  **counts on** — so the fill has a **mode**, and it says which:
  `copy` and `series`. The **default is the series**, because the
  tree's command defaults to the series too.
- The patterns of the series are the tree's: a **number** counts on by
  one, and **text with a number in it** — `Item 7`, `Q003x` — counts
  its number on and keeps the **width** of the digits. Anything else is
  **copied**.
- The **target holds the source at a corner**: a fill from `A1` into
  `A1:A10` goes **down**, a fill from `A10` goes **up**, and a fill
  into `A1:C1` goes **right**. A target that does not hold the source
  is refused, and so is a source that is not at a corner.
- The fill is **bounded**: the tree refuses a fill whose source or
  target is bigger than five million cells — "range too large" — and
  this one refuses a fill that would write more than **ten thousand**
  cells.
- A source that holds a **formula** is refused: the tree copies the
  formula and shifts its references, and that is a thing of its own.
  A source that is **empty** is refused, and so is a mode that is not a
  mode, and so is a sheet that is not there.

### What the port found

- **The tree has four fills and they differ in one cell.** The tree's
  plain drag of a lone number **copies** it — a drag of `1` gives
  `1, 1, 1` — and so does the tree's **series**, which is the tree's
  *default*: it is the tree's right-drag **Fill Series** (`extend`) and
  its `Ctrl`+drag (`alternate`) that count a lone number up. So "fill"
  is four different things in the tree, and a command that picked one
  of them silently would be wrong most of the time. Here the fill
  **says** which one it is — and the tree's own command says too:
  `edit.autoFill` takes a mode, and there are nine of them (`copy`,
  `alternate`, `formats`, `values`, `extend`, `days`, `weekdays`,
  `months`, `years`), and **the series is the default**.
  **§270 said the tree's series counted a lone number up, and that was
  wrong: the series copies it, and the `extend` counts it up.** The
  correction is in §274, where the modes are the tree's.
- **The tree's corner rule is the shape of the operation.** The tree's
  `holds_source_in_corner` says that a target must contain the source
  and that the source must sit in one of its corners, and the tree
  refuses a fill that does not: "the target must contain the source in
  one of its corners". A fill has a **direction**, and the direction
  comes from where the source is in the target.
- **The tree's series is a pattern, and the patterns are read off the
  source.** The tree's `Pattern::detect` finds a numeric series, a
  text with a number in it, or a list of days and months, and the
  pattern decides what every cell of the range holds. Here the numeric
  series and the text with a number are here, and the **lists** — the
  days, the months, the quarters — are not: a text that is a day of
  the week is copied here, and the tree would step through the week.
- **The tree's numbers are rounded to fifteen digits.** The tree's
  `round15` keeps a series of numbers from growing a tail of floating
  point noise, and here the same: `0.1` plus `0.2` counts on as
  `0.3` and not as `0.30000000000000004`.
- **The tree's overflow is a nothing and not a wrap.** The tree's
  series near the largest number yields nothing: the cell keeps what
  it had, rather than wrapping around. Here the same: a cell whose
  number would overflow is not written.

### What it cost

- **Thirteen tests** in the grid battery (`tests/fill.rs`): a copy
  fill copies the value, a series fill counts a number on, a series
  fill counts the number in a text on, a text with no number is copied,
  the fill goes up, the fill goes right, a target that does not hold
  the source is refused, a source that is not at a corner is refused, a
  source that holds a formula is refused, an empty source is refused, a
  mode that is not a mode is refused, a fill that is too large is
  refused, and a sheet that is not there is refused.
- **One command** (`grid.range.fill`). The grid battery now carries
  **9** commands and the MCP server **358**.

### What it does not settle

- **A formula is not filled** — and that is no longer true: a formula
  is filled, and its references are shifted (§275).
- **The tree's dates and lists are not here** — and the **dates** are
  here now (§276), and the **lists** are not: the tree's **quarter**
  (`Q1`, `Q2`, `Q3`, `Q4`) and its **ordinal** (`1st`, `2nd`) are not
  here either.
- **The tree's source may be a range.** The tree fills lane by lane
  from a source that is a range of cells; here the source is one cell.

---

## 271. The number format of a cell

The spreadsheet battery could set a cell and could not say how the cell
is **written**.

### What was built

- The command `grid.cell.format` puts a **number format** on a cell.
  The number formats this tree has are `general`, `0`, `0.00`, `#,##0`,
  `#,##0.00`, `0%` and `0.00%` — and they are a **grammar**, so
  `0.0000` and `#0` are codes too. A format that is **not a number
  format of that shape** is refused, and so is a format that is **too
  long** — the tree's own bound of 255 characters.
- The command `grid.cell.text` reads the **text the cell shows**: the
  value of the cell written with its format. The value of a **formula**
  cell is computed, so this is the calculation.
- A **percentage** is multiplied by a hundred, the **thousands** are
  separated, and a number is **rounded away from zero** — the tree's
  rounding.
- A cell may be formatted **before it has a value**, setting a value
  or a formula in a cell keeps its **format**, and the **fill** copies
  the format of the source.
- A **text** is not changed by a format, and a cell that is **not
  there** — a sheet that is not there — is refused.

### What the port found

- **The tree's format is a style, and a style is shared.** In the tree
  a cell has a **style** and the style holds the format, so a hundred
  cells with one format carry one format and changing the style changes
  them all. Here the format is a **field of the cell**, so a hundred
  cells with one format carry a hundred formats — and the tree's style
  also carries a font, a fill, borders, an alignment and a protection,
  none of which are here. The port found the same bargain the compositing battery
  made with its paths: the thing that is too many to be a node goes in
  the payload, and the plugin owns it.
- **The tree's format is a language and this one is a subset.** The
  tree's `NumberFormat` parses sections, colours, fills, dates, times,
  currency, accounting, fractions, scientific notation and text
  sections; and it **never fails** — an unknown part of a code becomes
  literal text, and a code that is too long becomes General, with the
  code kept as it is. Here a code that is neither a number format of
  this shape nor one of the nine dates is **refused**: the tree
  degrades quietly, and a format that is quietly ignored is a format
  the user believes in and the program does not have.
- **The number formats of this tree are a grammar, and the date
  formats are a list — and §271 said that both were lists.** It said
  "a code that is not one of them is refused", and named seven. The
  seven are the ones the tree's own tests use; the **code** takes any
  number of decimals and any arrangement of `0` and `#`, so `0.0000`
  and `#0` are formats this tree has had since §271. The truth is that
  the number formats are a small **grammar** — the thousands, a whole
  part of placeholders with at least one `0` in it, up to fifteen
  decimals and a percent sign — and that the date formats are a **list**
  of nine, because the tree's date formats are a language and this one
  has nine shapes of it (§276). The claim is corrected here, and the
  crate's own words with it.
- **The tree's General format is about a screen.** The tree's General
  format fits the number to the **width of the column** — fewer
  decimals, then scientific notation, then `####` — because a cell is
  drawn in a column that is not wide enough. Here the General format is
  the number as it is: a document is not a screen, and the width of a
  column is not in it.
- **The tree's rounding is away from zero, and it is not Rust's
  default.** The tree's numbers are written with the digits the format
  asks for, rounded the way a spreadsheet rounds: `0.125` with two
  decimals is `0.13`. Rust's own formatting rounds halves to even and
  would write `0.12`, so here the number is scaled and **rounded away
  from zero** before it is written.

### What it cost

- **Twelve tests** in the grid battery (`tests/format.rs`): a number is
  written with its decimals, the thousands are separated, a percentage
  is multiplied by a hundred, a number is rounded away from zero, a
  cell with no format shows its value, a text is not changed by a
  format, a formula cell shows what it computes, a format that is not
  one of ours is refused, a format that is too long is refused, a cell
  may be formatted before it has a value, the fill copies the format,
  and a sheet that is not there is refused.
- **Two commands** (`grid.cell.format` and `grid.cell.text`) and a
  **field** on the cell: the format. The grid battery now carries **11**
  commands and the MCP server **360**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's currency, accounting, fractions and scientific
  formats are not here**, and neither are the tree's **sections** — a
  format with one code for positive numbers and another for negative
  ones is not here. The tree's **dates** are here now, and they are a
  list of nine shapes (§276), and its **times** are here (§287).
- **The tree's style is not here**: a style is shared between cells and
  carries a font, a fill, borders, an alignment and a protection, and
  here the format is the cell's own.
- **The tree's `TEXT` function is not here** — and it is now (§278):
  the tree's `TEXT` writes a value with a format code inside a
  formula, and a formula in this tree has the codes of the format.

---

## 272. The lifting of a range

The tree has two ways of taking a **range** of a track away: the
**lift**, which leaves the gap, and the **extract**, which closes it.
The lift is here.

### What was built

- The command `film.clip.lift` takes the clips that are **in a range**
  of a track away, and the gap they leave is a **gap**: the clips that
  were after the range stay where they are, and the track is shorter by
  the length of the range.
- A clip that **spans an edge** of the range is **refused**, and the
  refusal names it: the tree splits it, and the split is a command of
  its own.
- A range that **ends before it starts** is refused, and so is a range
  that is **not whole frames**, and so is a node that is not a track,
  and so is a node that is not there.

### What the port found

- **The tree's lift is a remove and a split.** The tree's `lift` calls
  `clear_track_range`, and that **splits the clips at the boundaries
  of the range** and then removes the clips that are inside it — so the
  range has two edges, and the material that was in the range is gone
  and the material around it is still there. Here the range has to
  have edges that exist: a clip that spans an edge is refused, and the
  split that would make the edge is a command of its own.
- **The tree's two ways of taking a range away differ in one thing.**
  The tree's `lift` removes the material and leaves the gap; the
  tree's `extract` removes the material **and closes the gap** by
  shifting the clips that were after the range up by the length of the
  range. So the tree's lift and this lift are the same operation, and
  the tree's extract is the lift plus one more thing — which is why
  they are two commands here too.
- **The tree's lift works on several tracks at once, and the extract
  works on the sync-locked ones as well.** The tree's `lift` takes a
  list of tracks; the tree's `extract` also closes the gap on the
  tracks that are **sync-locked** with the target, so that a group of
  tracks stays together. Here a track is a track, and there is no lock
  to be in.

### What it cost

- **Seven tests** in the film battery (`tests/lift.rs`): the clips in
  the range are taken away, the clips outside the range stay where they
  are, a clip that spans an edge is refused, a range that ends before
  it starts is refused, a range that is not whole frames is refused, a
  node that is not a track is refused, and a node that is not there is
  refused.
- **One command** (`film.clip.lift`). The film battery now carries
  **12** commands and the MCP server **361**.

### What it does not settle

- **The extract was not here — §273 is where it came.** The tree's
  **sync-locked** tracks and its **locked** tracks are still not here.
- **The tree's links and transitions are not here**, and neither is the
  tree's **caption tracks**, which the extract also closes the gap on.

---

## 273. The extracting of a range

The tree's other way of taking a range of a track away is the
**extract**: the same removal, and the gap **closes**.

### What was built

- The command `film.clip.extract` takes the clips that are **in a range**
  of a track away **and closes the gap**: the clips that were after
  the range move **up** by the length of the range, so the time the
  range took is time that is free again.
- A clip that **spans an edge** of the range is refused, as it is for
  the lift: the tree splits it, and the split is a command of its own.
- A range that **ends before it starts** is refused, and so is a node
  that is not a track.

### What the port found

- **The tree's extract is the tree's lift plus one shift.** The tree's
  `extract` calls the same `clear_track_range` the lift calls, and
  then **shifts** the clips that were after the range up by the length
  of the range: `shift_track_from(tr, range.end(), -range.duration)`.
  So the two tree commands are one operation and one operation plus a
  shift — and here they are two commands, because a command that
  removes a range and closes a gap does two things.
- **The tree's extract moves the sync-locked tracks as well.** The
  tree's extract closes the gap on the tracks that are **sync-locked**
  with the target, and refuses when a locked track would have to move
  into time that is taken: "this edit would break sync: `A2` is
  sync-locked and has a clip in the way". Here a track is a track, and
  there is no lock to be in.
- **The tree's extract and lift share the removal, and the removal
  splits.** Both tree commands call `clear_track_range`, which splits
  the clips at the edges of the range and removes the clips inside
  it. Here the split is refused rather than done, so the two commands
  here share the *finding* of the clips and not the splitting.

### What it cost

- **Four tests** in the film battery (`tests/extract.rs`): the gap
  closes, a clip that spans an edge is refused, a range that ends
  before it starts is refused, and a node that is not a track is
  refused.
- **One command** (`film.clip.extract`). The film battery now carries
  **13** commands and the MCP server **362**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's sync-locked tracks are not here**, and neither is its
  **locked** track, its **links**, its **transitions** nor its
  **caption tracks** — the tree's extract closes the gap on the
  caption tracks that are sync-locked as well.

---

## 274. The modes of the fill

§270 gave the fill **two** modes, and one of them was the tree's
`extend` and not the tree's `series`. The tree has **four**, and they
differ in what they do with a lone number — so the modes here are the
tree's now.

### What was built

- The modes are the tree's: `copy`, `series` — the tree's **default** —
  `extend` and `alternate`. And the tree's table is the table:

  | the source | `copy` | `series` | `extend` | `alternate` |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | one number | copied | **copied** | counts up | counts up |
  | two or more numbers | copied | the **trend** | the trend | copied |
  | text with a number | copied | counts on | counts on | copied |
  | text | copied | copied | copied | copied |

- Two or more numbers are continued by the **trend**: the **least
  squares** line through them, so `1, 3` goes on as `5, 7`.
- The source may be a **range**, and the fill goes **lane by lane**:
  each column of the source continues down its own lane, and each row
  of the source continues along its own lane.
- A mode that is **not a mode** is refused, and the refusal names the
  four that are.

### What the port found

- **§270 was wrong about the tree's series, and the tree's own tests
  say so.** The tree's test `ctrl_drag_fill_swaps_copy_and_series` says
  it in a line: "a plain drag copies a lone number" — and the plain
  drag is the tree's *default* mode, which is the series. The tree's
  `extend` is the right-drag **Fill Series** ("a lone number counts
  up, everything else extends as a plain drag"), and the tree's
  `alternate` is the `Ctrl`+drag, which counts a lone number up and
  copies what a plain drag would extend. The port found this by
  reading the tree's `Pattern::detect`, which **copies** a single
  number, and the tree's `alternate`, which turns that copy into a
  count.
- **The tree's trend is a least squares line, not a difference.** The
  tree's `Pattern::detect` fits the **least squares** line through the
  numbers of the source — the trend Excel uses — and continues it. So
  `1, 3` goes on as `5, 7`, and a source of `1, 2, 4` goes on as
  `5.33`, `6.83`, `8.33`: the line through the numbers, and not even
  through the last of them — the tree continues the **fitted** line,
  not the last value. Here the same: the fill continues the line.
- **The tree's source may be a range, and then the fill is a fill per
  lane.** The tree's `fill` takes the **lanes** of the source — its
  columns when the fill goes down, its rows when it goes along — and
  every lane continues its **own** pattern. Here the same: a source of
  `A1:B1` fills two lanes, and each lane counts on by itself.
- **The tree's source with no common pattern continues each cell's own
  series.** The tree's `per_cell` finds, for a source whose cells have
  no pattern in common, the pattern of **each cell alone** and
  continues it: a source of `Product 1` and `On backorder` goes on as
  `Product 2` and `On backorder`, and then `Product 3` and
  `On backorder`. Here the same: in the series and the extend modes a
  copied lane continues each of its cells.

### What it cost

- **Seventeen tests** in the grid battery (`tests/fill.rs`): a copy
  fill copies the value, the series copies a lone number, the extend
  counts a lone number up, the alternate counts a number up and copies
  a text, two numbers are a trend, a series fill counts the number in a
  text on, a text with no number is copied, a range source fills lane
  by lane, the fill goes up, the fill goes right, a target that does
  not hold the source is refused, a source that is not at a corner is
  refused, a source that holds a formula is refused, an empty source
  is refused, a mode that is not a mode is refused, a fill that is too
  large is refused, and a sheet that is not there is refused.
- **No new command**: the command is the same one, with the tree's
  modes. The grid battery still carries **11** commands and the MCP
  server **362**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's lists are not here** — and they are now (§282): the
  days of the week, the months and the quarters. The tree's `days`,
  `weekdays`, `months` and `years` **modes** were not here either, and
  they are now (§277).
- **The tree's `formats` and `values` modes are not here** — and they
  are now (§279): the first copies the style without the value, the
  second copies the value without the style.
- **A formula is not filled** — and that is no longer true: a formula
  is filled, and its references are shifted (§275). The tree's **flash
  fill**, which reads the pattern out of the text beside the source, is
  now (§286).

## 275. The fill of a formula

§274 left the fill of a formula out and said so: the tree copies a
formula and **shifts its references**. That is the tree's
`shift_relative`, and it is here now.

### What was built

- A source that holds a **formula** is filled with the formula, and
  the references of it are shifted for every cell that is written:
  `=B1` in `A1` becomes `=B2` in `A2` and `=B3` in `A3`.
- The **anchoring** of an address is in the model: `$A$1` does not
  move, `A$1` keeps its row, `$A1` keeps its column, and `A1` moves in
  both.
- A reference that would **leave the sheet** is refused, and the
  reference is named.
- A fill that would make a cell **read itself** is refused, and the
  whole fill with it — not a part of it.
- The formula language grew a **printer**: a formula is written out
  again, and the copy a fill writes is the printer's text.

### What the port found

- **The `$` is a part of the address, and the port had thrown it
  away.** v2's `CellRef::parse` skipped the `$` and read `$A$1` as
  `A1` — so here a formula that named an anchored cell and one that
  named a plain cell were the same thing, and the difference the tree's
  `$` makes could not be made at all. Now an address is an address
  **and** its anchoring, and the anchoring is what says whether a
  reference moves. And a command that names a cell names a cell:
  `grid.cell.set` with `A$1` is refused, because `$A$1` is the address
  of a *reference* and not the address of a cell.
- **The tree's shift moves the relative parts and keeps the anchored
  ones — and it moves the references of another sheet too.** The tree's
  `shift_relative` shifts every reference of the expression, whether it
  names this sheet or another: `Sheet2!A1` is a relative reference to
  another sheet and it moves with the copy. Here the same: a fill of
  `=Sheet2!A1` writes `=Sheet2!A2`.
- **The tree's `#REF!` is a value, and a value that says "this
  reference is broken".** The tree's `shift_anchor` refuses an address
  that leaves the sheet, the formula becomes `#REF!`, and the cell
  still holds a formula — a broken one. Here the whole **fill** is
  refused and the reference is named: a refusal that never truncates,
  and a tree that would rather break a formula than stop.
- **A fill can make a cell read itself, and the tree does not look.**
  The tree's fill copies a formula and moves its references, and
  nothing in the fill asks whether the copy reads the cell it is
  written in: `=B1` in `A1`, filled into `A2`, reads `B2` — and if
  `B2` reads `A2` the two cells read each other. Here the copy is
  checked against the **workbook** before it is written and the fill is
  refused, with the cell named — the same rule the formula command has,
  where the cycle is found at the point the formula is set and not
  later in the middle of a recalculation.
- **A formula cell has no value to offer a pattern.** The tree's fill
  detects its pattern from the cells' **values**, and a formula cell's
  value in the tree is the tree's **cached** one. Here a formula cell's
  value is derived and never written down, so a lane's pattern is made
  from the cells that hold values, and a cell that holds a formula is
  given its formula instead.

### What it cost

- **Twelve tests** in the grid battery (`tests/formula_fill.rs`): a
  fill of a formula shifts its references, a copy of a formula holds a
  formula and not a value, an anchored reference does not move, a range
  in a formula shifts as a whole, a reference to another sheet keeps
  its sheet, the mode does not matter for a formula, a fill that makes
  a cell read itself is refused, a reference that would leave the sheet
  is refused, the value of a copied formula is derived, a fill of a
  range of formulas shifts every one of them, a fill of a formula
  copies the format, and a text is not a formula.
- **One test taken away**: `tests/fill.rs` had a test that said a
  source that holds a formula is refused, and it is not true any more.
- **The formula model changed**: `Expr::Cell` and `Expr::Range` carry
  an **anchor** now, the language has a printer, and the printer's text
  is what a fill writes.
- **No new command**: the grid battery still carries **11** commands and
  the MCP server **362**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's flash fill** is not here: it reads the pattern out of
  the text beside the source, and that is a thing of its own — and it is
  now (§286).
- **The tree's `formats` and `values` modes** are still not here, and
  neither are its **lists** — the days, the months, the quarters — nor
  its **dates**: the `formats` and `values` modes are now (§279), the
  dates are now (§276), and the lists are not.
- **The tree's whole-column and whole-row references** — `A:A`, `1:1`
  — are refused by the parser here, and so are the tree's **defined
  names**, its **arrays** and its `INDIRECT`: a call this tree does not
  have is kept and its value is an error.

## 276. The date of a cell

§271 said the tree's dates were not here, and named them among the
things that are missing. They are here now.

### What was built

- A **date format** is a format, and there are **nine** of them:
  `yyyy-mm-dd`, `dd/mm/yyyy`, `m/d/yyyy`, `d-mmm-yyyy`, `mmm`, `mmmm`,
  `ddd`, `dddd` and `yyyy`. A code that is not one of them is refused,
  and the refusal names them.
- A **date is a number with a date format on it** — the number of days
  since the 30th of December 1899 — and the command `grid.cell.date`
  puts both of them in a cell.
- A date may be written the **tree's** way: `2026-10-26`,
  `10/26/2026` or `4-Mar-2026`, and the format the date is written with
  is the **shape it was written in**.
- A date that **did not happen** is refused: the 30th of February is
  not a date.

### What the port found

- **A date in a spreadsheet is not a value: it is a number and a
  format.** The tree's cell holds a `Value` and a `Style`, and the
  style carries the number format; a date is the number of days and the
  format that says so. Here the format is the cell's own field (§271)
  and the date is the same shape: the number, and the format. That is
  why a date and a number are not two kinds of thing here — they are
  one kind of thing with a format on it.
- **The tree's calendar has a day that never happened.** The 1900
  system counts from the 30th of December 1899 and — like Lotus 1-2-3
  and Excel, and for a mistake that is a hundred and twenty-five years
  old — it treats 1900 as a **leap year**: the serial 60 is the
  fictitious 29th of February 1900. So the tree's first two months of
  1900 have sixty serials and fifty-nine days, and the tree's serial 1
  is the 1st of January and its serial 61 is the 1st of March. Here the
  same: `1900-02-29` is a date this tree accepts, and it is the
  serial 60.
- **The tree's weekdays follow the fictitious calendar, and after the
  phantom day they are right.** The tree's `datetime_from_serial`
  computes the weekday from the serial alone, so the serial 1 is a
  Sunday — a day out from the truth — and the serial 61 is the Monday
  the 1st of March 1900 really was. Here the same: the weekday comes
  from the serial and not from the date, and the 26th of October 2026
  is a Monday.
- **The tree's date formats are a language, and here they are a
  list.** The tree's `numfmt` parses a code with `y` and `m` and `d`
  and `h` and `s` in it, with sections, with colours and with fills;
  `mmm` is the month in three letters and `dddd` is the day of the week
  in full, and the tree renders them. Here a date format is one of
  nine shapes and a code that is not one of them is refused.
- **The tree turns what you type into a date, and it reads the month
  first.** The tree's `parse_date` reads `2026-10-26` as the year
  first, `10/26/2026` as the **month** first — so `26/10/2026` is not
  a date to it — and `4-Mar-2026` with the month by its name; and it
  reads a year of two digits as this century below thirty and as the
  last one above thirty. Here the same, and the shape a date was
  written in is the format it is written with.
- **The tree rolls a date over and this tree refuses it.** The tree's
  `serial_from_ymd` is `DATE()`: the month 13 is the January of the
  next year and the day 0 is the last day of the month before. A cell
  that holds a date holds a date that **was**, so here the 30th of
  February is refused.

### What it cost

- **Thirteen tests** in the grid battery (`tests/dates.rs`): a date is a
  number with a format on it, the 1st of January 1900 is the serial 1,
  the tree has a day that never happened, a date that did not happen is
  refused, a date that is not written as one is refused, a format that
  is not a date format is refused, a date may be written in any of its
  shapes, a date may be written the tree's way, the tree reads the
  month first, a year of two digits is the tree's, a number with a date
  format is a date, a format this tree does not have is refused, and a
  number that is not a date is a number.
- **One new command**: `grid.cell.date`. The grid battery now carries
  **12** commands and the MCP server **363**.
- **The format list grew**: seven number formats and nine date
  formats, and the refusal that names them names sixteen.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's 1904 date system is not here** — and it is now (§296):
  it is the system of the old Macintosh Excel, and the system is a fact
  of the workbook, so a workbook that says which system it uses is a
  workbook that was made somewhere else.
- **The tree's times are not here** — and they are now (§287): there is
  `hh:mm`, there are seconds, there is a.m. and p.m., and a date with
  a time in it is still a number here.
- **A fill of dates is not here yet**: the tree's `days`, `weekdays`,
  `months` and `years` modes step through the calendar, and the
  arithmetic they need is here but the modes are not (§274).
- **The tree's date and time parsing is not here**: the tree reads a
  time of day as well as a date, and a date with a time in it, and
  here a date is a date — a date **written** the tree's way is here
  (§276), and a time of day is now (§287), and a date with a time in
  it is not.

## 277. The fill of dates

§276 gave the grid a **date**, and §274 said the tree's four date fills
were not here. They are here now.

### What was built

- The fill has **four more modes**, and they are the tree's: `days`,
  `weekdays`, `months` and `years`.
- A fill of **days** steps by days, and the step is the difference
  between the first two dates: two dates a week apart are a fill of
  every seventh day.
- A fill of **weekdays** skips the Saturday and the Sunday.
- A fill of **months** keeps the day of the month and **clamps** it to
  the month it lands in — the 31st of January, the 28th of February,
  the 31st of March — and it does not drift.
- A fill of **years** steps by years, and a year is twelve months.
- A source that is **not dates** extends like a plain drag, as the
  tree has it.

### What the port found

- **The tree's date modes are not the plain series with a different
  step: they are a pattern of their own.** The tree's `Pattern::dates`
  is asked for the date modes first, and it needs the source to be
  numbers under a **date format**; when it cannot have that it falls
  back to the plain detection, and a lone number is copied. So the
  modes are a fill of dates and nothing else, and a fill of a number
  in the `days` mode is a plain drag. Here the same: the date modes
  ask the source whether it holds dates, and a source that does not
  extends like a plain drag.
- **The tree's `days` step is the difference between the first two
  dates, and not one day.** Two dates a week apart are a fill of every
  seventh day — and two dates on the same day are a fill of one day,
  because the tree's rule is that a step of zero is one. Here the same.
- **The tree's `weekdays` step counts the weekdays between the first
  two dates, and skips the weekend on the way.** The tree's
  `add_weekdays` moves to the next weekday first — so a fill that
  starts on a Saturday starts on the Monday — and then counts five
  weekdays to the week. Here the same.
- **The tree's months are clamped and they do not drift, and that is
  the tree's own comment on it.** The tree's `add_months_clamped`
  keeps the day of the month and clamps it to the length of the month
  it lands in, and it always measures from the **original** date, so
  a series is the 31st of January, the 28th of February, the 31st of
  March and the 30th of April — and not the 28th of February, the 28th
  of March and the 28th of April, which is what a fill that added a
  month to the cell before it would give. Here the same.
- **The tree's plain series knows about dates too, and the port had
  forgotten.** The tree's `Pattern::detect` looks at the format of the
  source: a **single date** counts a day on — where a single *number*
  is copied — and two dates of the **same day of the month** go on by
  months and not by a line through them. Here the same, and that is a
  rule the tree had and this tree did not: the port had a fill of
  numbers and a fill of texts, and a date was a number with a format
  on it and the fill never looked at the format.
- **The tree's year is twelve months, and its month step is a count of
  months and not a count of days.** Two dates two years apart are a
  fill of every second year, and the tree's rule is that a count of
  zero is one — so two dates in the same month are a fill of a year.
  Here the same.

### What it cost

- **Eleven tests** in the grid battery (`tests/date_fill.rs`): a fill
  of days steps by days, two dates a week apart step by a week, a fill
  of weekdays skips the weekend, a fill of months clamps the day and
  does not drift, a fill of years steps by years, two dates years apart
  step by years, a source that is not dates extends like a plain drag,
  a single date in a plain series counts a day on, two dates of the
  same day go on by months, two dates of different days go on by a
  line, and a mode that is not a mode is refused.
- **One test changed**: the refusal of a mode that is not a mode now
  names eight modes and not four.
- **No new command**: the command is the same one, with four more
  modes. The grid battery still carries **12** commands and the MCP
  server **363**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's lists are not here**: the days, the months, the
  quarters and the ordinals — and the days, the months and the
  quarters are now (§282). The **ordinals** are not.
- **The tree's flash fill is not here**: it reads the pattern out of
  the text beside the source — and it is now (§286).
- **The tree's `formats` and `values` modes are not here** — and they
  are now (§279): the first copies the style without the value, the
  second copies the value without the style.

## 278. The `TEXT` of a formula

§271 said the tree's `TEXT` was not here, and said why: "a formula in
this tree has no format code in it". §276 gave the tree its date
formats, so the reason is gone — and the reason was wrong in any case.

### What was built

- The formula language has the tree's **`TEXT`**: `TEXT(value, code)`
  writes a value with a **format code** and the answer is a text.
- The code is **evaluated**, so it may be a cell that holds a code.
- A code that this tree does not have is an **error**, and the error
  names the code.

### What the port found

- **The reason §271 gave was wrong, and the port had carried it for
  eleven arcs.** §271 said a formula in this tree has no format code
  in it — and the truth is that a formula may name **any** code, and
  what it does with it is the question. The codes are here (§271 for
  the numbers and §276 for the dates), so `TEXT` is a function of the
  format module and not a new thing.
- **The tree's `TEXT` takes the second argument as a value, not as a
  code.** The tree's `TEXT` evaluates both of its arguments and then
  asks the second one for its text: so `TEXT(A1, B1)` writes `A1` with
  whatever code is **in** `B1`. Here the same: the code is a value, and
  a value may be in a cell.
- **The tree's `TEXT` is an error when the value is an error, and it
  does not go on to write anything.** Here the same: the error of the
  value is the error of the `TEXT`, and a `TEXT` with one argument or
  with three is `#VALUE!`.
- **The number formats of this tree are a grammar, and §271 said they
  were a list.** §271 named seven number formats and said "a code
  that is not one of them is refused" — and the seven are the ones the
  tree's own tests use, while the **code** takes any number of
  decimals and any arrangement of `0` and `#`. So `0.0000` and `#0`
  have been formats this tree has had since §271, and the claim in
  the README and in the crate's own words was false. It is corrected
  here: the number formats are a small **grammar** — the thousands, a
  whole part of placeholders with at least one `0` in it, up to
  fifteen decimals and a percent sign — and the date formats are a
  **list** of nine, because the tree's date formats are a language
  and this one has nine shapes of it.
- **A format that is refused by `grid.cell.format` is not refused by
  `TEXT`, and that is a difference worth naming.** The command refuses
  a code it does not have, because a command that sets a format is a
  user writing a format; a formula that writes a value with a code it
  does not have is an **error in a cell**, and the tree's own way of
  saying that is the cell's error.

### What it cost

- **Nine tests** in the grid battery (`tests/text_function.rs`): a
  `TEXT` writes a number with a format code, a `TEXT` of a percentage
  multiplies it, a `TEXT` of a date writes the date, the code may be
  in a cell, a code this tree does not have is an error, a `TEXT` with
  the wrong arguments is an error, a `TEXT` of a text is the text, a
  `TEXT` of a general format is the value, and a code with four
  decimals is a code this tree has.
- **Two claims corrected**: §271's list of seven number formats and
  the reason it gave for the tree's `TEXT` not being here.
- **No new command**: a function is not a command, and the formula
  command is the same one. The grid battery still carries **12**
  commands and the MCP server **363**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's `TEXT` takes the tree's whole format language** and
  this one takes the grammar and the nine dates of this tree: a code
  with a section, a colour or a fill is an error here and a text in
  the tree.
- **The tree's other functions are not here**: its `IF`, its `INDEX`,
  its `XLOOKUP`, its `LET` and its `LAMBDA`, and the tree's
  **volatile** functions.

## 279. The formats and the values of a fill

The tree has **ten** ways of filling a range. Eight of them are here
(§274 and §277), and the last two are the ones that are about the
**format**.

### What was built

- The fill has the tree's **`formats`** mode: the cell is given the
  **format** of the source and keeps its own value.
- The fill has the tree's **`values`** mode — the tree's *Fill Without
  Formatting*: the cell is given the **value** of the source and keeps
  its own format, and it extends like a plain drag.
- The fill **replaces** the format of the cell with the format of the
  source, as the tree replaces the style — and a source with no format
  takes the format away.

### What the port found

- **The tree's fill replaces the style of the cell, and the port had
  copied the format only when the source had one.** The tree's fill
  builds the new cell as a **copy of the source cell** — with the
  value put in it — and so the style of the target is the style of the
  source and not the style the target had. A source with the default
  style gives the target the default style, and a target with a
  hundred decimals loses them. Here the same: the format of the cell
  is replaced by the format of the source, and a source with no format
  takes the format away.
- **The tree's style is more than a format, and the port's bargain
  shows here.** The tree's style carries the font, the fill, the
  borders, the alignment and the protection, and the tree's fill
  copies **all of it**. Here the format is the cell's own field
  (§271) and the fill copies the format and nothing else — so a fill
  here is a fill of a spreadsheet with one property, and the tree's
  is a fill of a spreadsheet with six.
- **The tree's values mode is the plain drag without the style.** The
  tree's `ValuesOnly` is in the tree's `extends_series`, so it
  continues a series like the plain drag does, and a lone number is
  copied; and the tree keeps the target's style. Here the same: the
  values mode is the series mode with the format left alone.
- **The tree's formats mode writes no value at all, and it says so in
  the outcome.** The tree's `Formats` takes the target's cell, puts
  the source's style in it and writes it back — so the value of the
  target is the target's own. Here the same: the cell is given its
  format and nothing else, and the outcome says which format.

### What it cost

- **Five tests** in the grid battery (`tests/formats_and_values.rs`):
  the formats mode gives the format and keeps the value, the values
  mode gives the value and keeps the format, the values mode extends
  like a plain drag, a source with no format takes the format away,
  and the formats mode with no format takes the format away.
- **One test changed**: the refusal of a mode that is not a mode now
  names ten modes and not eight.
- **No new command**: the command is the same one, with two more
  modes. The grid battery still carries **12** commands and the MCP
  server **363**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's style is not here**, and only its format is: the
  font, the fill, the borders, the alignment and the protection are
  not here, and a fill copies the format and not the style.
- **The tree's lists are not here**: the days, the months, the
  quarters and the ordinals — and the days, the months and the
  quarters are now (§282). The **ordinals** are not.
- **The tree's flash fill is not here**: it reads the pattern out of
  the text beside the source — and it is now (§286).

## 280. The interpolation of a keyframe

§265 said the shape of the curve was the tree's business, and that a
keyframe here was a frame and a value. The shape of the curve is
here now.

### What was built

- A keyframe has an **interpolation** on the side it leaves on, and it
  is one of the tree's three: `linear`, `bezier` and `hold`.
- A **bezier** has an **ease** — a **speed** and an **influence** — and
  the ease is what shapes the curve.
- The command `fx.keyframe.interp` sets the interpolation and the ease
  of a keyframe.
- The value at a frame follows the curve: the line, the hold, or the
  bezier.
- The interpolation is **kept** when the value of a keyframe is
  changed, as the tree's `set_key` keeps it.

### What the port found

- **The tree does not keep a curve: it keeps a speed and an
  influence.** The tree's `Ease` is two numbers — the speed in value
  units per second and the influence, the fraction of the segment the
  handle takes — and the curve is a cubic Bezier in the (time, value)
  plane whose handles those two numbers make. That is the finding: the
  tree's curve is not a curve in the document, it is a **speed** and a
  **place**, and the shape is computed. Here the same, and the speed
  is in units per **frame**, because a frame is the unit of this tree
  and there is no clock in a frame.
- **A bezier at the speed of the straight line is the straight line.**
  The tree's arithmetic says so: the handle is then on the chord, and
  the curve is the chord. It is worth knowing, because it means the
  tree's ease is not a shape and a speed but one number — and that a
  speed of nothing with an influence of nothing is the line too.
- **The tree's keyframe has an interpolation on **each** side, and the
  segment between two keyframes is shaped by both.** The out side of
  the first keyframe and the in side of the second. Here a keyframe
  has the side it leaves on, and the side it is entered on is linear —
  and the tree's linear side is not a plain line either: it is a
  handle at a third of the segment, so a segment with a bezier on one
  end and a linear one on the other is not a straight line.
- **The tree's hold is the business of the keyframe the segment
  leaves.** The tree's `segment_value` holds the earlier value when
  `a.out_interp` is `Hold` — and the in side of the later keyframe
  does not matter at all for a hold. Here the same: the hold is the
  out side's.
- **§265 said the port had no curve to keep, and that was true then
  and is not true now.** The tree's `set_key` keeps the interpolation
  and the eases when the value of a key changes — the curve is the
  keyframe's and the value is a thing that comes and goes. There is a
  curve to keep now, and it is kept.

### What it cost

- **Ten tests** in the fx battery (`tests/interp.rs`): a linear
  keyframe moves the value in a line, a hold keyframe does not move the
  value at all, a bezier is not a line, a bezier at the speed of the
  line is the line, an influence is a fraction of the segment, a list of
  numbers is eased number by number, the interpolation is kept when the
  value is changed, an interpolation that is not one of the three is
  refused, an influence that is not a fraction is refused, and a
  keyframe that is not there is refused.
- **One new command**: `fx.keyframe.interp`. The fx battery now carries
  **8** commands and the MCP server **364**.
- **The keyframe's payload changed**: it carries the interpolation and
  the ease beside the frame and the value.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's spatial handles are not here.** A spatial property
  moves along a **path** with tangents of its own, sampled through an
  arc-length table, and the path is a thing the tree computes and does
  not store.
- **The tree's auto-bezier and continuous-bezier are not here**: the
  tree derives the tangents of a key from its **neighbours**, and a
  key that asks for it has no tangents of its own.
- **The tree's in side is not here**: a keyframe has the side it leaves
  on, and the side it is entered on is linear.
- **The expression is not here**, and the tree's expressions may
  drive a property that has keyframes as well.

## 281. The reversal of a clip

The tree's clip may play its media **backwards**, and the flag is not a
property of the media — the media is the same — it is a property of the
**direction** the clip plays in. It is here now.

### What was built

- The command `film.clip.reverse` turns a clip around.
- The **trim** of a reversed clip consumes the media at the **other
  end** of its range: its in edge takes the media *after* its out point
  and its out edge takes the media *before* its in point.
- The **split** of a reversed clip keeps the content continuous: the
  piece before the place shows the later media and the piece after it
  shows the earlier media.
- A clip's payload keeps what it carries when its clocks are written,
  so a reversal survives a trim, a move, an insert, a lift and a
  ripple.

### What the port found

- **The tree's reversal is a direction and not a media.** The tree's
  clip has a `reverse` flag and the media it plays is the same media
  either way; what changes is which end of the media the clip's head
  is at. That is a different thing from "the clip plays the other
  file" — and it is the tree's flag and not a second item that says
  so.
- **The tree's `move_edge` is where the tree says it, and it is a
  swap.** For a clip that plays forwards, the in edge moves the source
  in point **forward** and the out edge leaves it alone; for a clip
  that plays backwards, the in edge leaves the source in point alone
  and the out edge moves it **backwards**. So the two edges take
  turns: the head of a reversed clip is the *end* of its media, and
  the tail is the *beginning* of it. Here the same — and the bound
  moves with it, because a reversed clip may not reach before the
  media begins.
- **The tree's split of a reversed clip keeps the content
  continuous, and the port had no idea that a split had a direction
  in it.** The tree's split writes the pieces' source in points in the
  other order when the clip plays backwards: the piece before the
  place takes the media the piece after it had, so that the two
  pieces show the same frames in the same order. Here the same, and
  the test says so: the first piece is at the later media and the
  second at the earlier.
- **The tree's `reverse` lives beside the clip's clocks, and a port
  that writes a payload from scratch loses it.** The trim, the split,
  the move, the insert, the lift and the ripple each wrote the
  clip's payload whole — three clocks and nothing else — so a flag
  that is not one of the three clocks was taken away by every one of
  them. The payload of a clip now keeps what it carries, and the
  clocks are written into it. That is the finding of this arc that is
  not about the reversal at all: **a command that writes a payload
  from scratch throws away everything the payload carried**, and the
  tree's `edit` crate writes one field at a time.
- **The tree's reversal and the tree's speed are one command.** The
  tree's `set_speed` takes the speed and the direction together, and a
  clip that is reversed at a speed of a half plays its media backwards
  at half the speed. Here the direction is a command of its own and
  the speed is not here.

### What it cost

- **Eight tests** in the film battery (`tests/reverse.rs`): a clip may
  play its media backwards, a clip reversed twice plays forwards again,
  the in edge of a reversed clip does not move the media, the out edge
  of a reversed clip takes the media before it, the out edge of a
  reversed clip stops at the media, the split of a reversed clip keeps
  the content continuous, the split of a clip that plays forwards moves
  the media, a clip that is not there is refused and a node that is not
  a clip is refused.
- **One new command**: `film.clip.reverse`. The film battery now
  carries **14** commands and the MCP server **365**.
- **Six commands changed**: the trim, the split, the move, the insert,
  the lift and the ripple write the clip's payload whole, and now they
  write its three clocks into the payload it has.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's speed is not here**, and the tree's speed and direction
  are one command: a clip reversed at a speed of a half plays its media
  backwards at half the speed.
- **The tree's frame hold is not here** — and it is now (§301): a clip
  may hold a frame for a while, and a held frame has no media to
  consume at one end.
- **The tree's transitions are not here**: a transition between two
  clips overlaps them, and the overlap is not a clip.

## 282. The lists of a fill

The tree's fill steps through a **list**: the days of the week, the
months and the quarters. That is here now.

### What was built

- A text that is in one of the tree's lists steps through it: the days
  of the week in three letters and in full, the months in three
  letters and in full, and the quarters.
- The list **wraps around**: a fill that runs past the end of the week
  begins again at the start of it.
- The **step** is the distance between the first two items of the
  source, so two days apart are a fill of every second day.
- The **case** of the source is the case of the list: a source in
  capitals fills with capitals.

### What the port found

- **The tree's list is found by membership and not by a name.** The
  tree keeps five lists — the days in three letters, the days in full,
  the months in three letters, the months in full and the quarters —
  and the fill looks at the source's texts and asks which of the lists
  holds **all** of them. There is no "this is a list" in the document:
  the list is a fact about the texts. Here the same, and the lists
  are the tree's five.
- **The tree's list has a case of its own, and the case comes from the
  source.** The tree's `Pattern::List` carries an `upper` and a `lower`
  flag, and they are read off the **first text** of the source: a
  source in capitals fills with capitals and a source in small letters
  fills with small letters. Here the same — with the tree's own
  subtlety kept: the items of the tree's lists begin with a capital,
  so the small-letter flag leaves them alone.
- **The tree's custom lists are not here, and they are a fact about the
  workbook and not about the sheet.** The tree's `lists()` is the
  tree's own five, and the tree's *custom* lists are the user's, kept
  in the workbook beside the sheets. A custom list is a thing a user
  made, and there is nowhere to keep it here.
- **The tree's ordinal is not here.** The tree's fill has a rule for
  `1st`, `2nd` and `3rd` — the number counts on and the suffix comes
  with it — and it is a rule of its own and not a list.

### What it cost

- **Eight tests** in the grid battery (`tests/lists.rs`): a fill of a
  day steps through the week, a fill of a day in full steps through the
  week, a fill of a month steps through the months, a fill of a quarter
  steps through the quarters, the list wraps around, two days apart are
  a fill of every second day, the case of the source is the case of the
  list, and a text that is not in a list is copied.
- **No new command**: the fill is the same one and it finds the list by
  itself. The grid battery still carries **12** commands and the MCP
  server **365**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's custom lists are not here**: a list the user made is a
  list of their own.
- **The tree's ordinal is not here**: `1st`, `2nd` and `3rd` are a rule
  of their own.
- **The tree's flash fill is not here**: it reads the pattern out of
  the text beside the source — and it is now (§286).

## 283. The locked track

The tree's track may be **locked**, and a locked track cannot be
edited. That is here now.

### What was built

- The command `film.track.lock` locks a track and unlocks it.
- Every command that would **edit** a track is refused when the track is
  locked: the add of a clip, the trim, the move, the insert, the
  split, the removal, the ripple, the lift and the extract.
- The refusal says which track is locked.

### What the port found

- **The tree's lock is a property of the track and not of the clip,
  and it is asked about at the moment of the edit.** The tree's
  `unlocked_track` is asked for the track of the clip that is being
  edited, and a locked track is the error `Locked`. So the lock is
  not a thing the clip remembers and not a thing the sequence decides:
  it is a fact about the track, and every edit asks the track.
- **The tree checks the lock before the edit and not after it.** The
  tree's `overwrite` and `insert` look at every track they are about to
  write to and refuse if any of them is locked — before anything is
  written, so that a refused edit leaves nothing half done. Here the
  same: the check is at the top of the command, and a refused edit
  changes nothing.
- **The tree's lock is not the tree's sync lock, and the two are
  different facts.** The tree's *sync-locked* track is one that moves
  with the others — an insert opens a gap on it too — and the tree's
  *locked* track is one that may not be touched. Here the lock is
  here and the sync lock is not.
- **The tree's lock is on the track and not on the sequence, and a
  caption track has one too.** The tree's caption tracks are locked
  and sync-locked as well, and a caption track is not a thing this
  tree has.

### What it cost

- **Nine tests** in the film battery (`tests/locked.rs`): a track may
  be locked and unlocked, and a locked track refuses a trim, a move, a
  split, a removal, a ripple, a lift, an extract and a new clip, and
  an unlocked track may be edited again.
- **One new command**: `film.track.lock`. The film battery now carries
  **15** commands and the MCP server **366**.
- **Nine commands changed**: the add, the trim, the move, the insert,
  the split, the removal, the ripple, the lift and the extract all ask
  the track whether it is locked.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's sync lock is not here**: a sync-locked track moves with
  the others, and an insert opens a gap on it too.
- **The tree's caption tracks are not here**, and they may be locked
  and sync-locked as well.
- **The tree's track solo and the tree's track freeze are not here**,
  and they are locks of another kind.

## 284. The fades of a range of a track

The tree's `sound.clip.fade` was here (§ the clip's own fade), and the
tree's **range** of fades was not: the tree's `create_fades` walks a
**selection** and fades what the selection touches. That is here now.

### What was built

- The command `sound.track.fade` fades a **range** of a track: a clip
  that **starts** inside the range fades in over the rest of the
  range, and a clip that **ends** inside it fades out over the
  beginning of the range.
- The command `sound.track.fade.delete` takes those fades away.
- A range that covers **neither** a start nor an end is **refused**,
  and the refusal says what the range must cover.
- The **shape** of the curve is the tree's: `linear`, `equal_power`,
  `s_curve`, `exponential` or `logarithmic`, and the default is the
  tree's default, the equal power.

### What the port found

- **The tree's fade is a property of the clip and not of the track.**
  The tree's `create_fades` walks the track's playlist and writes the
  fade onto the *clip* — `c.fade_in = Fade { len, shape, curvature }` —
  and the tree's clip holds its fade and takes it with it when it
  moves. So a "fade of a range" is a thing a range *causes* and not a
  thing a range *is*: the range is looked at once and the clips are
  written. Here the same.
- **The tree's fade is a length, a shape and a bend, and the port had
  all three.** The tree's `Fade` is three numbers, and v2's clip has
  carried all three since the clip's own fade was ported — what was
  missing was not the fade but the **range**: the tree's fades are made
  over a *selection*, and the selection is what says which clips are
  faded and how long. That is what this arc adds, and the fade itself
  was already here.
- **The tree's range decides by the clip's start and by the clip's
  end, and it is an `else if`.** The tree's rule is that a clip that
  starts inside the range fades in, and a clip that ends inside it
  fades out — and a clip that does both gets only the fade in, because
  the tree's second test is an `else if`. Here the same.
- **The tree refuses a range that covers nothing, and says what a
  range must cover.** The tree's `fades_create` counts the fades it
  made and **fails when the count is zero**: "the selection must cover
  a clip start, end or the boundary between two clips". Here the
  refusal names the two of the three that are here, and the third —
  the boundary — is the crossfade and is not here yet.
- **The tree's delete clears the fades of every clip that *touches*
  the range, and it counts the clips that had one.** A clip that
  touches the range and has no fade is still touched, and the tree
  does not count it. Here the same.

### What it cost

- **Nine tests** in the sound battery (`tests/rangefades.rs`): a range
  that covers a start fades the clip in, a range that covers an end
  fades the clip out, the shape may be the tree's other shapes, a shape
  that is not a shape is refused, a range that covers nothing is
  refused, an empty range is refused, the fades of a range may be taken
  away, a fade in and a fade out may both be made, and a track that is
  not there is refused.
- **Two new commands**: `sound.track.fade` and `sound.track.fade.delete`.
  The sound battery now carries **129** commands and the MCP server
  **368**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's crossfade is not here**: a range that covers the
  **boundary** between two clips makes the two clips **overlap**, and
  each is extended into the other's territory using its handle — the
  material before it and the material after it. That is the third case
  of the tree's rule and it is a thing of its own.
- **The tree's delete trims the overlapping neighbours back to the
  midpoint** — the undo of the crossfade — and that is not here.
- **The tree's fade to is not here**: a fade that runs to the start of
  the next clip.

## 285. The crossfade

§284 left the third case of the tree's rule out: a range that covers the
**boundary** between two clips. That is here now.

### What was built

- A range that covers the boundary between two clips makes them
  **overlap**: each is extended into the other's territory using its
  **handle** — the material before it and the material after it.
- The two fades **meet in the overlap**: the first clip fades out over
  it and the second fades in over it.
- Taking the fades away takes the **overlap** with them: the two clips
  are trimmed back to the **midpoint**, and they are as long as they
  were.

### What the port found

- **The tree's crossfade is an edit of two clips and not a fade of
  one.** The tree's `create_fades` extends the first clip by the
  material it has *after* it and starts the second clip earlier by the
  material it has *before* it — and the two overlap. The crossfade is
  that overlap, and the fades are the two curves that meet in it.
- **The tree's handles are the material a clip does not play.** The
  material after a clip is the source's frames less what the clip
  plays, and the material before it is its offset. A crossfade cannot
  reach further than the handles allow, and the tree takes what it can:
  a clip with no material before it cannot be extended backwards.
- **The tree's handles are measured in the source's samples while the
  clip's length is in the timeline's, and the tree does not follow the
  stretch.** Here the handles are measured in the **timeline's**
  samples and the two agree whenever the clip is not stretched — and
  the difference is the stretch, which the tree does not correct for.
- **The tree's delete undoes the overlap by trimming to the
  midpoint.** The tree's `delete_fades` clears the fades of every clip
  that touches the range and then trims the overlapping neighbours
  back to the middle of the overlap: the two clips are as long as they
  were and the overlap is gone.
- **The tree's crossfade needs the clips to be next to each other.**
  The tree's test is that the second clip starts exactly where the
  first one ends, and a gap between them is not a boundary: the range
  fades the two apart instead, and the clips do not overlap.

### What it cost

- **Five tests** in the sound battery (`tests/crossfade.rs`): a range
  that covers a boundary makes the clips overlap, the fades meet in the
  overlap, a crossfade is limited by the handles, taking the fades away
  takes the overlap with them, and two clips with a gap between them are
  not a crossfade.
- **No new command**: the crossfade is what `sound.track.fade` does
  when the range covers a boundary. The sound battery still carries
  **129** commands and the MCP server **368**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's fade to is not here**: a fade that runs to the start of
  the next clip, and the tree's fade to the playhead.
- **The tree's crossfade of uncorrelated material** is the tree's
  `EqualPower` shape, and it is here as a shape — but the tree's
  renderer chooses between the shapes by whether the two clips are of
  the same material, and that choice is not here.

## 286. The flash fill

The tree's fills (§270, §274, §275) all copy a value or a series. The
tree has one fill that does neither: it **learns**.

### What was built

- A column is **flash filled**: the column beside it is the **source**,
  the rows that are filled are the **examples**, and what the examples
  say is a **program** — literals, tokens of the source and the first
  letter of a token — that is then run on the rows that are empty.
- The program is learned from the **shown text**: a date is read as the
  date it shows and not as the number it holds.
- The fill takes the **format** of the top of the column it fills, as
  the tree's fill takes the style of the top of the column.
- Four things are **refused**: the first column, which has nothing
  beside it to learn from; a column with no filled rows, which has
  nothing to learn from; a column whose examples share no program; and
  a column that is already full, which has nothing to fill.

### What the port found

- **The tree's flash fill learns a program and not a pattern.** Its
  pieces are a literal, a token by index with a case, and the first
  letter of a token; the target is cut greedily — the longest token that
  starts the rest of it wins, and whatever is left over becomes a
  literal. "Smith, John" is the second token, a literal `", "`, and the
  first token.
- **The tree tries two index conventions.** The first program counts
  the tokens from the front and the second counts them from the back,
  so "the last name" is one program written `-1`.
- **The tree's flash fill reads what the cell shows.** A date is the
  date it shows, so a column of dates is a column of texts and a date
  written in one shape can be rewritten in another.
- **The tree's learning cannot fail on a single example.** "Write this
  text" is always a program, so the tree's own test — one example, and
  the program that explains it — always finds something. Only two
  examples that disagree can fail, and then the tree writes nothing.
- **The tree's flash fill is silent when it cannot learn.** It returns
  zero and the caller cannot tell a refusal from a column that was
  already full. Here both are refusals, and the refusal says which.
- **The tree's flash fill writes the style of the top of the column**,
  which is a style and is shared. Here a format is the cell's own, and
  the format of the top cell is copied onto the cells that are written.
- **The tree's own comment overstates it.** The tree's `flash_fill`
  says it supports "fixed-position substrings", and its program has no
  piece for one: there are literals, tokens and initials, and nothing
  else.

### What it cost

- **Twelve tests** in the grid battery (`tests/flash.rs`): a token is
  learned and filled, the initials are learned, a literal is learned,
  the shown text of a date is read, the format of the column is taken,
  the first column is refused, a column with no examples is refused,
  examples that share no program are refused, a full column is refused,
  a cell that holds a formula is not empty, the outcome says what was
  written, and the value that is written is a text.
- **One new command**: `grid.flash.fill`. The grid battery now carries
  **13** commands and the MCP server **369**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's flash fill is the editor's, and the editor names a
  selection.** Here the command names the cell whose column is filled,
  and the region is the run of the source column around it.
- **The tree's examples are the rows of the source column and the
  target together; the region's ends are the ends of the source
  column.** A row whose source is empty ends the region, and the tree
  counts it in neither.
- **The tree's program is only ever tried on the rows that are
  filled.** A program that explains the examples may not fit a source —
  and then the tree writes nothing for that row and says nothing about
  it. Here the same: a row the program does not fit is left alone, and
  the count in the outcome is the count of the rows that were written.
- **The region's ends are the ends of the run of the source column
  around the cell that named it.** A row above or below that run is not
  in the region at all, and a row in the middle whose source is empty
  is in it: the program is run on an empty source, it does not fit, and
  the row is left alone.

## 287. The time of a cell

§276 gave the grid a **date**: a number and a format. The tree has one
more thing of that shape, and it is here now.

### What was built

- A cell may hold a **time**: a **number** and a **format**, like a
  date. The number is the **fraction of the day** and the format says
  that the number is a time and how it is written.
- The **thirteen time formats** the tree has are here: `h`, `hh`,
  `h:mm`, `hh:mm`, `h:mm:ss`, `hh:mm:ss`, `h AM/PM`, `h:mm AM/PM`,
  `h:mm:ss AM/PM`, `hh:mm:ss AM/PM`, and the three **elapsed** shapes
  `[h]:mm`, `[h]:mm:ss` and `[mm]:ss`.
- A time is **written** the tree's way — `13:45`, `13:45:30`,
  `1:45 pm` — and the shape it was written in is the format it is
  written with, as a date's shape is (§276).
- A time that **did not happen** is refused: the sixtieth minute is
  not a minute, and a lone number is not a time.

### What the port found

- **A time is a fraction of a day and not a kind of value.** The tree's
  `time_fraction` is `(h × 3600 + m × 60 + s) / 86400`, and the tree's
  own `General` format shows a time as a number — so the number is the
  time and the format is what says so. That is the same bargain a date
  makes, and it is made twice.
- **The tree's clock has two faces and the format chooses.** The same
  number is `18:00` under `h:mm` and `6:00 PM` under `h:mm AM/PM`, and
  the twelve-hour face has the noon as the twelve and the midnight as
  the zero — and the midnight is `12:00 AM`, never `0:00 AM`.
- **The tree's elapsed shapes are a different thing entirely.** The
  clock shapes look at the *time of day* and throw the day away; the
  elapsed shapes look at the *whole number* and count it — a day and a
  half is thirty-six hours under `[h]:mm`, and the hours do not stop
  at twenty-four. The tree's square brackets are what say so, and they
  are the tree's own convention.
- **The tree rounds a time to the nearest second, and the rounding
  carries.** A time of 12:00:59.6 is 12:01:00, and a time of
  23:59:59.7 is 00:00:00 — the tree rounds the milliseconds to the
  second and a second that rounds to the next one carries into the
  minute and into the day.
- **The tree's written time is half of a day at the noon and a half of
  a day at the midnight.** `12:00 pm` is 0.5 and `12:00 am` is 0.0,
  because the tree reads a clock of twelve: the twelve of the morning
  is the zero of the day.
- **The tree's parser refuses more than it accepts.** A lone `13` is
  not a time, `13:60` is not a time, and `1:45:30.5` is not a time
  either — the tree's parser has no thousandths. Here the same three
  are refused.

### What it cost

- **Seventeen tests** in the grid battery (`tests/times.rs`): a time is
  put in a cell, a time is a number, the clock is of twenty-four
  hours, the clock of twelve says the half of the day, the midnight is
  twelve in the morning, the noon is twelve in the afternoon, the
  seconds are written, the time is rounded to the second, the elapsed
  hours do not stop at twenty-four, the elapsed minutes are the
  minutes, a time on a clock of twelve is written as it was, the noon
  and the midnight written with a half of the day, a time that did not
  happen is refused, a number on its own is not a time, a format that
  is not a time format is refused, and a time may be written with
  another format.
- **One new command**: `grid.cell.time`. The grid battery now carries
  **14** commands and the MCP server **370**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's thousandths are not here.** The tree's clock can show
  `mm:ss.0` and `mm:ss.00`, and the tree's parser reads a fraction of a
  second; here a time is a whole second and a code with a point in it
  is refused.
- **The tree's `[s]` is not here**: the elapsed seconds on their own
  are a shape the tree has and this one does not.
- **The tree's `a/p` is not here**: the tree writes `6 a` and `6 p`,
  and here the half of the day is `AM` or `PM`.
- **The tree's date with a time in it is not here**: `2026-10-26
  13:45` is a date and a time in the tree, and here it is neither a
  date nor a time — a date is a date and a time is a time.

## 288. The ordinals of a fill

§270 gave the grid a fill that counts a **text with a number** in it on.
The tree counts more than the number.

### What was built

- A text with an English **ordinal ending** is filled with the ending
  rewritten to suit the new number: `1st Period` is filled as
  `2nd Period`, `3rd Period` and `4th Period`.
- The eleventh, the twelfth and the thirteenth end in **th**, as they
  do in English.
- The ending keeps the **case** it was written in: `1ST` is filled as
  `2ND`.
- A text after the ending that starts a **word** is not an ordinal, and
  the ending is kept as it is.

### What the port found

- **The tree's ordinal is a rule about the text after the number.** The
  fill splits a text into the text before the number, the number and
  the text after it, and the *first two letters* of that last part are
  the ending. `1st Period` is the empty text, the number `1` and
  `st Period`, and the ending is `st`.
- **The tree refuses an ending that is followed by a word.** `1stx` is
  filled as `2stx`: the ending is not rewritten when what follows it
  starts an alphanumeric, because `1stx` is not an ordinal and the
  tree does not make it one.
- **The tree's case rule is about the ending and not about the text.**
  The ending is in capitals when the two letters it was written in are
  both capitals, and the rest of the text keeps its own case.
- **The tree's number in a text is the *last* run of digits.** `1st2` is
  the text `1st` and the number `2`, and it is filled as `1st3` — the
  ending is not the ending of the text at all, because the text's
  number is the one at the end.

### What it cost

- **Seven tests** in the grid battery (`tests/ordinals.rs`): the
  ending is rewritten, the eleventh and the twelfth and the thirteenth
  end in th, the ending keeps its case, a text that starts a word is
  not an ordinal, a text with no ordinal is filled as it is, the number
  is still a number, and the number is the last run of digits.
- **No new command**: this is what `grid.range.fill` does with a text
  that has an ordinal in it. The grid battery still carries **14**
  commands and the MCP server **370**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's `n-th` in every language is not here**: the four
  English endings are the four the tree has, and `1er` and `2ème` are
  not.
- **The tree's quarters in a text are not here**: `Qtr3` and
  `Quarter 4` wrap after four in the tree, and here they count on.

## 289. The fill of a time

§287 gave the grid a **time**, and §288 gave a fill an **ordinal**. The
tree's fill knows about the time as well.

### What was built

- A single number under a **time format** counts an **hour** on when it
  is filled: `9:00` is filled as `10:00` and `11:00`.
- The fill carries over the **midnight**: `23:30` is filled as `0:30`,
  and the day counts on with it.

### What the port found

- **The tree's time is a number, and so the tree's fill of a time is
  the tree's fill of a number.** The tree's `detect` looks at the
  **format code** and not at the value: a code with an `h` in it is a
  time, and a single number under one steps by `1/24` — an hour. A
  single number under a date format steps by a day, and a single number
  under no format at all is copied.
- **The tree's time and its date are told apart by the code.** The
  tree's test is `fmt.contains('d') || fmt.contains('y') || (fmt
  .contains('m') && !fmt.contains('h'))` — the `h` is what says a
  format is a time and not a date, and the `m` of a month is not a
  month when the code has an `h` in it.
- **The tree's time in a cell is a typed time.** The tree's own test
  fills a cell that holds the text `9:00` and gets `10:00` and
  `11:00`, because the tree's parser reads a typed time as a number
  under a time format. Here a time is put in a cell by a command (§287)
  and a typed `9:00` is a text — so the fill of a *text* that looks
  like a time is a text that counts its last run of digits, and that
  is a difference the tree does not have.

### What it cost

- **Five tests** in the grid battery (`tests/time_fill.rs`): a time
  counts an hour on, the fill carries over the midnight, a date counts
  a day on, a number with no format is copied, and the fill keeps the
  format of the time.
- **No new command**: this is what `grid.range.fill` does with a
  number under a time format. The grid battery still carries **14**
  commands and the MCP server **370**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's typed time is not here**: the tree's parser reads a
  typed `9:00` as a time, and here a typed text is a text — a time is
  put in a cell by `grid.cell.time` (§287) and the tree's own typed
  input is not here.
- **The tree's time in a fill of two cells is a line and not an
  hour.** The tree's `detect` steps by an hour only when there is a
  single number; two or more are a least squares line, and so are they
  here.

## 290. The quarters in a text

§282 gave the grid the **list** of the quarters, and a list wraps. The
tree has the rule twice.

### What was built

- A text that says a **quarter** wraps after four, as the list does:
  `Qtr3` is filled as `Qtr4` and `Qtr1`, and `Quarter 4` is filled as
  `Quarter 1`.

### What the port found

- **The tree's quarter in a text is the list of the quarters again,
  with a prefix.** The tree's list holds `Q1`, `Q2`, `Q3` and `Q4`, and
  a text that is one of them is filled from the list. A text that says
  a quarter in **words** — `Qtr3`, `Quarter 3` — is not in the list, so
  the tree has a second rule for it: the text before the number, with
  its spaces trimmed and its case lowered, is `Q`, `Qtr` or `Quarter`.
- **The tree's second rule is about the source and not about the
  value.** The tree tests the number it is filling *from*: `Qtr7` is
  not a quarter — seven is not one of the four — and it counts on to
  `Qtr8`. The test is on the source so that a fill that starts at a
  quarter stays a quarter all the way round.
- **The tree's second rule wants nothing after the number.** `Qtr3x` is
  not a quarter, because the text after the number is not empty, and it
  counts on.

### What it cost

- **Five tests** in the grid battery (`tests/quarters.rs`): a quarter
  wraps after four, a quarter in words wraps, a number that is not a
  quarter counts on, a text with a suffix is not a quarter, and the
  list of the quarters wraps as well.
- **No new command**: this is what `grid.range.fill` does with a text
  that says a quarter. The grid battery still carries **14** commands
  and the MCP server **370**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's other quarter words are not here**: `Q` and `Qtr` and
  `Quarter` are the three the tree has, and `Trimester` is not.
- **The tree's own list of words is not here**: the tree's fill may be
  given a list of words to step through, and here the lists are the
  tree's five (§282).

## 291. The in side of a keyframe

§280 gave the fx battery the **interpolation** of a keyframe, and it
gave it the side the keyframe **leaves** on. The tree has two sides.

### What was built

- A keyframe has an interpolation on **each** side: the side it leaves
  on and the side it is entered on, and both are set by the same
  command with the **side** it names — `out` or `in`.
- The segment between two keyframes is shaped by **both** sides: the
  side the first leaves on and the side the second is entered on.

### What the port found

- **The tree's out side decides the shape of the segment and the in
  side shapes the handle.** The tree's `segment_value` asks the out
  side first: a hold out side holds the value, whatever the in side
