  says. The in side only ever moves the handle that comes in.
- **The tree's in side that is not a bezier is a linear side.** The
  tree's test is `b.in_interp != Interp::Bezier`, so a **hold** in
  side shapes the segment it ends like a line — the tree says so in a
  comment: a hold in side only matters for the segment it ends, which
  the out side decides, and it shapes the incoming segment like a
  linear side, as the Graph Editor and the Lottie export do.
- **The tree's linear side is a third of the segment.** The tree's
  linear side is not a line drawn from the two values but an *ease*:
  a speed of the whole difference over the duration and an influence
  of a third. That is the same curve as the line — the handles are a
  third of the way to the other value — and it is what makes the
  tree's two eases interchangeable with a linear one.
- **The tree's linear out side with a bezier in side is a curve.** The
  tree's `lin_out && lin_in` is the test for a plain line, and a
  bezier in side makes it false: the segment is a Bezier whose out
  handle is the linear one and whose in handle is the bezier one.

### What it cost

- **Nine tests** in the fx battery (`tests/insides.rs`): the in side is
  set on its own, the side that is not named is the out side, the in
  side shapes the segment, a hold on the in side is a linear side, the
  out side decides the shape, a linear out side with a bezier in side
  is a curve, the ease of the in side is kept, a side that is not a
  side is refused, and the outcome says which side was set.
- **No new command**: `fx.keyframe.interp` takes the side it sets, and
  the fx battery still carries **8** commands and the MCP server
  **370**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's auto-Bezier is not here.** The tree's keyframe may be
  an *auto* key, whose ease is the slope to its neighbours and whose
  influence is a sixth — the tree's `auto_bezier`. Here the ease is
  always written down.
- **The tree's ease is per dimension and here it is one.** The tree
  keeps an ease for each dimension of the value, so a list of numbers
  may curve one way and another way; here the ease is the ease of the
  whole value.
- **The tree's spatial handles are not here**: they are the same idea
  in three dimensions, along a path, and they are a thing of their
  own.

## 292. The auto bezier of a keyframe

§291 gave the fx battery the **in side** of a keyframe. The tree has
one more thing about a keyframe's ease, and it is the opposite of
writing it down.

### What was built

- A keyframe may be an **auto** bezier: its ease is not written down
  but comes from its **neighbours** — the slope from the keyframe
  before to the keyframe after — and its influence is a **sixth**.
- So an auto keyframe **follows** its neighbours: move one and the
  curve moves with it.
- A **written** ease is a manual one, and it clears the auto flag: the
  keyframe follows its neighbours again only when nobody has said
  otherwise.

### What the port found

- **The tree's auto ease is the slope to the neighbours, and not the
  slope to the segment.** The tree's `effective_ease` takes the value
  of the keyframe before and the value of the keyframe after and the
  time between them: the slope is `(after − before) / (after time −
  before time)`. The time of the keyframe itself is not in it — the
  auto key's ease does not know where it sits between its neighbours.
- **The tree's auto ease has an influence of a sixth, and the sixth is
  the tree's own default.** The tree's `Ease::default` is a speed of
  nothing and an influence of a sixth, and the auto ease is that
  default with the speed filled in.
- **The tree's auto key needs a neighbour on each side.** The tree's
  test is `k.auto_bezier && i > 0 && i + 1 < keys.len()`, so the first
  and the last keyframe of a property are never auto: there is no
  slope to the other side.
- **The tree's ease is per dimension and the written ease here is
  not.** The tree keeps an ease for each dimension of the value, so a
  list of numbers may curve one way and another way. Here an ease is
  one speed and one influence for the whole value, and every number of
  a list is curved by that same written ease. The **auto** slope is
  the slope of each dimension, as the tree's is — an auto key of a
  list still curves each number its own way.
- **The tree's manual ease is not an auto one.** The tree's
  `easy_ease` sets the ease and clears `auto_bezier`, so the two are
  not together.

### What it cost

- **Seven tests** in the fx battery (`tests/auto.rs`): an auto
  keyframe follows its neighbours, the auto flag is kept, the auto flag
  is cleared, a written ease clears the auto flag, a keyframe with no
  neighbour is not an auto one, the auto on a keyframe that is not
  there is refused, and the outcome says the auto.
- **One new command**: `fx.keyframe.auto`. The fx battery now carries
  **9** commands and the MCP server **371**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's continuous bezier is not here**: the tree's keyframe
  also has a `continuous` flag, whose ease is the slope to the
  **segment** — the keyframe before for the in side and the keyframe
  after for the out side — and that is a thing of its own.
- **The tree's spatial auto bezier is not here**: it is the same idea
  in three dimensions, along a path, with tangents instead of slopes.
- **The tree's written ease per dimension is not here**: an ease is
  one speed and one influence for the whole value, and every number of
  a list is curved by it.

## 293. The transitions of a track

The tree's timeline has one thing this battery did not have: a thing
that sits **over the cut** between two clips.

### What was built

- A track may carry a **transition**: a node in the track, with a
  payload — the two clips it joins, its span, its duration, its
  alignment and its kind.
- A transition sits on the **cut** by its alignment: `center` (half of
  it before the cut), `start` (all of it after) or `end` (all of it
  before).
- A transition may be **changed** — its duration and its alignment — and
  it may be **taken away**, and the clips it joins are not touched.
- Three things are **refused**: two clips that are not next to each
  other, a transition that would leave the clips it joins, and a locked
  track.

### What the port found

- **A transition joins two clips that are next to each other.** The
  tree looks for the cut: the clip before must *end* exactly where the
  clip after *begins*. A gap is not a cut, and a transition over a gap
  is not a thing.
- **The tree's alignment is a placement and not a shape.** The
  transition's start follows from the alignment and the cut: a centred
  one starts half its duration before the cut, one that starts at the
  cut starts at it, and one that ends at the cut is its whole duration
  before it. So changing the duration of a centred transition moves
  **both** of its ends, and changing the duration of one that ends at
  the cut moves only its beginning.
- **The tree's transition may not leave the clips it joins, and the
  tree says why.** The tree's bounds are the outgoing clip's start and
  the incoming clip's end, and the tree's own comment is that it does
  not check the material the clips have beyond the cut — the *handles*
  — so a transition may cover at most the clips it joins.
- **A transition is a thing of the track and not of either clip.** The
  tree keeps the transitions in the track, and the tree removes a
  transition whose clip is gone (`remove_orphan_transitions`).
- **The tree's transition over the same cut is replaced, and not
  stacked.** The tree's `add_transition` removes the transitions that
  overlap the new one and join one of the same clips, so that there is
  one transition over a cut and not two.
- **The tree's transition kind is a name in a registry, and the
  registry is not here.** The tree has a table of transitions and a
  cross dissolve is the default for a video track. A registry is a
  thing of its own, so this tree has the one the tree's default names
  and refuses the rest.

### What it cost

- **Fourteen tests** in the film battery (`tests/transitions.rs`): a
  transition is centred on the cut, it may start at the cut, it may end
  at the cut, it is a thing of the track, two clips that are not next
  to each other are refused, a transition that does not fit is refused,
  a locked track refuses it, a transition that is already there is
  replaced, a transition can be taken away, the duration may be
  changed, the alignment may be changed, an alignment that is not an
  alignment is refused, a transition this tree does not have is
  refused, and a transition of no frames is refused.
- **Three new commands**: `film.transition.add`, `film.transition.set`
  and `film.transition.remove`, and a **kind**: `film.transition`. The
  film battery now carries **18** commands and the MCP server **374**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's one-sided transitions are not here**: a fade from
  nothing or to nothing is a transition with one clip and not two, and
  the tree has a rule for where it sits — at the cut, or its whole
  duration before it.
- **The tree's custom start is not here**: a transition dragged off
  the centre of its cut is a fourth alignment, and the tree's rule for
  it is that the ends move equally around where it is now.
- **The tree's transition parameters are not here**: the tree's
  transition is an *effect* with parameters of its own, and the
  parameters are the effect's business.
- **The tree's linked clips are not here**, and so a transition over
  the cut of a linked pair is not here either: a linked clip is a
  thing of its own.

## 294. The speed of a clip

The film battery had **two clocks** and a clip that played its media
as it was. The tree has a third thing.

### What was built

- A clip may play its media **faster or slower** than it is: a new
  command, `film.clip.speed`, and a `speed` in the clip's payload.
- The clip's **length follows**: a clip that plays twice as fast is
  half as long, and it plays the **same material**.
- The **trim** and the **split** count the media through the speed: a
  trim of five frames of a clip that plays twice as fast moves the
  media ten frames, and a split cuts the media at the speed's worth.

### What the port found

- **The tree's speed is the third thing that joins the two clocks.**
  The tree's clip has a `start` and a `duration` in the timeline's
  ticks, a `source_in` in the media's ticks, and a `speed` — and the
  media a clip plays is `duration × speed`. The tree's own `move_edge`
  says so: the media a trim takes is `src_of(delta, speed)`.
- **The tree's speed keeps the media the same.** The tree's
  `set_speed` computes the new length as `source length / speed`, so
  the clip is the same material at another rate — and not a different
  material at the same rate.
- **The tree's speed is not the tree's reverse.** The tree's speed may
  be negative and a negative speed is a reverse, and the tree's
  `move_edge` takes the absolute value. Here the direction is a
  property of the clip and not of the speed (§281), so a speed here is
  a number that is more than nothing.
- **The tree's speed may not run into the next clip.** The tree bounds
  the new length by the space there is — `new_dur.min(next_start -
  it.start)` — so a clip that would grow into its neighbour is
  shortened by the tree and **refused** here.
- **The tree's rounding is a bound of its own, and the tree has no
  such bound.** Fifty frames of media at three times the speed is
  seventeen frames long, and seventeen frames at three times the speed
  is fifty-one frames of media: the rounding of the length may make a
  clip play a frame more of the media than it did. The tree's `check`
  looks at the length of a clip, at the time bounds and at the
  transitions — and **not** at the media, so the tree says nothing
  about a clip that plays past the end of its item. Here it is
  refused.

### What it cost

- **Nine tests** in the film battery (`tests/speed.rs`): a faster clip
  is shorter, a slower clip is longer, the media is the same material,
  a speed that is not a speed is refused, a locked track refuses a
  speed, a clip that would overlap is refused, the trim moves the
  media by the speed, the split cuts the media at the speed, and the
  media may not run past its end.
- **One new command**: `film.clip.speed`. The film battery now carries
  **19** commands and the MCP server **375**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's ripple is not here**: the tree's speed change may
  ripple — the later material moves with the clip — and here the clip
  changes and the gap it leaves is a gap.
- **The tree's speed on a group of linked clips is not here**: the
  tree changes the speed of a clip and its linked partners as one
  edit, and the linked clips are not here either.
- **The tree's rate and stretch are not here**: the tree's
  `rate_stretch` changes the speed by dragging an edge, and the speed
  it leaves is the speed of the new length.

## 295. The link of a clip

The tree's timeline has a thing that is not on the timeline: two clips
that are **the same thing on two tracks** — a picture and its sound.

### What was built

- Two clips may be **linked**: a new command, `film.clip.link`, and a
  `link` in the clip's payload. A clip may be **unlinked** with
  `film.clip.unlink`.
- A **move** of a linked clip moves its **partners** by the same
  offset, on their own tracks.
- A partner on a **locked** track stays where it is.
- A partner left **alone** in its link is unlinked too: a link with
  nothing to follow reads as if it were something.

### What the port found

- **The tree's link is a number in the clip, and the clips with the
  same number are the group.** The tree's `TrackItem` has a `link:
  Option<u64>` and the tree's edit context allocates the number. Here
  the link is the id of the **first clip of the group** — the smallest
  id in it — so the group has a name that is in the document and two
  groups can be merged by taking the smaller name.
- **The tree's move of a linked clip moves the partners by the same
  offset and not to the same place.** The tree's `timeline.move` puts
  each partner at `partner.start + offset` on **its own track**: the
  picture and the sound keep their own places on their own tracks and
  stay in step.
- **The tree's partner on a locked track stays.** The tree's move
  looks at the tracks that are not locked and leaves the partners on
  the locked ones alone — the same rule the locked track has for
  every other edit (§283).
- **The tree's group of one is not a group.** The tree's link command
  says so in its own words: "a partner left alone in its link is
  unlinked too: a one-member link would read as linked with nothing
  to follow".
- **The tree's link command is a command on a *selection*.** The tree
  links everything that is selected, and it pairs a video clip with
  the audio clip of the same item that overlaps it. Here two clips
  are named, and nothing is guessed.

### What it cost

- **Ten tests** in the film battery (`tests/links.rs`): two clips are
  linked, a move moves the partner, a partner on a locked track stays,
  an unlinked clip leaves the others, a partner left alone is unlinked,
  a clip that is not linked cannot be unlinked, a clip may not be
  linked to itself, two clips in different sequences are refused, the
  trim of a linked clip is refused, and the split of a linked clip is
  refused.
- **Two new commands**: `film.clip.link` and `film.clip.unlink`. The
  film battery now carries **21** commands and the MCP server **377**.

### What it does not settle

- **The trim of a linked clip is refused, and it is not here yet** —
  and it is now (§299): the tree trims the group as **one edit**, with
  the delta that every member can take — the smallest of their bounds —
  and it applies that delta to all of them.
- **The split of a linked clip is refused, and it is not here yet.**
  The tree splits the group as one edit and the right-hand pieces get
  a **new** link, so that they stay linked to each other and not to
  the left-hand ones.
- **The tree's copy of a linked clip is not here**: the tree's copies
  of linked clips are linked to each other and not to the originals.
- **The tree's selection is not here**: the tree links what is
  selected and pairs a video clip with the audio clip of the same item
  that overlaps it; here two clips are named.

## 296. The date system of a workbook

§276 gave the grid a **date**, and the date was a number in one
calendar. The tree has **two** calendars and a workbook says which one.

### What was built

- A workbook says which **calendar** its serials are counted in: the
  `1900` system or the `1904` system, and a new command,
  `grid.workbook.date.system`, that says it.
- The system is a fact of the **workbook**, as it is in the tree: every
  date in every sheet of a workbook is read in that workbook's
  calendar.
- A date before the **calendar's own first day** is refused: the 1904
  system begins at the 1st of January 1904 and the 1900 system at the
  1st of January 1900.

### What the port found

- **The tree's date system is a field of the workbook.** The tree's
  `Workbook` has a `date_system: DateSystem` and every date in the book
  is read in it — the tree's `serial_in_system` shifts a serial by
  **1462 days**, and the shift is the whole difference between the two
  systems.
- **The tree's 1904 system has no day in it that never happened.** The
  1900 system has the fictitious 29th of February of 1900 — the serial
  60 — and the 1904 system counts from the 1st of January 1904, so its
  serial 0 is that day and its serial 60 is the 1st of March 1904.
- **The tree's weekdays are the tree's own in the 1900 system and the
  real ones in the 1904 system.** The tree's 1900 calendar has the
  day that never happened in it, so every date before the 1st of March
  of 1900 is a day later than the day it really is: the 1st of
  January 1900 was a Monday and the tree's calendar says the Sunday.
  After March the tree's dates and its weekdays are the real ones, and
  the two systems agree on the weekday of every date they share.
- **The tree's maximum serial is the system's.** The tree's
  `max_serial` is 2 958 465 in the 1900 system and 1462 less in the
  1904 system, so the two books end on the same day.
- **The tree's workbook is where the system lives and not the sheet.**
  That is why the system's change moves *every* date in the book: the
  serial of a date is the same number in both systems only when the
  system is the same.

### What it cost

- **Ten tests** in the grid battery (`tests/systems.rs`): a workbook is
  in the 1900 system, the system may be changed, a system that is not
  a system is refused, the two systems are 1462 days apart, the
  weekday is the one of the system, a date before the calendar is
  refused, the 1904 system has no day that never happened, the system
  belongs to the workbook, a fill of dates is in the system, and the
  same serial is a different date.
- **One new command**: `grid.workbook.date.system`. The grid battery
  now carries **15** commands and the MCP server **378**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's system is set when the file is read and not by a
  command.** The tree's workbook carries the system in the file, so a
  file that was made somewhere else keeps its calendar. Here the
  system is set by a command, and a file that says nothing is in the
  1900 system.
- **The tree's `DATE()` is not here**, and it takes the system's
  calendar and rolls a month over into the next year.
- **The tree's time zone is not here**: the tree's serial is a time
  without a zone, and here it is too.

## 297. The continuous keyframe

§292 gave the fx battery the **auto** bezier, whose ease is not
written down. The tree has one more way a keyframe's ease may be
decided.

### What was built

- A keyframe may be **continuous**: its two sides are **locked** to each
  other, so the outgoing side takes the ease of the incoming one and
  the curve is smooth at the keyframe. A new command,
  `fx.keyframe.continuous`, and a `continuous` in the keyframe's
  payload.
- The ease that is **given** is written to both sides; when none is
  given, the side the keyframe is **entered** on is the master and the
  other takes its ease.
- Both sides become **beziers**, the **auto** flag is cleared, and the
  flag may be **cleared** again without touching the eases.

### What the port found

- **The tree's continuous flag does not change the curve.** The tree's
  `effective_ease` — the function that decides a side's ease — reads
  the `auto_bezier` flag and not the `continuous` one. So the curve of
  a continuous keyframe is the curve of the eases that were written,
  and the flag is a **memory** of the writing.
- **The tree's continuity is a way of *writing* the two sides.** The
  tree's velocity dialog is where the flag lives: "Continuous" makes
  the outgoing velocity follow the incoming one, so the side that is
  not named takes the ease of the side that is — and the tree's dialog
  writes the two sides *together*.
- **The tree's two sides are the same ease in the same sense.** The
  tree's `side_ease` presents the incoming side's speed as the
  **forward** rate of the segment and the outgoing side's speed as the
  forward rate too, so copying one to the other gives the two handles
  as **mirrors** — and the curve is smooth at the keyframe. Here the
  eases are in the tree's sense as well (§280), so the mirror is a
  mirror.
- **The tree's manual ease is not an auto one, and a continuous ease is
  a manual ease.** The tree's velocity command clears `auto_bezier`
  when it writes, and so does this one.

### What it cost

- **Nine tests** in the fx battery (`tests/continuous.rs`): the two
  sides are locked, the sides are beziers, the continuous flag is
  kept, the flag may be cleared, the auto flag is cleared, the curve is
  smooth at the keyframe, the in side is the master, a keyframe that
  is not there is refused, and an influence that is not a fraction is
  refused.
- **One new command**: `fx.keyframe.continuous`. The fx battery now
  carries **10** commands and the MCP server **379**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's continuous flag is not read by the tree's own curve**,
  and here it is not read either: the flag is a memory and the eases
  are the truth. A keyframe marked continuous whose eases were changed
  afterwards is not continuous, and that is the tree's behaviour too.
- **The tree's velocity dialog is not here**: it presents the ease of
  each side as it is, writes a speed and an influence per dimension,
  and keeps the parts that were not named. Here one ease is written to
  both sides.
- **The tree's ease per dimension is not here**: the tree keeps an ease
  for each dimension of the value, so a continuous keyframe of a list
  curves each number its own way; here one ease is written and every
  dimension is curved by it.

## 298. The custom lists of a workbook

§282 gave the grid the tree's **five lists** — the days of the week,
the months and the quarters. The tree has a sixth place for lists, and
it is empty.

### What was built

- A workbook may carry **lists of your own**: the words a fill steps
  through. Two new commands, `grid.workbook.list.add` and
  `grid.workbook.list.remove`, and a `custom_lists` in the workbook's
  payload.
- The tree's own lists are tried **after** the workbook's, so a list of
  your own may **shadow** one of the tree's.
- The words are given **one per line**; a list of **one** word is not a
  list, and a word that is in the list **twice** is refused — the fill
  finds a list by membership and would find the first of the two and
  never the second.

### What the port found

- **The tree's custom lists are a field with no writer.** The tree's
  `Workbook` has a `custom_lists: Vec<Vec<String>>` and the tree's
  fill reads it — the tree's `fill` does `cx.wb.custom_lists.clone()`
  and the tree's `Pattern::detect` tries them — but **nothing in the
  tree ever writes one**: no command, no file reader, no user interface.
  So the tree's custom lists are always empty, and the code that reads
  them is the tree's own dead branch.
- **The tree tries the lists of the workbook first.** The tree's
  `Pattern::detect` does `custom.iter().cloned().chain(lists())`, so a
  list of your own is tried **before** the days of the week — and a
  list of your own that says `Mon`, `Tue`, `Wed` shadows the tree's
  list of the days.
- **The tree's list is found by membership and not by a name.** The
  tree's test is that every text of the source is in the list, and the
  index of each text in the list is where the fill starts — so a list
  of two words may be stepped through in either direction, and the
  case of the source is the case of the list (§282).
- **The tree's list has no duplicate rule.** The tree's `position`
  finds the **first** match, so a list with the same word twice is a
  list with one of them unreachable — and the tree says nothing. Here
  the list with the word twice is refused.

### What it cost

- **Ten tests** in the grid battery (`tests/custom_lists.rs`): a custom
  list may be added, a fill steps through a custom list, a custom list
  wraps, a custom list is found by membership, a custom list shadows a
  tree list, a list of one word is refused, a word twice is refused, a
  custom list may be taken away, a list that is not there is refused,
  and the lists belong to the workbook.
- **Two new commands**: `grid.workbook.list.add` and
  `grid.workbook.list.remove`. The grid battery now carries **17**
  commands and the MCP server **381**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's list has no writer and this one has two.** A list in a
  workbook is a fact here and a dead field there, and the difference
  is the finding: the tree's fill honours a thing nothing ever puts
  there.
- **The tree's list is written in a user interface and not by a
  command**: the tree's field is the *Options › Custom Lists* of a
  spreadsheet, and here the words are given one per line.

## 299. The trim of a linked group

§295 gave the film battery the **link** between two clips, and it
refused the trim of a linked clip. The tree has no such refusal.

### What was built

- The trim of a linked clip trims the **whole group**: every member
  takes the same delta, and the media of every member moves with it.
- A member that **cannot take** the delta refuses the whole trim, and
  the refusal names the member.
- A clip that is **not** linked is trimmed on its own, as before.

### What the port found

- **The tree's trim of a group is one edit and not many.** The tree's
  `clamp_trim_linked` and `trim_delta_linked` take the **delta** every
  member can take: the tree computes the bound of each member and uses
  the smallest, so the picture and the sound are trimmed by the same
  number of frames and stay in step.
- **The tree clamps and this tree refuses.** The tree's trim computes
  the biggest delta the trim may have and uses that, so a drag that
  goes too far stops at the bound and the editor never says that it
  did (§287's rule, §285's too). Here a trim that a member cannot take
  is an **error** that says which member stopped it, and the group is
  as it was.
- **The tree's group trim is the same delta for every member** — the
  tree's `trim_delta_linked` returns one delta for the whole group and
  every member is trimmed by it. So a picture and its sound are
  trimmed by the same number of frames, and the media they play moves
  with them.

### What it cost

- **Five tests** in the film battery (`tests/linked_trim.rs`): the
  partner is trimmed too, the in edge moves the media of every member,
  a member that cannot take it refuses the trim, the outcome names the
  group, and a clip that is not linked is trimmed on its own.
- **No new command**: this is what `film.clip.trim` does with a linked
  clip. The film battery still carries **21** commands and the MCP
  server **381**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's clamp is not here**: the tree's trim takes the biggest
  delta it may and says nothing about it; here the trim is refused and
  the member that could not take it is named.
- **The split of a linked group is refused, and it is not here yet** —
  and it is now (§300): the tree splits the group as one edit and the
  right-hand pieces get a **new** link, so that they stay linked to
  each other and not to the left-hand ones.

## 300. The split of a linked group

§299 gave the film battery the **trim** of a linked group. The split
is the last of the tree's link rules.

### What was built

- The split of a linked clip splits the **group**: every member that
  covers the place is cut at the same frame, and the media of every
  member moves with the cut.
- The **right-hand pieces** are a **new group**: they are linked to
  each other and not to the left-hand ones, as the tree's split does.

### What the port found

- **The tree's split of a group mints a new link for the right-hand
  pieces.** The tree's `split_track_at` takes a map of the old groups
  to the new ones and gives the right-hand piece a link from it — so
  the two pieces of a group are still linked **to each other** and not
  to the left halves. A split does not break a link; it makes a new
  one.
- **The tree's split of a group cuts the members that are under the
  place.** The tree's `razor_items` splits the tracks of the given
  clips, and only where the item at the place is one of them: a
  partner that does not reach the place is not cut, and the group is
  one link smaller for it.
- **The tree's split is the same place for every member** — the
  timeline frame, not the source frame. So a picture and its sound are
  cut at the same moment on the timeline, and each of them takes the
  media that goes with its own cut.

### What it cost

- **Five tests** in the film battery (`tests/linked_split.rs`): the
  partner is split too, the right-hand pieces are a new group, the
  media moves with the cut, a member that does not cover the place is
  left alone, and a place that is not inside is refused.
- **No new command**: this is what `film.clip.split` does with a
  linked clip. The film battery still carries **21** commands and the
  MCP server **381**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's transitions are not here** — and they are now (§302):
  the tree's split moves the transitions that follow the cut onto the
  right-hand piece, and it takes away the ones that span it only when
  they are a fade to nothing. Here a split moves the transitions that
  follow it, and nothing is taken away.
- **The tree's group split is a **razor** of the whole group**: the
  tree's razor may be given a track and cuts everything on it, and
  the groups it cuts are made new links as well. Here a split is of
  one group and its members.

## 301. The frame hold of a clip

§294 gave the film battery the **speed** of a clip. The frame hold is
the third thing that changes what a clip plays: a clip may play its
media up to a point and then **hold** one frame to the end of itself.

### What was built

- A clip may **hold a frame**: it plays its media up to a frame of the
  media and then holds that frame to the end of the clip. Two commands:
  `film.clip.hold` and `film.clip.hold.delete`.
- The hold is a **source** frame — a frame of the media and not a frame
  of the timeline — because it is the media that stops and not the
  timeline.
- The **trim honours it**: a held clip has no head handle, so a trim of
  its in edge moves the clip and leaves the media where it is, and the
  media does not bound a held clip at all.

### What the port found

- **A held clip has no media length.** The tree's `media_len` answers
  *nothing* when a clip holds a frame: the media does not bound the
  clip, and the bound is the hold. So a held clip's material is
  **shorter** than the clip — it ends at the hold, and the rest of the
  clip is that one frame.
- **A held clip has no head handle.** The tree's `head` gives a held
  clip its own source in point, so there is no media before it to be
  taken: a trim of the in edge moves the clip and not the media. The
  tree says it in the same place — *a frame hold needs no source head*.
- **The tree's hold is a tick of the media, snapped to the rate.** The
  tree clamps it to zero and snaps it to the frame rate of the item.
  Here it is a whole number of frames, and a number that is not a
  whole number is refused.
- **The tree's Add Frame Hold is two edits, and the hold is not one of
  them.** The tree's `add_frame_hold` **razors** the clip at the
  playhead and gives the right-hand piece the hold — so the tree's
  command is a split and a hold in one, and the hold belongs to a clip
  that did not exist before it. Here the split is its own command
  (`film.clip.split`) and the hold is a fact about a clip that is
  already there: **one command per thing**.
- **The tree's hold has five ways to be named** — the in point, the out
  point, the playhead, the sequence time and the source timecode — and
  every one of them is the same source frame by another route. Here
  there is one way: the frame itself.

### What it cost

- **Nine tests** in the film battery (`tests/hold.rs`): the clip holds
  the frame, the frame is a frame of the media, a frame outside the
  media is refused, a frame past the material is refused, a locked
  track refuses the hold, the hold may be taken away and may not be
  taken away twice, and the two edges of the trim of a held clip move
  the clip and not the media.
- **Two new commands**: `film.clip.hold` and `film.clip.hold.delete`.
  The film battery now carries **23** commands and the MCP server
  **383**.
- **One rule changed** in the trim: the media bound does not apply to a
  held clip, because the tree's `media_len` is nothing for one.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's frame hold options are not here**: the tree may hold
  the frame at the in point, the out point, the playhead, the sequence
  time or the source timecode, and it snaps the hold to the frame
  rate. Here the frame is given as a number.
- **The tree's hold filters are not here**: the tree's `hold_filters`
  says whether the filters keep running over the held frame. Here the
  hold is the picture alone.
- **The tree's insert-frame-hold-segment is not here**: the tree may
  insert a new clip that holds a frame for so many seconds. Here a
  clip that holds a frame is a clip that is already there, and making
  one is a clip that is added.

## 302. The transitions of a split

§293 gave the film battery the **transitions** of a track. §300 gave it
the **split** of a linked group. This is where the two meet: a cut
through a clip has to answer for the transitions that sit over it.

### What was built

- A split moves the **transitions that follow it**: a transition that
  begins at or after the cut now joins the piece after the cut.
- The split **says** which transitions it moved, so that an agent
  driving it does not have to go looking.

### What the port found

- **The tree's rule is about the transition's start, and not about the
  cut it sits on.** The tree's `split_track_at` moves a transition
  whose `start` is at or after the cut and that names the split clip as
  its **outgoing** side. A transition that **spans** the cut — its
  span covers it — keeps the piece before it, and the two clips it
  joins are then no longer next to each other. The tree allows that,
  and so does this tree.
- **The tree's removal of a spanning transition is for the fades to
  nothing.** The tree's `retain` drops a transition that spans the cut
  and names the split clip only when it does **not** join two clips —
  that is, a fade in from nothing or a fade out to nothing. Every
  transition in this tree joins two clips, so here nothing is taken
  away. The tree's own sentence — *a transition spanning the cut on
  this clip's interior is removed* — is about the fades, and the
  earlier draft of this README said it was about every transition,
  which was wrong.
- **Only the outgoing side moves.** The tree rewrites `from` and never
  `to`: a transition that ends at the split clip still ends at the
  piece before the cut, because that is where the cut it sits on now
  is.

### What it cost

- **Six tests** in the film battery (`tests/split_transitions.rs`): a
  transition after the cut joins the piece after it, a transition that
  spans the cut keeps the piece before it, a transition that ends at
  the clip is not moved, a transition of another cut is not touched,
  the transitions of a linked group follow the cut on every track, and
  the split says which transitions it moved.
- **No new command**: this is what `film.clip.split` does. The film
  battery still carries **23** commands and the MCP server **383**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's fades to nothing are not here**, so the tree's rule that
  takes away a transition spanning the cut has nothing to take away.
- **The tree's trim does not move the transitions here**: the tree
  keeps a transition within the clips it joins after a trim, and it
  moves them when a ripple or a speed change moves the cut. Here only
  the split moves them.
- **The tree's transitions carry a kind of their own** — a registry of
  them — and this tree has the one the tree's default names.

## 303. The average of the points of a path

The tree's average puts the **selected** points of a path on one line,
in one column, or all in one place. It is a small thing, and it is
here because it says something about what this tree does with a
selection.

### What was built

- The **average** of the points of a path: the command
  `vector.path.average` puts the points that are given on one line
  (`horizontal`), in one column (`vertical`), or all in one place
  (`both`, which is the default).
- The points are given **one per line**, as `contour:point`, because
  this tree has no selection: a range is a fact and a selection is
  not.
- The **handles** move with the point they belong to, as they do in the
  tree.

### What the port found

- **The tree's average is a command about the selection, and this
  tree's is a command about the points.** The tree's `path.average`
  works on the anchors that are directly selected, across **several**
  paths at once: it gathers their positions, works out the mean, and
  moves each anchor to it. Here the points are a **parameter**, one
  path per command, because a command works on one node.
- **The tree's unknown axis is `both`, and says nothing about it.** The
  tree's handler matches `horizontal` and `vertical` and falls through
  to the centre for everything else — so a typo is a different edit
  and no warning. Here an axis that is not an axis is **refused**.
- **The tree's average of nothing is nothing.** The tree gathers the
  points, and if there are none it returns without editing anything —
  a command that did nothing and said nothing. Here there is nothing
  to average and that is **refused**.
- **The tree's average does not move the handles of a point it did
  not average**, and neither does this one: a point carries its two
  handles, and the handles of an averaged point move with it.

### What it cost

- **Ten tests** in the vector battery (`tests/average.rs`): the three
  axes, the axis that is left out, the handles that move with the
  point, an axis that is not an axis, a line that is not a point, a
  point that is not there, no points at all, and the same point twice.
- **One new command**: `vector.path.average`. The vector battery now
  carries **32** commands and the MCP server **384**.
- **One rule of the SDK's**: the parameter kinds are number, text,
  bool, node, document and either — and there is no list. So the points
  are one **text**, one point to a line.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's average of several paths at once is not here**: a
  command works on one path, so averaging points of two paths is two
  commands and not one.
- **The tree's other point commands are not here**: the tree's
  `path.convertAnchors` turns the direct-selected points into corner
  or smooth points, and its `path.deleteAnchors` takes them away.

## 304. The removal of a page

The PDF battery could take an **object** away; it could not take a
**page** away. A page is not only an object: it is a page of the tree
of pages, and everything that pointed at it has to stop pointing at it.

### What was built

- The command `pdf.page.remove` takes a **page** away: the node goes,
  the **tree of pages** is right afterwards, and the **destinations**
  that went to the page go with it.
- The **count** of the children of the tree of pages is **derived**:
  it is worked out from the edges that are left, and not kept.
- The **last page** cannot go: a file with no pages is not a file.

### What the port found

- **The tree's destination goes whole.** The tree's
  `drop_destinations_to` looks at the bookmarks and at the link
  annotations of the pages that stay, and for each of them: a `/Dest`
  that goes to a page that is gone loses its key, and a `/A` that is a
  `GoTo` whose `/D` goes to a page that is gone loses its key. Half a
  destination is not a destination — the tree does not leave a lonely
  `Fit` behind where the destination was. This tree's rule for taking
  an **object** away is the plain one: a list loses the one element
  that names the object, and the rest of the list stays, so a
  destination would have been left broken. The page rule is the
  tree's.
- **The tree's rule is about the holders it names**, and here it is
  about every dictionary: the tree looks at the bookmarks and at the
  links of the pages that stay; this tree looks at every object and
  every stream that has a `/Dest` or an `/A`. The same rule, and more
  of the file.
- **The tree frees the number of the page.** The tree's `free` marks
  the object number as free and its generation one higher, and the
  file writes that number as a free entry, so that the numbers of the
  file do not move. Here the number is free the moment the object
  goes, and a new object may take it: this tree has no pool of freed
  numbers and no generation to raise.
- **The tree rebuilds the tree of pages.** The tree's rebuild moves
  the attributes a page inherits — the media box, the resources, the
  crop box, the rotation — down into the pages that are left and takes
  them out of the root, so that the root says nothing but the tree.
  Here the attributes stay where they are, and the pages that are left
  inherit them as they did.
- **The tree's form fields leave the form.** The tree takes the
  widgets of a page that is gone out of the form, so that a field
  does not point at a page that is not there. Here they stay: an
  annotation of a page that is gone is an object of its own, and it
  stays — which is the rule this tree already had for a removed
  object, and the tree's rule is the better one.
- **The tree takes several pages at once.** The tree's `delete_pages`
  takes a list of indices and refuses the whole list when it would
  leave no pages. Here a command takes one page, so several pages are
  several commands.

### What it cost

- **Eight tests** in the PDF battery (`tests/page_removal.rs`): a page
  may be taken away, the last page cannot go, the tree of pages is
  right afterwards, a destination that went to the page goes with it,
  an action that goes to the page goes with it, what the page held
  stays, a node that is not a page is refused, and a page that is not
  there is refused.
- **One new command**: `pdf.page.remove`. The PDF battery now carries
  **21** commands and the MCP server **385**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's form fields do not leave the form here** — and they do
  now (§307): the widgets of a page that is gone stay in the document
  and in the form.
- **The tree's rebuild is not here**: the attributes that a page
  inherits stay with the tree of pages and are not moved down.
- **The tree's freed numbers are not here**: there is no pool of them
  and no generation, so a number that is free may be taken by a new
  object.
- **Several pages at once are not here**: one command, one page.

## 305. The removal of an anchor

The vector battery could add an anchor to a segment. It could not take
one away, and taking one away is not the same thing as not adding it:
the contour has to answer for the gap.

### What was built

- The command `vector.path.anchor.remove` takes an **anchor** away.
- The segments that touch it go with it, and the contour becomes the
  **stretches** that are left: a closed contour is a cycle and stays
  one stretch, an open contour is a line of points and becomes the two
  stretches on either side of the gap.
- A stretch with fewer than two points is not a stretch, and it is
  gone.

### What the port found

- **The tree's rule is about the stretches and not about the points.**
  The tree removes the selected anchors *and* the segments that touch
  them, and then keeps the surviving stretches **separate** rather
  than joining across the gap: the path does not heal over the hole.
  A stretch that is left with fewer than two anchors is dropped, so a
  contour may go entirely.
- **A closed contour is a cycle, and it stays one stretch.** The tree's
  closed contour has an explicit closing segment, and taking an anchor
  out of the cycle leaves one path — not two. This tree's closed
  contour has no closing segment: the closing is **implicit**, and it
  is a straight line. So the cut makes that edge explicit, and it is a
  straight line here as well.
- **The tree's handles at the ends of a stretch are cleared.** The tree
  clears the dangling handles of the first and the last anchor of a
  stretch, because a handle that leads nowhere is not a handle. Here
  the handles belong to the segments and not to the points, so the
  segments that went took their handles with them and there is nothing
  left to clear.
- **The tree's anchor is a selection.** The tree's `path.deleteAnchors`
  works on the anchors that are directly selected, and it also handles
  a whole path that was caught by a marquee. Here the anchor is a
  **parameter**, because this tree has no selection: a range is a fact
  and a selection is not.

### What it cost

- **Ten tests** in the vector battery (`tests/anchor_remove.rs`): an
  anchor may be taken away, a closed contour stays one stretch, an
  open contour splits into two, the points that survive keep their
  places, a closed contour is open afterwards, a contour with one
  point is gone, the segments that survive keep their shape, and three
  refusals.
- **One new command**: `vector.path.anchor.remove`. The vector battery
  now carries **33** commands and the MCP server **386**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's other anchor commands are not here**: its
  `path.convertAnchors` turns the selected points into corner points
  or into smooth ones, and its `path.removeAnchor` takes one point
  away by its own name — the two are the same edit here, because this
  tree has one command for one thing.
- **The tree's segment pick is not here**: a segment that is picked may
  be cut on its own, keeping every curve around it.
- **The tree's marquee is not here**, and with it the removal of a
  whole path that a marquee caught.

## 306. The transitions of a trim

A transition joins two clips, and it may not leave them. So a trim
that makes a clip shorter has to answer for the transitions that join
it: the tree brings them back inside the clips they join.

### What was built

- A **trim** brings the transitions that join the trimmed clip back
  inside the two clips they join, and it **shortens** a transition when
  the clips are now shorter than it.
- The **alignment** is worked out again from where the transition ends
  up: one that starts at the cut starts at it, one that ends at the cut
  ends at it, and any other is centred.

### What the port found

- **The tree's rule is a bound and not a move.** The tree's
  `keep_within_clips` leaves a transition alone when it is already
  inside the two clips, and otherwise does two things: the duration
  becomes the shorter of the transition's duration and the length of
  the two clips together, and the start is brought back inside them.
  So the transition is shortened first and moved second, and a
  transition that is longer than the clips together is cut down to
  their length.
- **The tree works the alignment out again.** The tree stores the
  alignment as one of *starts at the cut*, *ends at the cut* and
  *centred at the cut*, and after a trim it reads the transition's new
  place and writes the alignment that place says. A transition that
  lands somewhere else is *centred* — the tree has no other variant
  for a transition between two clips.
- **The tree's rule is about the two clips and not about the gap.** The
  bounds are the first clip's start and the second clip's end, so a
  gap between the two clips is inside the bounds and the transition
  may lie across it. The tree's regular trim cannot move a cut, so the
  cut of a transition between two clips does not move either.
- **The tree's other edits move the transitions as well.** The tree's
  `transitions_follow_cuts` shifts a transition by as much as its cut
  moved, after a ripple trim, a roll, a slide and a ripple speed
  change. Here the trim moves the clip and nothing else — there is no
  ripple here — so only the bound applies.

### What it cost

- **Six tests** in the film battery (`tests/trim_transitions.rs`): a
  transition that reaches past the clips is moved back inside them, a
  transition that is too long is shortened, the alignment is worked out
  again, a transition that fits is left alone, a transition of another
  cut is not touched, and a transition that starts at the cut keeps
  that.
- **No new command**: this is what `film.clip.trim` does. The film
  battery still carries **23** commands and the MCP server **386**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's ripple is not here**, so the transitions do not follow a
  cut that moves: only the bound is here.
- **The tree's fades to nothing are not here**, so the tree's rule
  that a one-sided fade follows the edge of its clip has nothing to
  follow.
- **The tree's speed change does not move the transitions here**: a
  clip that gets shorter because its speed changed keeps its
  transitions as they are.

## 307. The widgets of a page that is gone

§304 took a page away. The tree does more: it takes the **fields** of
that page out of the **form**, because a field that points at a page
that is not there keeps that page — with its content — in the file that
is written.

### What was built

- The **widgets** of a page that is gone **leave the form**: a widget
  is taken out of the field that holds it, or out of the form's fields
  when the widget is a field itself.
- A field left with **no children** leaves the form as well: it is
  taken out of the field that holds it, or out of the form.
- The widget itself **stays** in the document: it is an object of its
  own, and an object that nothing refers to any more is still an
  object.

### What the port found

- **The tree's reason is the file and not the document.** The tree
  says it in one sentence: *the deleted pages go for good — bookmarks,
  links and widgets that still point at one would otherwise keep it,
  with its content, in the saved file*. So the widget leaves the form
  because of what the **file** would carry, and not because of what
  the document holds.
- **The tree's field that is left with no children goes as well.** The
  tree's `drop_widgets` unlinks the widget from the field's `/Kids`,
  and when the field's children are all gone the field is unlinked in
  turn — from the field above it, or from the form. So the chain of
  fields empties upwards, one field at a time.
- **The tree's widget is not freed.** The tree frees the **page** and
  its number; the widget objects stay in the document as objects that
  nothing refers to any more. That is the rule this tree already had
  for a removed object, and it is the tree's rule too.
- **The tree's form may be a dictionary inside the catalog.** The tree
  resolves the root's `AcroForm`, and it may be a reference to an
  object or a dictionary in the root itself. Here the form is an
  object of its own, and the catalog names it.

### What it cost

- **Four tests** in the PDF battery (`tests/page_widgets.rs`): the
  widget of a page that is gone leaves the form, a field left with no
  children leaves the form, the widgets of a page that stays are not
  touched, and a file with no form is not troubled.
- **No new command**: this is what `pdf.page.remove` does. The PDF
  battery still carries **21** commands and the MCP server **386**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's widget objects are not freed**: they stay in the
  document, with their content and their appearance.
- **The tree's form inside the catalog is not here**: the form is an
  object of its own here.
- **The tree's fields that are not widgets are not here**: a field
  that a page does not hold is not touched, because a page does not
  hold it.

## 308. The corner of a point

A point with handles on it is a curve. A point with its handles pulled
back to it is a **corner**, and the two sides leave it as straight
lines. The tree's smooth point was here; the corner was not.

### What was built

- The command `vector.path.corner` makes a point of a path a
  **corner**: the handles at the point are pulled back to it, and the
  two sides leave it as straight lines.
- The handles at the **other ends** of those sides are not touched:
  they belong to other points.
- A point with **no handles** is refused: it is a corner already.

### What the port found

- **The tree's command is one command for two things.** The tree's
  `path.convertAnchors` takes a `to` that says `corner` or `smooth`,
  and does one or the other. This tree has one command for each: the
  smooth one was `vector.path.smooth` and the corner one is
  `vector.path.corner`. One command per thing.
- **The tree's corner is the handles pulled back to the point.** The
  tree's `retract` sets the point's two handles to the point itself,
  and the segments on either side become straight lines. The handles at
  the other ends of those segments are untouched — they belong to the
  other points.
- **The tree's smooth is not the same rule.** The tree's
  `smooth_anchor` puts the handles along the line from the previous
  point to the next one, a third of the way to each; a corner is the
  opposite of that, and the two are the two halves of one idea: where
  the handles are says whether the point is a corner or a curve.
- **The tree does nothing when there is nothing to do.** The tree's
  command on a point that is already a corner changes nothing and says
  nothing. Here a point with no handles is **refused**, as the smooth
  command refuses a point with no handles to smooth.

### What it cost

- **Six tests** in the vector battery (`tests/corner.rs`): the handles
  at the point are pulled back, the handles at the other ends are not
  touched, the point does not move, and three refusals.
- **One new command**: `vector.path.corner`. The vector battery now
  carries **34** commands and the MCP server **387**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's selection is not here**: the tree's command works on
  every selected point at once, and here a command works on one point.
- **The tree's anchor kind is not here**: the tree remembers whether
  an anchor is a corner or a smooth one, and this tree's points do not
  carry that — the handles say it.

## 309. The currency of a cell

The tree's format is a whole language, and a **currency** is one of
the things in it. This tree's number formats were a grammar without a
symbol in it.

### What was built

- A cell may have a **currency**: a number with a **symbol** on it.
  The symbol is a literal in **quotes**, as the tree writes it:
  `"$"#,##0.00`, or `#,##0.00" kr"` with the symbol behind the
  number.
- The **sign** is in front of the symbol, and the thousands are
  separated when the format says so.

### What the port found

- **The tree's currency is not a renderer.** The tree asks what a
  format *is* before it renders it, and the answer is a currency when
  the number section has a currency flag and some digits. The
  rendering is then the ordinary number rendering with the literal in
  it. So the tree's currency is a number format **plus a literal**, and
  not a shape of its own.
- **The tree's symbol is a quoted literal.** The tree's own test says
  `"$"#,##0.00` is a currency. The quotes are what make it a literal
  and not a placeholder — and the tree's literal may be anywhere in
  the code.
- **The tree's sign is in front of the literal.** A single-section
  format writes the minus sign before the code's own tokens, so a
  negative currency is `-` and then the symbol and then the number.
- **The tree's sections are not here.** A format with a second section
  for the negative numbers — `"$"#,##0.00;("$"#,##0.00)` — is not
  here, so the negative currency has a sign and not brackets. The tree
  says as much: a multi-section format never adds the minus sign
  itself.

### What it cost

- **Seven tests** in the grid battery (`tests/currency.rs`): the
  symbol and the number, the symbol behind the number, a currency with
  no decimals, a negative currency, the separated thousands, and two
  refusals.
- **No new command**: this is what `grid.cell.format` does. The grid
  battery still carries **17** commands and the MCP server **387**.
- **One rule of the number format was pulled out of the parser**: the
  shape of a number format — the decimals and the separated thousands
  — is now one function, and the currency uses it as well.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's sections are not here**: a currency with a second
  section for the negative numbers is not a currency this tree has.
- **The tree's literal may be anywhere in the code**: here the symbol
  is in front of the number or behind it.
- **The tree's accounting format is not here**: it is a currency in
  another shape, and the tree tells the two apart.

## 310. The sign of a number that rounds away

A negative number that rounds to zero is written **without its sign**.
The sign of a number that is not there is not written — and this tree
was writing it.

### What was built

- A negative number that **rounds to zero** is written without its
  sign: `-0.0033` with two decimals is `0.00` and not `-0.00`.
- A negative number that **rounds away from zero** keeps its sign:
  `-0.005` with two decimals is `-0.01`.
- The rule holds for the **currency** as well: a currency that rounds
  to zero has no sign.

### What the port found

- **The tree's rule is about the number that is written and not about
  the number that was given.** The tree's test says it in one line: *a
  negative number that rounds to zero shows no minus sign*. The sign
  belongs to the written number, and the written number is zero.
- **The tree's rounding is away from zero**, so the boundary is
  exact: `-0.005` with two decimals is `-0.01` — the sign is there,
  because the number that is written is not zero — and `-0.4` with no
  decimals is `0`, and `-0.5` is `-1`.
- **The tree's sign is a sign and not a section.** A format with a
  second section for the negative numbers writes the section's own
  text, and the tree says that a multi-section format never adds the
  minus sign itself. Here the sign is the sign, and it goes when the
  number is not there.

### What it cost

- **Six tests** in the grid battery (`tests/negative.rs`): a negative
  number that rounds to zero, one that rounds away, a whole number
  that rounds to zero, one that rounds away, one that is not near
  zero, and a currency that rounds to zero.
- **No new command**: this is what the number format does. The grid
  battery still carries **17** commands and the MCP server **387**.
- **One rule changed** in the number format and in the currency: the
  sign is written when the number that is written is not zero.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's sections are not here**: a format with a second section
  for the negative numbers is not a format this tree has, so the
  negative number is written with a sign and not with the section's own
  text.
- **The tree's scientific formats are not here**, and their sign is
  the tree's as well.

## 311. The styles of a workbook

The tree's format is a **style**, and a style is **shared**: a hundred
cells with one format carry one format. This tree's format was a field
of the cell, and a hundred cells with one format carried a hundred
formats. Now a cell may name a **style**.

### What was built

- A **style** is a named format of the **workbook**, and a cell may
  name one: the commands `grid.style.add`, `grid.style.set`,
  `grid.style.remove` and `grid.cell.style`.
- The format of a cell is **derived**: a cell that names a style is
  written with the style's format, and changing the style changes
  every cell that names it.
- The tree's rule that is here: a style whose format is *General* does
  not change the cell's format — the cell keeps its own.

### What the port found

- **The tree's style is a whole thing.** The tree's style carries the
  font, the fill, the border, the alignment and the number format, and
  the tree's cell holds a style. Here a style carries a **format** and
  nothing else, because a format is the only thing this tree writes on
  a cell.
- **The tree's named styles are built in.** The tree's `home.cellStyle`
  finds a style in a list of the tree's own — *Normal*, *Title*,
  *Explanatory Text*, *Comma*, *Currency*, *Percent* and the rest — or
  in the ones the file carries. Here a style is a style of the
  workbook, and it is **written**: added, changed and taken away.
- **The tree's style is found by its name and without regard to
  case.** The tree's `cell_style` compares the names with
  `eq_ignore_ascii_case`, so two styles whose names differ only in
  case are one style. Here a name that is taken is refused — and a
  name that is not there is refused as well, and never quietly
  ignored.
- **The tree's rule about the number format is the one that is here.**
  The tree's number-format styles — *Comma*, *Currency*, *Percent* —
  change the number format and nothing else; and a style whose number
  format is *General* leaves the cell's own number format alone. Here
  a style carries a format and nothing else, so the second half of the
  rule is the whole of it.

### What it cost

- **Eleven tests** in the grid battery (`tests/styles.rs`): a style may
  be added, a cell that names one is written with it, changing it
  changes every cell that names it, a style with a general format
  leaves the cell alone, a style that is taken away leaves the cell
  with its own format, an empty name means the cell has no style, and
  four refusals.
- **Four new commands**: `grid.style.add`, `grid.style.set`,
  `grid.style.remove` and `grid.cell.style`. The grid battery now
  carries **21** commands and the MCP server **391**.
- **One rule of the cell changed**: the format of a cell is now
  **derived** — the style's format when the cell names a style, and
  its own otherwise — and the cell text, the fill and the flash fill
  all read the derived one.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's style carries more than a format**: the font, the
  colour and the alignment are not here.
- **The tree's built-in styles are not here**: there is no *Normal* and
  no *Title*; a style is one the workbook has.
- **The tree's style is not written here by the tree**: the tree's
  styles come from the file and are applied by a command, and here a
  style is a fact of the workbook that three commands write.

## 312. The spatial path of a property

The tree's spatial property does not move along the straight line from
one keyframe to the next. It follows a **path** in the plane, and the
time maps to the **length** along that path. That is the whole of the
difference, and it is a large one: the property travels at the speed
of the path and not at the speed of the chord.

### What was built

- A property may be **spatial**: the command `fx.prop.spatial` sets
  the flag, and the value of a spatial property at a frame is the
  point on its **path** at that time.
- The **path** is a cubic through the two keyframes, with the **auto**
  tangents as its handles: a sixth of the way from the keyframe before
  to the keyframe after, and the key times play no part in it.
- The **length** of the path is worked out with a **table** — the
  curve is cut into ninety-six cells, the length of each cell is
  added up, and the point at a given length is found by walking the
  table and refining with Newton steps.
- The time maps to that length: the **eases** of the two sides say how
  fast the value is moving **along the path**, and the ease's speed is
  scaled by the time over the path's length.
- A property that is spatial needs **keyframes** and **points**: a
  value that is not a point, a property that is not animated, and a
  property whose keyframes are of two widths are all refused.

### What the port found

- **The tree's spatial property is a motion path, and the time is a
  length.** The tree does not interpolate the two points; it walks the
  path, and the fraction of the segment is a fraction of the path's
  length. So the property is *behind* the straight line at the middle
  of a curved segment — it has covered half the **path**, and half
  the path is more than half the chord.
- **The tree's tangents are the auto ones, and they ignore the time.**
  The out tangent is a sixth of the way from the keyframe **before** to
  the keyframe **after**, and the in tangent is its mirror; the times
  play no part. A keyframe at the end of the list uses the one
  neighbour it has, so the path leaves the first keyframe and enters
  the last one.
- **The tree's path is measured, not parameterised.** The tree cuts
  the curve into cells and adds up the length of each with a
  five-point Gauss-Legendre rule, and then finds the point at a given
  length by refining the cell's linear guess with Newton steps on the
  true length. The position is smooth along a curved path and not
  piecewise linear per cell — and that smoothness is the reason the
  tree does it this way.
- **The tree's straight path is the chord itself.** When both control
  points lie on the chord, the tree interpolates the line exactly
  instead of walking the table, so a property on a line is not
  slightly off it.
- **The tree's ease of a spatial side is a speed along the path.** A
  linear side is the length of the path over the time it takes, and a
  third; and the speed of the ease is divided by the path's length,
  because the ease says how fast the value moves and the path is
  longer than the chord.
- **The tree's spatial is a property of the value, not of the
  property.** The tree decides a keyframe is spatial by looking at
  whether its value is a pair or a triple of numbers. Here the
  property carries the flag, and the command refuses to set it on a
  property whose keyframes are not points — so the two agree, and the
  disagreement is caught rather than ignored.

### What it cost

- **Twelve tests** in the fx battery (`tests/spatial.rs`): a straight
  path is the chord, the ends of the path are the keyframes' own
  values, a path that turns leaves the chord, the time maps to the
  length of the path, the flag is what makes the path, the flag is
  kept, the flag is cleared, and five refusals — a property that is
  not animated, a value that is not a point, keyframes of two widths,
  a property that is not there, and a triple that is a point too.
- **One new command**: `fx.prop.spatial`. The fx battery now carries
  **11** commands and the MCP server **392**.
- **One new module** (`src/spatial.rs`): the cubic, its table, the
  auto tangents, the chord test and the progress of a segment.
- **The keyframe's value is visible to the crate.** The command that
  sets the flag has to look at the keyframes' values, and the keyframe
  is the module's own, so the field is `pub(crate)` now.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's spatial tangents may be written down.** The tree keeps
  a keyframe's spatial tangents and uses them when the keyframe is not
  an **auto** one, and its graph shows handles that may be dragged into
  a curve. Here every path has auto tangents and there is no command
  that writes them down.
- **The tree's roving keys are not here.** The tree re-times the
  keyframes of a run so that the speed along the path is even, and
  that is a different edit from the one that moves a keyframe.
- **The tree's velocity is not here**: the speed of a spatial property
  at a time, and the graph of it.
- **The path is in the value's own plane.** A pair or a triple is a
  point and a point has a path; a value of four numbers is not a
  point here and is refused.

## 313. The free numbers of a file

A PDF file numbers its objects, and a number that is not in use is
**free**. The file says which numbers are free, and the tree's rule is
the finding: a number that is taken away is **not given back**.

### What was built

- A number whose object is taken away is **free**: the commands
  `pdf.object.remove` and `pdf.page.remove` free it, and the file
  says so.
- A free number is **not used again**: the command `pdf.object.add`
  refuses a number that is free.
- The command `pdf.file.free` says which numbers are free, and what
  the **next** number is — the next number is past them all, because a
  free number is a number something had.
- The **table** that is written has a row for each free number, and a
  row for the number zero, which is always free.
- The **size** of the file that is written is the next number, and not
  the count of its objects.
- A file that is **loaded** keeps the free numbers it says.

### What the port found

- **The tree's free number is a slot, and a slot has a generation.**
  The tree frees a number by writing a slot that says *freed* with
  the generation **one more** than the number had, and the number is
  never used again: the tree's `next_num` only ever grows, and a
  freed number is a number something had.
- **The tree's free row is an offset of zero and a kind of `f`.** The
  classic table says the number is free with `0000000000 00001 f` —
  and the generation in the row is the generation the number gets if
  it is used again.
- **The tree writes the number zero as free, with the generation
  65535**, and the first row of the table is its own. Here the table
  had no row for the number zero at all, and a table whose first row
  is not the number zero is not the table the file's own rules ask
  for.
- **The tree's size is the next number.** The tree's trailer says
  `/Size` is `next_num` — the highest number in the file plus one —
  and not the count of the objects, because a file with a free number
  in it has more numbers than it has objects. Here the size was the
  count of the objects, which was wrong for every file whose numbers
  were not one after another.
- **The tree's free numbers are the incremental save's business.** The
  tree's full save renumbers the objects from one and writes only the
  ones that are reachable, so a full save has no free numbers at all;
  the free numbers are what an incremental save carries. Here the file
  is always written whole and keeps its own numbers, so the free
  numbers are written as they are.
- **The tree's free number may be used again.** The tree's `set` puts
  an object on a number that was free, and the number comes back with
  the generation the free row gave it. Here a free number is refused:
  a number that is free is not used again, and the file says so.

### What it cost

- **Ten tests** in the pdf battery (`tests/free_numbers.rs`): a file
  that is loaded keeps its free numbers, an object that is taken away
  frees its number, a page that is taken away frees its number, a
  free number is not used again, the next number is past the free
  ones, the table has a row for the free number, the number zero is
  free, the size of the file is the next number, the free number
  survives the round trip, and a number that is not free is not free.
- **One new command**: `pdf.file.free`. The pdf battery now carries
  **22** commands and the MCP server **393**.
- **The writer changed**: the table has a row for the number zero and
  a row for each free number, and the trailer's size is the next
  number.
- **Two claims of the battery were wrong, and are corrected here**:
  the module of the page said that the widgets of a page that is gone
  do not leave the form — they do, since the widgets came in — and the
  module of the filters said that the predictors are not here — they
  are, in the module of their own.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's incremental save is not here.** The file is written
  whole, with the numbers it has; a file that was saved again has one
  table and not two.
- **The tree's full save renumbers the objects** from one and writes
  only the ones that are reachable, so an object that nothing refers
  to any more is not in the file at all. Here every object is written,
  reachable or not.
- **The generation of a live object is not here.** Every object of
  this tree is written with the generation zero, so a number that is
  freed gets the generation one — the one after the generation it had.

## 314. The ripple of a speed change

A speed change makes a clip longer or shorter, and the space after it
may not be there. The tree has two ways out, and the second one is a
**ripple**: the clips that were after the clip move **up** by the
change in its length, and the time the clip took is time that is free.

### What was built

- The command `film.clip.speed` takes a **`ripple`**: the clips that
  were after the clip move up by the change in its length, and the
  track's material after the clip moves with it.
- The **transitions** follow the cuts: one whose cut moved moves with
  it, and one that no longer fits inside the two clips it joins is
  brought back inside them.
- Without a ripple the change is still **refused** when the clip
  would run into its neighbour.

### What the port found

- **The tree's first way out is a clamp, and a clamp is a quiet lie.**
  The tree bounds the new length by the space there is and takes the
  shorter length, so the clip's **speed** says one thing and its
  **length** says another, and nothing says that the length was not
  the one that was asked for. Here the change that does not fit is
  **refused**: the clip does not move at all, and the caller is told
  why.
- **The tree's ripple moves the clips that start at or after the OLD
  end of the clip that changed** — not the new one, and not the start
  of it. A clip that is still running when the change happens is left
  where it is.
- **The tree's ripple moves the sync-locked tracks as well.** The
  tracks that are **sync-locked** with the track that changed move
  with it, so that a group of tracks stays together, and the clips on
  them move by the same shift — one shift for all of them, and the
  largest of the changes when several clips changed at once. Here only
  the track the clip is on moves.
- **The tree's transitions follow the cuts by their anchor.** The tree
  works out how far each transition's anchor moved between the
  sequence before the change and the sequence after it, moves the
  transition by that much, and then keeps it inside the two clips it
  joins. Here the same: a transition whose cut moved moves with it,
  and one that no longer fits is brought back and shortened.
- **The tree refuses a ripple that would move later clips past the
  end of the timeline.** Here the length of a track is **derived** —
  it is the end of its last clip — so there is no end to pass, and the
  clips may move as far as they like.

### What it cost

- **Eight tests** in the film battery (`tests/speed_ripple.rs`): a
  change that does not fit is refused, a ripple moves the clips after
  it, the moved clips keep their length, a shorter clip moves them
  down, the clips before it do not move, the transitions follow the
  cuts, a transition that no longer fits is brought back, and a locked
  track refuses the ripple.
- **No new command**: `film.clip.speed` takes the `ripple`, and the
  film battery still carries **23** commands and the MCP server
  **393**.

### What it does not settle

- **The sync-locked tracks are not here**: a ripple moves the track
  the clip is on and no other.
- **The tree's end of the timeline is not here**: the length of a
  track is derived, so nothing refuses a change that moves a clip past
  the end of it.
- **The tree changes several clips at once.** The tree's command takes
  a list of clips and a group of them changes speed as one edit, and
  the ripple is one shift for all of them. Here one clip changes at a
  time.

## 315. The fraction of a cell

A number may be written as a **fraction**: not the decimals of the
number but a fraction that stands for it — a half, a third, an eighth.

### What was built

- A cell may carry a **fraction** format: `# ?/?`, `# ??/??`, `?/?` and
  `# ?/4` — a whole part, a numerator, a bar and a denominator.
- The fraction is the **nearest** one: the best rational number whose
  denominator is no bigger than the **limit**, found with continued
  fractions.
- The **limit** is what the code says: one digit of denominator is
  nine, and two are ninety-nine.
- A code may **name** the denominator: `# ?/4` is a quarter, and the
  fraction is written with that denominator.
- The **whole** part is written beside the fraction when there is one,
  and a whole number is written as a whole number.

### What the port found

- **The nearest fraction is not the closest one.** The tree takes the
  **semiconvergent**: the best of the two ends of the last step of the
  continued fraction, because the best fraction with a denominator no
  bigger than the limit is often one step short of the next
  convergent. So `0.3` with a limit of nine is **2/7** and not `1/3`:
  the error of the second is bigger.
- **The limit is the number of the denominator's placeholders.**
  `10^digits - 1`: one digit is nine, two are ninety-nine, and the
  tree takes the last seven digits of a denominator that has more.
- **The numerator may be bigger than the denominator, and is then
  carried into the whole part.** `0.99` with a limit of nine is the
  whole number **1** — the fraction is below one, so the whole part
  takes the rest.
- **A named denominator is not reduced.** `0.5` with `?/8` is
  **`4/8`** and not `1/2`: the code names the denominator and the
  fraction is written with it.
- **The tree's sign is dropped when the number is written as zeros**,
  which is the same rule the fixed formats have: the sign of a number
  that is not there is not written.
- **The tree pads the fraction to its placeholders.** The `?`
  placeholders leave blanks where a part is hidden and the `0`
  placeholders pad with zeros, so the tree writes `" 1/4"` and
  `"3 14/99"`. Here the parts are written as they are.

### What it cost

- **Fourteen tests** in the grid battery (`tests/fractions.rs`): the
  nearest fraction, the whole part beside it, a whole number, zero,
  the numerator carrying the whole value, the limit the placeholders
  say, the nearest fraction being the best one, a named denominator
  used as it is, a named denominator with a whole part, the sign of a
