  tree's indents are clamped to between minus fifteen hundred and
  eighty-four points and its spacing to between zero and the same, and
  a number outside the range is quietly brought into it. Here a number
  outside the range is **refused**, and the refusal says the range.
- **The tree's indents cancel the character indents and this tree's
  do not.** The tree's `cancel_char_indents` reaches into the
  characters of the paragraph and undoes the letter-by-letter
  indents. Here a paragraph's runs carry a length, a bold and an
  italic, and there is no character indent to cancel — so there is
  nothing to cancel.
- **The tree's alignment has a word for each edge and this tree's has
  the tree's words.** The tree refuses an alignment it does not know,
  and so does this one, and the refusal says what they are.

### What it cost

- **Ten tests** in the prose battery (`tests/paragraphs.rs`): a
  paragraph being told how it stands, the logical edges being the
  tree's own, an alignment that is not one being refused, a paragraph
  being indented, an indent out of range being refused, a paragraph
  having space around it, a space out of range being refused, a table
  not being a paragraph, a node that is not there being refused, and
  the properties being saved.
- **Three new commands**: `prose.block.paragraph.align`,
  `prose.block.paragraph.indent` and `prose.block.paragraph.spacing`.
  The prose battery now carries **13** commands and the MCP server
  **451**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's line spacing is not here.** The tree's spacing of the
  lines inside a paragraph is a multiple, or a minimum, or an exact
  number of points, and it is a thing of its own. Here the space
  around a paragraph is here and the space between its lines is not.
- **The tree's character indents are not here.** The tree may indent
  the characters of a run — a letter at a time — and its paragraph
  indents cancel them. Here a run carries a length, a bold and an
  italic, and the indents of a paragraph are the paragraph's own.

## 345. The hiding of a row and a column

A row may be **hidden** and a column may be hidden, and a hidden one is
still there: its cells are still there, they still hold what they hold,
and they are still worked out. The tree's hidden row is not a row that
is gone; it is a row that is not shown.

### What was built

- The command `grid.row.hide` hides a row and the command
  `grid.row.show` shows it again.
- The command `grid.column.hide` hides a column and the command
  `grid.column.show` shows it again.
- A row or a column that is **already** hidden may not be hidden again
  and one that is **not** hidden may not be shown: a command that does
  nothing did not do anything.

### What the port found

- **The tree's hidden row is a flag on the row and this tree's is a
  list on the sheet.** The tree's sheet carries a line of information
  for every row, hidden or not, and the hidden flag is on that line.
  Here a sheet carries the **list** of the rows that are hidden and the
  list of the columns that are hidden, and a row that is not on the
  list is shown.
- **The tree's hidden row has its own size.** The tree's row of no
  height is a hidden row, and the tree's height command and its hide
  command are two ways of saying the same thing. Here they are not: a
  size of nothing is **refused** (§343) and the hiding is a fact of
  its own.
- **The tree's `SUBTOTAL` leaves the hidden rows out and this tree's
  formulas do not.** The tree's `SUBTOTAL` skips the hidden rows when
  the function number says so, and its `SUM` does not. This tree has
  no `SUBTOTAL` — so nothing here changes what a formula reads, and a
  hidden row is a row that is not shown and that is all it is.

### What it cost

- **Twelve tests** in the grid battery (`tests/hiding.rs`): a row
  being hidden, a hidden row still being a row, a row that is already
  hidden refused, a hidden row being shown, a row that is not hidden
  refused, a column being hidden and shown, a column that is already
  hidden refused, a column that is not hidden refused, a column that is
  not a column refused, a row that is not there refused, a node that is
  not a sheet refused, and the hiding being saved.
- **Four new commands**: `grid.row.hide`, `grid.row.show`,
  `grid.column.hide` and `grid.column.show`. The grid battery now
  carries **42** commands and the MCP server **455**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's `SUBTOTAL` is not here**, and it is the one thing that
  reads the hidden rows. It is a function of its own, with its own
  rules about the nested totals it leaves out, and it is not a
  function of this tree yet.
- **The tree hides a row and the rows above it.** The tree's
  `home.hideRows` hides the rows that are chosen and the tree's
  filter hides the rows that do not match. Here a row is hidden by
  itself, and a filter that hides rows is a thing this tree has not
  got.

## 346. The subtotal of a range

`SUBTOTAL` is the tree's own function: it sums a range the way a total
row does, and it leaves out what a total row leaves out. The tree
names it with a **function number**, and this tree does too — and the
hiding of a row (§345) is what makes it mean something.

### What was built

- The function `SUBTOTAL(code, range...)` in the grid's formula
  engine.
- The **hundred-and-more form** (`101` to `111`) leaves the hidden rows
  out as well; the plain form does not. That is the tree's own rule and
  not Excel's, and the tree's comment says so.
- A **nested subtotal** — a cell whose own formula holds a
  `SUBTOTAL(` — is left out, in both forms.
- The function numbers that this tree has are `1` (AVERAGE), `2`
  (COUNT), `3` (COUNTA), `4` (MAX), `5` (MIN) and `9` (SUM). A number
  that names a function this tree does not have is **refused**, and the
  refusal says what the numbers are.
- A subtotal may read **two ranges** and it may read a **name**.

### What the port found

- **The tree's rule is not Excel's rule.** The tree's `SUBTOTAL`
  leaves out the rows a **filter** hides whatever the function number,
  and the hundred-and-more form leaves out the rows hidden **by hand**
  as well. Excel does the opposite for the rows hidden by hand. This
  tree ports the tree: the hundred-and-more form leaves the hidden rows
  out and the plain form does not.
- **The tree's eleven function numbers are not all here.** The tree's
  `SUBTOTAL` can be a `PRODUCT`, a `STDEV`, a `STDEVP`, a `VAR` or a
  `VARP` — and this tree has none of those functions, so a subtotal
  that names one is refused and says so. The functions of this tree
  are the six the numbers stand for.
- **The tree's nested rule is a rule about the formula's text.** The
  tree leaves out a cell whose formula **contains** `SUBTOTAL(` or
  `AGGREGATE(` — anywhere in it, even inside a word — and so does
  this one. It is a rule about the text and not about what the formula
  means.

### What it cost

- **Ten tests** in the grid battery (`tests/subtotal.rs`): a subtotal
  summing a range, the hundred-and-more form leaving the hidden rows
  out, a nested subtotal being left out, the other functions working, a
  function number that is not one being refused, a function number out
  of range being refused, a subtotal with no range being refused, a
  subtotal reading two ranges, a subtotal reading a name, and the
  subtotal being saved.
- **The formula engine learned the hidden rows.** The book carries the
  hidden rows of each sheet, and the subtotal reads them.
- **No new command**: `SUBTOTAL` is a function and not a command, so
  the grid battery still carries **42** commands and the MCP server
  **455**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's `AGGREGATE` is not here.** It is the tree's other
  function over a range, with its own options — whether it skips
  errors, whether it skips hidden rows, whether it leaves out nested
  totals — and it is a function of its own.
- **The tree's filter is not here**, and so the rows a filter hides are
  not a thing this tree knows: a hidden row here is a row hidden by
  hand, and the subtotal leaves it out only in the hundred-and-more
  form.

## 347. The filter of a sheet

A filter is a **column** and a **criterion**, and the criterion is an
operation and a value: `B` is `>` `10`, and the rows whose `B` is not
more than ten are the rows the filter **hides**.

### What was built

- The command `grid.filter.set` filters a sheet by a column, and the
  command `grid.filter.clear` takes the filter away.
- The command `grid.filter.rows` says which rows the filter hides.
- The rows a filter hides are **derived**: they are worked out from the
  cells each time they are asked for, and they are not written down.
- The operation is one of the tree's own — `=`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`
  or `>=` — and a name that is not one of them is refused.
- The tree's `*` is a **wildcard**: `*abc*` is "contains abc" and
  `abc*` is "begins with abc".
- The comparison operations compare **numbers**, and a value that is
  not a number is refused when the filter is written; the equality
  operations compare the **text** of the cell, without case.
- A **subtotal** leaves the rows a filter hides out, whatever the
  function number — that is the tree's rule — and a plain `SUM` does
  not.

### What the port found

- **The tree's filter has many kinds of criterion and this one has
  one.** The tree's criterion may be a list of values, a pair of
  comparisons joined by and or or, a top-ten, an above-the-average or
  a colour. Here a criterion is **one** operation and **one** value —
  the pair of comparisons — and the other kinds are commands of their
  own when they come.
- **The tree's filter is over a range and this one's is over a
  column.** The tree's filter has a range and a criterion for each
  column of it. Here a sheet has **one** filter and it is over one
  column, and the rows it hides are the rows of the sheet.
- **The tree's comparison is Excel's and this one's is simpler.** The
  tree compares two numbers rounded to fifteen significant digits,
  treats an empty cell as zero, as `""` or as `FALSE` depending on
  the other side, and orders values of different kinds by rank. Here
  the comparison operations compare **numbers** — an empty cell is
  zero — and the equality operations compare the **text** of the cell,
  without case, with the tree's `*`.
- **The tree's filter and the tree's hiding are two facts.** The tree
  knows whether a row is hidden by a filter and whether it is hidden
  by hand, and its `SUBTOTAL` treats them differently. Here they are
  two facts too — a list of rows hidden by hand and a criterion — and
  the rows a filter hides are derived from the criterion.

### What it cost

- **Twelve tests** in the grid battery (`tests/filters.rs`): a filter
  hiding the rows that do not match, the rows being derived, the
  wildcard being the tree's, the text being compared without case, a
  subtotal leaving the filtered rows out, a sum not leaving them out,
  the filter being taken away, a sheet that is not filtered being
  refused, an operation that is not one being refused, a comparison
  with text being refused, a column that is not a column being
  refused, and the filter being saved.
- **The book carries the filters**, and the subtotal reads them.
- **Three new commands**: `grid.filter.set`, `grid.filter.clear` and
  `grid.filter.rows`. The grid battery now carries **45** commands
  and the MCP server **458**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's other criteria are not here.** A list of values, a
  top-ten, an above-the-average and a colour are four criteria of
  their own, and each of them is a command with its own rules.
- **The tree's sort is not here.** The tree may sort the rows of a
  filtered table, and the order of the rows is then a fact of the
  sheet. Here the rows are where they were put.

## 348. The switch of one effect

An effect on a layer may be switched **off** and leave its values
where they are: the tree's `effect.toggle`.

### What was built

- The command `fx.effect.toggle` switches one effect of a layer off or
  on, and the values of the effect stay where they are.
- With no value given the switch is **toggled** — the tree's own rule.
- An effect is **on** when it is put on a layer.
- The **effects that run** are derived: the ones that are enabled and
  the layer's own effects switch is on. The evaluator says how many
  there are.

### What the port found

- **The tree's instance has a group with an `enabled` flag and this
  tree's has a field.** The tree's effect instance is a property
  group with a uid, a label and an `enabled` flag, and the flag is
  what the tree's `effect.toggle` writes. Here the instance is a group
  in the property tree and the flag is a field of it — and the
  instance is addressed by its **number**, as the paths address it.
- **The tree's toggle takes the value or flips the flag, and this
  tree's does the same.** The tree's `effect.toggle` reads an optional
  `value` and flips the flag when there is none, and returns what the
  flag is now.

### What it cost

- **Nine tests** in the fx battery (`tests/toggle.rs`): an effect
  being on when it is put on, an effect being switched off with its
  values left in place, an effect with no value being toggled, the
  effects that run being derived, the layer's own switch saying
  whether they run, an effect that is not there being refused, an
  effect being counted from one, a node that is not a layer being
  refused, and the switch being saved.
- **One new command**: `fx.effect.toggle`. The fx battery now carries
  **24** commands and the MCP server **459**.
- The **switches evaluator** says how many of a layer's effects run.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's reorder of the stack is not here.** The tree may move
  an effect up or down the stack, and the tree's instance has a uid so
  that moving it does not move what addresses it. Here the instance is
  addressed by its number, and a reorder has to say what it does to
  the paths — which is why it is not here yet.
- **The tree's duplicate and reset of an instance are not here**
  either: they are commands on an instance and they come with the
  reorder.

## 349. The line spacing of a paragraph

The space **around** a paragraph is here (§344) and the space
**between** its lines was not: the tree's spacing is one of three
things — a **multiple** of single spacing, a **minimum** number of
points, or an **exact** number of points.

### What was built

- The command `prose.block.paragraph.linespacing` says how the lines of
  a paragraph are spaced.
- Only **one** of the three may be said: a spacing of nothing is
  refused and a spacing of more than one is refused.
- A number outside the tree's own range is **refused**: a multiple is
  between 0.06 and 132, a minimum of points is between 0 and 1584, and
  an exact number of points is between 0.7 and 1584.

### What the port found

- **The tree clamps the numbers and this tree refuses them.** The
  tree's `line_spacing` clamps each of the three into its own range
  and says nothing about it. Here a number outside the range is
  **refused**, and the refusal says the range.
- **The tree takes the three in an order and this tree takes one.**
  The tree's command reads `atLeast`, then `exactly`, and takes a
  multiple when neither is there — so a call with two of them keeps
  the first. Here a call with two of them is **refused**, because a
  spacing that is two things is not a spacing.
- **The tree's spacing is one enum and this tree's is one field with
  a kind.** The tree's `LineSpacing` is a multiple, a minimum or an
  exact number, and it is written down as such. Here the paragraph
  carries the kind and the number, and the kind is one of the tree's
  three names.

### What it cost

- **Nine tests** in the prose battery (`tests/linespacing.rs`): the
  lines being spaced by a multiple, by a minimum and by an exact
  number, a spacing of nothing refused, a spacing of more than one
  refused, a multiple out of range refused, a minimum and an exact out
  of range refused, a table not being a paragraph, and the spacing
  being saved.
- **One new command**: `prose.block.paragraph.linespacing`. The prose
  battery now carries **14** commands and the MCP server **460**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's character spacing is not here.** The tree may space
  the characters of a run — a letter at a time — and the tree's
  paragraph indents cancel it. Here a run carries a length, a bold and
  an italic, and there is no character spacing to cancel.
- **The tree's reading view has its own spacing** — the spacing the
  reader sees, which is not the spacing of the document — and that is
  the state of the view and not a fact of the document.

## 350. The conditional formats of a sheet

A **conditional format** is a **range** of cells, a **criterion** and a
**format**: the cells of the range whose value matches the criterion are
written with that format. It is the tree's conditional formatting
without the colours.

### What was built

- The command `grid.conditional.set` puts a conditional format on a
  range, and the command `grid.conditional.clear` takes one away.
- The command `grid.conditional.check` says which cells a range's
  conditional format holds for, and the cells are **derived**: they are
  worked out from the cells each time they are asked for.
- The criterion is the **same** one the filter of a sheet uses (§347) —
  an operation and a value, with the tree's `*` as a wildcard — and an
  operation that is not one of the tree's own is refused.
- The format is one of the tree's own **number formats**, and a format
  that is not a format is refused.
- A range may have **one** conditional format: a second one for the
  same range replaces the first.
- The conditional format is **on top** of the cell's own format: the
  cell is written with the conditional format when it matches, and with
  its own otherwise.

### What the port found

- **The tree's rule is a style and this one's is a format.** The
  tree's conditional format carries a style — a fill, a font colour, an
  icon set — and a style is shared between cells. Here it carries a
  **number format**, which is a cell's own thing in this tree.
- **The tree's criteria are many and this one's is one.** The tree's
  rule may be a comparison, a colour scale, a data bar, an icon set or
  an expression. Here a rule is a **comparison** — the same criterion
  the filter uses — and the other kinds are commands of their own when
  they come.
- **The tree's rules are ordered and the first that matches wins.**
  The tree's rules are in a list and it walks them in order. Here they
  are in a list too, and the **first** one that matches the cell is the
  one that writes it.
- **The tree's conditional format wins over the cell's own format, and
  so does this one.** In the tree the conditional format's style is
  drawn on top of the cell's own; here the number format that writes
  the cell is the conditional one when it matches.

### What it cost

- **Eleven tests** in the grid battery (`tests/conditional.rs`): a
  conditional format writing the cells that match, the cells being
  derived, the conditional format being on top, a cell outside the
  range not being written, a second format for a range replacing the
  first, a conditional format being taken away, a range with no
  conditional format being refused, a range that is not a range being
  refused, an operation that is not one being refused, a format that is
  not a format being refused, and the conditional format being saved.
- **The criterion is now a thing of its own.** The filter's criterion
  and the conditional format's criterion are the same type, and the
  filter says so.
- **Three new commands**: `grid.conditional.set`,
  `grid.conditional.clear` and `grid.conditional.check`. The grid
  battery now carries **48** commands and the MCP server **463**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's colours are not here.** A conditional format in the
  tree is a fill and a font colour and an icon set, and this tree's
  grid has number formats and no colours — so a rule that says "this
  cell is red" has no place to say it.
- **The tree's colour scales, data bars and icon sets are not here**,
  and neither is its **expression** rule: a rule that is a formula
  judged for every cell of the range.

## 351. The other commands on an effect

An effect on a layer has three more commands of its own: its
parameters may be put back to their **defaults**, it may be **copied**,
and it may be **moved** in the stack.

### What was built

- The command `fx.effect.reset` puts the parameters of an effect back
  to their defaults, and it is **refused** when a parameter carries
  **keyframes**: the reset would lose them.
- The command `fx.effect.duplicate` copies an effect, and the copy
  goes **right after** the one it is a copy of and holds the same
  values.
- The command `fx.effect.reorder` moves an effect in the stack, and a
  place that is **not there** is refused — the tree clamps it and says
  nothing. The answer says which number the effect is now, because the
  paths address an effect by its number.
- An effect that is already in that place may not be moved: a command
  that does nothing did not do anything.

### What the port found

- **The tree's instance has a uid and this tree's has its number.** The
  tree's instance is a group with a uid, so moving it in the stack
  does not move what addresses it. Here the instance is addressed by
  its **number** — `effects/#2/radius` — so a move changes what a
  path says, and the answer says which number the effect is now.
- **The tree's reset keys the value and keeps the keys.** The tree's
  `effect.reset` writes the value at the layer's current time and
  leaves the keys where they are. This tree has no current time in a
  command, so a reset of an animated parameter would lose the keys —
  and it is **refused** and says so.
- **The tree's duplicate gives the copy a new uid and a unique name.**
  Here the copy is a copy of the group: the same effect, the same
  values and the same switch, and the paths say which number it is.

### What it cost

- **Eleven tests** in the fx battery (`tests/instance.rs`): the
  parameters being reset, a reset that would lose the keyframes
  refused, an effect being copied, the copy going right after, an
  effect being moved, a move saying where the effect is now, a place
  that is not there refused, an effect that is already there refused,
  an effect that is not there refused, a node that is not a layer
  refused, and the commands being saved.
- **Three new commands**: `fx.effect.reset`, `fx.effect.duplicate` and
  `fx.effect.reorder`. The fx battery now carries **27** commands and
  the MCP server **466**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's effects are applied in an order and this tree's order is
  the order of the list** — and nothing here *renders* it, so the
  order is a fact and not a picture.
- **The tree's own colours are not here** (§350), and neither are its
  other kinds of rule.

## 352. The marks of a media

A **media** may carry a **mark in** and a **mark out**, and the
material a clip plays is between them: the tree's media has marks, and
a clip of a marked media may not play outside them.

### What was built

- The command `film.item.mark` puts the marks on a media. Only what is
  **named** is changed: a mark in alone leaves the mark out as it was,
  and a mark out alone leaves the mark in.
- A mark that is **outside the media** is refused and says how long the
  media is; a mark in that is **after** the mark out is refused and says
  why; a frame that is **not a whole number** is refused.
- A media with **no marks** is all of itself: the clip may begin at its
  first frame and run to its last, and the refusals say the media's
  length as they always did.
- A marked media **bounds** the clip: the trim, the slip and the speed
  all stop at the marks and not at the end of the media, and the
  refusal says where the media begins or what its marks are.

### What the port found

- **The tree's marks are the media's own and so are these.** The tree's
  item carries a `mark_in` and a `mark_out` in media time, and the
  tree's clip's `source_in` is in media time as well. Here the clip's
  `source_in` is in media time too — it has always been — and the marks
  say which part of that media may be played.
- **The tree's marks are optional and so are these.** A media without a
  mark in or a mark out is all of itself, and a mark in of nothing is
  the media's own beginning and a mark out of nothing is its end.
- **The tree clamps a trim against the media and this tree refuses it.**
  The tree's trim works out the biggest delta it may have and uses that;
  here the trim that would cross the mark is refused and says which
  bound stopped it — the same rule as every other bound in this tree.

### What it cost

- **Eleven tests** in the film battery (`tests/mediamarks.rs`): the
  marks being put on a media, only what is named being changed, a mark
  outside the media refused, a mark in after the mark out refused, a
  frame that is not a frame refused, a node that is not a media
  refused, a clip not running past the mark out, a clip not beginning
  before the mark in, a slip staying between the marks, a media with no
  marks being all of itself, and the marks being saved.
- **One new command**: `film.item.mark`. The film battery now carries
  **35** commands and the MCP server **467**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's marks may be set on the media and on the sequence.** The
  tree's sequence carries its own `mark_in` and `mark_out` for the media
  it plays, and they are the marks of the *sequence* and not of a media.
  Here the marks are the media's and a sequence's marks are not here.
- **A mark does not change what a clip plays.** The clip's `source_in`
  still says where it begins, and the marks only say what it may begin
  at — so a clip that already plays outside the marks is left as it is
  and is refused when it is edited.

## 353. The name of a sheet

A sheet's **name** is not a label: it is the way a formula reaches the
sheet, and a name that is taken is a name that means nothing. So a
name has rules, and a rename is more than a rename.

### What was built

- The command `grid.sheet.rename` renames a sheet. The name it takes
  is checked against the tree's rules: not **blank**, at most **31
  characters**, holding none of `:`, `\`, `/`, `?`, `*`, `[` or `]`, not
  **beginning or ending** with an apostrophe, and not **taken** by
  another sheet of the workbook — the tree's comparison ignores case,
  so `ledger` does not save a name that `Ledger` has.
- The **formulas follow**: every formula of every sheet that names the
  sheet is rewritten, and the answer says how many followed. A formula
  that does not name the sheet is left exactly as it was written.
- The **names follow**: a name of the workbook that stands for a range
  in the sheet now stands for a range in the new sheet.
- The same rules are the rules of the **name**, so `grid.sheet.add`
  refuses a bad name and a taken one too — the tree's `check_sheet_name`
  is one rule with two doors, and here it is one rule as well.

### What the port found

- **The tree renames by rewriting the expression, and here the formula
  is text.** The tree keeps a formula parsed and prints it again, so a
  rename is a change of the expression. Here a cell holds the formula's
  **text** — the text the caller wrote — so a rename parses the text,
  names the sheet again and prints it. The cost is honest and worth
  saying: a formula that follows is the **printer's** spelling of it
  (`A1 + A2`, where the caller wrote `A1+A2`), and a formula that does
  not follow keeps its own text untouched.
- **The tree's sheet-qualified names are not here.** The tree's
  `Old!MyName` is one string and the printer adds the quotes. Here a
  name stands for a **range**, and the range names its sheet, so a
  rename moves the sheet in the range and the name stays as it is.
- **The tree's uniqueness is per workbook and so is this one.** Two
  workbooks may hold sheets of one name, because each workbook is its
  own book of sheets.

### What it cost

- **Ten tests** in the grid battery (`tests/sheetnames.rs`): a sheet
  being renamed, a blank name refused, a name that is too long refused,
  a name holding a forbidden character refused, a name with an
  apostrophe at either end refused, a name that is taken refused (and
  the case not saving it), the formulas that name the sheet following
  it and the one that does not staying as it was, a name that stands
  for a range following, a node that is not a sheet refused, and a
  sheet that is added with a bad name refused.
- **One new command**: `grid.sheet.rename`. The grid battery now
  carries **49** commands and the MCP server **468**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's protection is not here.** The tree refuses to rename a
  sheet in a workbook whose structure is protected, and this tree has
  no protection of a workbook yet.
- **The tree's charts and pivot tables follow a rename and this tree
  has neither.** A chart's series and a pivot table's link name a
  sheet, and the tree rewrites them with the sheet; here there is
  nothing of that kind to rewrite.
- **A renamed sheet's own formulas follow it too, and the tree's do as
  well** — but the tree's sheets are held in a list and this tree's are
  nodes, so a formula that names the sheet it is in is rewritten the
  same way as any other.

## 354. The taking away of a sheet

A sheet may be **taken away** from its workbook, and the workbook must
keep **one visible sheet**: the tree's rule, and the rule the hiding of
a sheet obeys too.

### What was built

- The command `grid.sheet.remove` takes a sheet away from its workbook.
- The **last visible sheet** may not be taken away, and the refusal says
  why: a workbook with no sheet to look at is not a workbook. The tree
  counts the sheets that are visible and refuses the taking away when
  there is one of them, so a **hidden** sheet may not be taken away
  either while it is the last one that can be looked at.
- A **formula that named** the sheet is left as it was written, and the
  cell's value is the error "there is no sheet `Ledger`" — which says
  which sheet is missing.
- A node that is **not a sheet** is refused, and so is a node that is
  not there at all.

### What the port found

- **The tree writes `#REF!` and this tree says what is missing.** The
  tree's `adjust::delete_sheet` turns a reference to a sheet that is
  gone into `#REF!` — a mark, and not a word. Here the reference is
  left alone and the **evaluation** produces an error value with the
  sheet's name in it. The error is **derived**, so it cannot be wrong:
  it is computed every time the cell is read, and a sheet that comes
  back makes the formula work again with nothing written down. The
  tree's `#REF!` is written into the file and stays there.
- **The tree's names of a deleted sheet become `#REF!` too, and here
  they are not touched.** A name of the workbook stands for a range, and
  a range in a sheet that is gone reads the same error.

### What it cost

- **Six tests** in the grid battery (`tests/removal.rs`): a sheet being
  taken away, the last visible sheet not being takeable, a hidden sheet
  not being takeable while it is the last visible one, a hidden sheet
  being takeable when another can be looked at, a formula that named
  the sheet reading the error that says which sheet is missing, and a
  node that is not a sheet refused.
- **One new command**: `grid.sheet.remove`. The grid battery now
  carries **49** commands and the MCP server **469**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's protection is not here.** The tree refuses to take a
  sheet away in a workbook whose structure is protected, and this tree
  has no protection of a workbook yet.
- **The tree's active sheet and selection are not here.** The tree
  moves the active sheet when the sheet it was on is taken away, and
  clears the selection; this tree has no active sheet and no selection,
  so there is nothing to move and nothing to clear.
- **The tree's sheet order is a list and this tree's is the tree.** The
  tree's sheets are held in a list and their indices are moved when one
  is taken away; here a sheet is a node and taking it away takes it
  out of the tree, and the order of the rest is their own.

## 355. The taking away of a track

A track may be **taken away** from its sequence, and the clips on it go
with it.

### What was built

- The command `film.track.remove` takes a track away, and the answer
  says which clips went with it.
- A **locked** track may not be taken away: a locked track is a track
  that cannot be edited, and the taking away of the track is an edit.
  A track that is unlocked again may be taken away.
- A node that is **not a track** is refused, and so is a node that is
  not there at all.

### What the port found

- **The tree's track is a lane and this tree's track is a node.** The
  tree holds its tracks in two lists — the video tracks and the audio
  tracks — and takes one away by dropping it from its list. Here a
  track is a **node** under the sequence and the clips on it are its
  **children**, so taking the track away takes the clips with it, and
  the **tree of the document** says so by itself: no list is walked
  and no child is counted.
- **The tree's lock is checked by the tree's edit, and here by the
  command.** The tree's `edit_sequence` asks for the track of every
  edit and refuses a locked one. Here every command that edits a clip
  asks for the track of the clip, and this command asks for the track
  it is taking away.

### What it cost

- **Five tests** in the film battery (`tests/trackremoval.rs`): a
  track being taken away, the clips on it going with it, a locked track
  not being takeable, an unlocked track being takeable, and a node
  that is not a track refused.
- **One new command**: `film.track.remove`. The film battery now
  carries **36** commands and the MCP server **470**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's tracks are two lists and here they are one.** The tree
  keeps the video tracks and the audio tracks apart, and a track's
  **kind** says which list it is in. Here a track's kind is in its
  payload and the tree under the sequence holds them all, so taking one
  away does not need to know which list it was in.
- **The tree's sequence keeps a **selected** track and this tree does
  not.** The tree's `deleteTrack` leaves the selection alone and the
  tree's editor falls back to another track; here there is no
  selection to fall back from.
- **The tree's markers of a track are not here.** The tree's markers
  live on the sequence and not on a track, so nothing of theirs goes
  with the track — and here the same is true.

## 356. The enable of a clip

A clip may be **disabled**: it is on the track and it takes its place
there, and it does not **play**.

### What was built

- The command `film.clip.enable` enables a clip or disables it. Without
  the `on` the flag is **toggled** and the answer says which way it
  went; with it the flag is **set** to what the caller asked for.
- The flag is a **fact** of the clip, and what plays is **derived**: the
  timeline says how many clips of a track play, and the clip's own
  evaluation says whether it plays.
- A clip that does not play is **still on the track**: it takes its
  place, it is counted among the clips and it is not counted among the
  ones that play.
- A node that is **not a clip** is refused, and so is a node that is
  not there at all.

### What the port found

- **The tree flips the flag and this tree sets it.** The tree's
  `clip.enable` inverts the flag of every clip of the selection, so a
  selection holding a mix of enabled and disabled clips ends up with
  the mix **inverted** and not normalised. Here the command takes the
  clip and says whether it plays, and a command that says nothing is a
  command that says nothing — so the flag is set to what was asked for.
- **The tree's track has an enable flag too, and here it does not.** The
  tree's disabled track plays nothing at all. Here a track's kind is in
  its payload and its clips are its children, and there is no flag on
  the track: a clip that does not play is a clip that does not play, and
  the track is not a thing that plays.

### What it cost

- **Seven tests** in the film battery (`tests/enabling.rs`): a clip
  playing when it is made, a clip being disabled, a clip that does not
  play still being on the track, the flag being toggled when the
  command does not say, the flag being set when it does, a node that is
  not a clip refused, and the flag being saved.
- **One new command**: `film.clip.enable`. The film battery now
  carries **37** commands and the MCP server **471**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's canvas is not here.** The tree's canvas skips a clip
  that is not enabled — the clip is there and it is not drawn. Here the
  film battery draws nothing at all, so the flag has no picture to
  change; it has the timeline, which says how many clips play.
- **The tree's selection is not here.** The tree's command works on the
  **selection** and flips every clip in it; here the command takes one
  clip, so there is no selection to flip and no mixed selection to
  invert.

## 357. The name of a clip

A clip may be **named**, and the name is the clip's own.

### What was built

- The command `film.clip.rename` names a clip. The name is trimmed, a
  name that is **blank** is refused, and a node that is **not a clip**
  is refused.
- The name **survives a move**: a clip that has been named is still
  called that when it is moved, trimmed, split at the head or slowed.
- A clip that has **not** been named is still shown by the place it is
  at — `clip at 120` — and that name **follows** the clip, exactly as
  before.
- The **split** of a named clip: the piece that keeps the clip's id
  keeps the name, and the piece that is new is a new clip and is shown
  by its own place.

### What the port found

- **The tree's clip has a name and this tree's had none.** The tree's
  clip is an item of a track and it has a name, and the name is what
  the timeline shows. Here a clip was named by the place it was at,
  and every edit that moved it wrote the name again — so a name was
  never a **fact** here, only a spelling of a place.
- **So the name of a clip is now a fact and a derivation, and the
  payload says which one it is.** A clip with a `name` in its payload
  has been given one and it keeps it; a clip without has not, and it is
  shown by where it is. The two are told apart by the payload and not
  by a flag that could drift.
- **The tree's rename takes an item or a clip, and here it takes a
  clip.** The tree's `clip.rename` renames the item when the caller
  names one and the clip otherwise; here the items of the project are
  named when they are added (`film.item.add`) and the clips are named
  by this command, and the two are two things with two commands.

### What it cost

- **Eight tests** in the film battery (`tests/naming.rs`): a clip that
  has not been named being shown by its place, a clip being named, the
  name surviving a move, an unnamed clip following its place, a blank
  name refused, the split of a named clip, a node that is not a clip
  refused, and the name being saved.
- **One new command**: `film.clip.rename`. The film battery now
  carries **38** commands and the MCP server **472**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's items are renamed by the same command and here they are
  not.** The tree's `clip.rename` renames an item of the project as
  well, and here `film.item.add` names an item and nothing renames it
  afterwards.
- **The tree's clip names are unique and here they are not.** The tree
  does not say so either, and here two clips may carry the same name —
  a name is a label and not a key.
- **The tree's timeline shows a clip's name in its own column and here
  the timeline shows the places.** The timeline here is a list of
  starts and lengths, and the name of a clip is in the clip's own
  evaluation.

## 358. The label of an item

The tree labels the **items of the project** and the **clips of the
sequence** with one command and one list of sixteen colours, and here
only the clips carried a label.

### What was built

- The commands `film.item.label`, `film.item.label.delete` and
  `film.item.label.group` do for a media item what the clip's own
  commands do for a clip: a label is put on it, taken off it, and the
  **group** of a label is derived from the labels and not written down.
- The list of colours is the tree's own **sixteen**, and a name that is
  not one of them is **refused** — the tree's list is closed, and a
  colour the tree does not have is not a colour.
- A node that is **not an item** is refused, and so is a node that is
  not there at all.

### What the port found

- **The tree's label is one command for two kinds of thing, and here it
  is two.** The tree's `edit.label` labels the items of the project and
  the clips of the sequence with one command, and it works on the
  **selection** — the items of the project and the clips of the
  sequence are selected separately in the tree. Here a command names
  the thing it acts on, so there is a command for an item and a
  command for a clip, and the **list of colours is one list** that
  both use.
- **The tree's label group is of clips, and here there is a group of
  items as well.** The tree's *select label group* takes every clip
  that carries one of the labels of the clips that are selected; the
  group of an item is the same derivation over the items, and it is
  derived the same way — it changes when a label is put on an item and
  not when it is written down.

### What it cost

- **Six tests** in the film battery (`tests/itemlabels.rs`): an item
  being labelled, a label that is not one of the tree's being refused,
  the label being taken away, the group of a label being derived, a
  node that is not an item refused, and the label being saved.
- **Three new commands**: `film.item.label`, `film.item.label.delete`
  and `film.item.label.group`. The film battery now carries **41**
  commands and the MCP server **475**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's one command is not here.** The tree's `edit.label` is
  one command that labels the selection of items and the selection of
  clips; here the two are two commands, because a command in this tree
  says which thing it acts on.
- **The tree's selection is not here**, so the tree's label group is
  built from a selection and this one is built from one item.

## 359. The order of the sheets

The sheets of a workbook are in an **order** — the tabs, left to right
— and a sheet may be **moved** in it.

### What was built

- The command `grid.sheet.move` moves a sheet to a place, counted from
  **one**, and the answer says the place it went to and the place it
  came from.
- A place that is **not there** is **refused** and the refusal says how
  many sheets the workbook has: the tree puts the sheet at the end when
  the place is past it, and here a place that is not there is refused.
- A place that is **not a whole number** is refused, and so is a node
  that is **not a sheet**.
- The order is the order of the sheets under the workbook in the
  **tree**, so it is saved with the document and no sheet is lost by a
  move.

### What the port found

- **The tree's sheets are a list and this tree's sheets are children.**
  The tree holds its sheets in a `Vec` and moves one by taking it out
  and putting it back at another index; the index of a sheet is then
  its position. Here a sheet is a **node** under the workbook, and the
  order of the children is the order of the tabs — so moving a sheet
  moves the child, and the tree of the document says which tab is
  first.
- **The tree clamps the place and this tree refuses it.** The tree's
  `sheet.move` puts the sheet at `to.min(n - 1)`, so a place past the
  end is the end and nothing is said. Here the place is refused and the
  refusal says what the places are — the rule this tree follows
  everywhere: refuse, and do not clamp.
- **The tree's place is an index and this tree's is counted from one.**
  The tree's `to` is a zero-based index into the list of sheets; here
  the place is the position of the tab, and it is counted from one,
  because every other count in this tree is counted from one.

### What it cost

- **Six tests** in the grid battery (`tests/tabsorder.rs`): a sheet
  being moved, a sheet being moved to the last place, a place that is
  not there refused, a place that is not a whole number refused, a
  node that is not a sheet refused, and the order being saved.
- **One new command**: `grid.sheet.move`. The grid battery now
  carries **50** commands and the MCP server **476**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's copy of a sheet is not here.** The tree's `sheet.move`
  copies a sheet when the caller says `copy`, and the copy gets a name
  of its own (`Ledger (2)`), its own copies of the names that referred
  to it and no tables. Copying a sheet is copying its **cells** and
  its formulas, and that is a command of its own.
- **The tree's active sheet is not here.** The tree's move makes the
  moved sheet the active one; here there is no active sheet.
- **The tree's protection is not here.** The tree refuses to move a
  sheet in a workbook whose structure is protected, and this tree has
  no protection of a workbook yet.

## 360. The media a clip plays

A clip plays a media, and it may play a **different** one.

### What was built

- The command `film.clip.replace` points a clip at another media. The
  clip keeps its id and its place, and the **edge** that says which
  media it plays is replaced: the old edge dies and the new one is
  made. The answer says the new media and the old one.
- The clip plays the new media from its **beginning**, and its speed
  goes back to one: the clip plays the new media as it is.
- A clip that would run **past the end** of the new media is
  **refused** and the refusal says where it would run to and how long
  the new media is. The clip is not shortened and the replace does not
  happen.
- A media with **no frames** is refused, a **locked** track may not
  have its media replaced, and a node that is **not a clip** — or that
  is not an **item** — is refused.

### What the port found

- **The tree's replace is three commands and here it is one.** The
  tree has *replace from source*, *replace from source, match frame*
  and *replace from bin*, and the three differ in where the new in
  point comes from: the source monitor, the frame under the playhead,
  or the beginning of the new media. Here the new in point is the
  **beginning of the new media** — the tree's *from bin* — because this
  tree has no source monitor and no playhead.
- **The tree clamps and this tree refuses.** The tree's replace keeps
  a clip's own in point when the caller says `keepSourceIn`, and clamps
  it to the nearest frame of a subclip that restricts its trims — and
  it says which clips were clamped. Here the in point is the beginning
  of the new media and a clip that would run past the end of it is
  **refused** and the clip is named: refuse, and do not clamp.
- **The tree's replace also changes the clip's name and label, and here
  it does not.** The tree's replace takes the new item's name and
  label for the clip; here a clip's **name** is the clip's own
  (§357) and its label is a colour the caller put on it, so neither is
  taken from the media.

### What it cost

- **Six tests** in the film battery (`tests/replacing.rs`): a clip
  playing a different media, the clip playing it from its beginning, a
  clip that would run past the end refused, a media with no frames
  refused, a locked track refusing, and a node that is not a clip
  refused.
- **One new command**: `film.clip.replace`. The film battery now
  carries **42** commands and the MCP server **477**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's source monitor is not here.** The tree's *replace from
  source* points a clip at the media in the source monitor and lines
  the source monitor's playhead up with the sequence's; here there is
  no source monitor and no playhead, so the media of the project is
  the only thing a clip may be pointed at.
- **The tree's subclip is not here.** The tree's replace keeps a
  clip's own in point inside a subclip that restricts its trims, and
  the media of a clip here is the media of an item with its own marks
  — so the in point of the new media is its beginning and not a frame
  near the old one.
- **The tree's video and audio are not checked here.** The tree skips
  a clip whose track has no video or no audio in the replacement; here
  a track's kind is a word and the media of an item has no channels,
  so there is nothing to check.

## 361. The gap on a track

A track may have a **gap** in it, and the gap may be **closed**.

### What was built

- The command `film.timeline.closegap` closes the gap that holds a
  place on a track. The gap runs from the end of the clip before it to
  the start of the clip after it, and the clips that were after it
  move **up** by the length of the gap. The answer says where the gap
  was and how long it was.
- A place that is **covered** by a clip is not a gap, and the refusal
  says so. A track with **no clip after** the place has no gap there
  either, and the refusal says that.
- A **locked** track may not have its gap closed: the other tracks
  would move while it stayed put — the tree's own reason.
- A place that is **not a whole number** is refused, and so is a node
  that is **not a track**.

### What the port found

- **The tree's gap is a selection and this tree's is a place.** The
  tree's *close gap* with no parameters closes the **selected** gap,
  and with none selected closes **every** gap of the sequence. Here the
  command says the **track** and the **place**, so there is no
  selection to read and no gap to guess: the gap is the one that holds
  the place, and the answer says which gap it was.
- **The tree's gap is measured in the track's own time and here it is
  measured in frames.** The tree's gap runs from the end of the clip
  before it to the start of the clip after it, and the clips that were
  after it move up by the length of the gap — the same rule, and the
  same result: the gap closes and nothing is cut.

### What it cost

- **Six tests** in the film battery (`tests/gaps.rs`): a gap being
  closed, a place that is covered not being a gap, a track with no clip
  after the place having no gap there, a locked track refusing, a place
  that is not a whole number refused, and a node that is not a track
  refused.
- **One new command**: `film.timeline.closegap`. The film battery now
  carries **43** commands and the MCP server **478**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's gap selection is not here.** The tree's timeline shows
  the gap under the pointer and closes it with a shortcut; here a gap
  is closed by naming the track and the place in it.
- **The tree's sync-locked tracks are not here.** The tree's close gap
  moves the tracks that are **sync-locked** with the track that lost
  the clip, so that a group of tracks stays together — and it refuses
  when a sync-locked track covers the gap. Here there is no sync lock
  and the gap closes on the track that was named.
- **The tree's sequence gaps are not here.** The tree can close every
  gap of the sequence in one step, and the gaps are the stretches that
  no track covers; here a gap is a gap on **one** track, and the
  tracks are not compared with each other.

## 362. The clearing of a cell

There are two things in a cell and they are cleared **apart**: what
the cell **holds**, and how it is **shown**.

### What was built

- The command `grid.cell.clear.contents` empties the cell of its value
  and its formula and keeps its format and its style.
- The command `grid.cell.clear.format` takes the number format and the
  style away and keeps what the cell holds.
- A **formula is a content**: it goes when the contents go, and it
  stays when the format goes.
- The clearing of the **whole cell** — `grid.cell.clear` — is still
  here and still takes everything.
- A cell that is **not there** is not refused: there is nothing to
  clear, and the answer says so. A cell that is **not a cell** is
  refused, and so is a **sheet** that is not there.

### What the port found

- **The tree's format is a style and this tree's format is the cell's
  own.** The tree's style is shared between the cells that name it, so
  the tree's *clear formats* clears the style of the cell — and the
  cells that share it keep theirs, because the tree's style is a
  reference and not a copy. Here the format is the cell's **own**, so
  clearing it is that cell's business alone; a **style** is still
  shared, and a cell that names one keeps the name and loses the
  format it had.
- **The tree's one command with a checkbox is two commands here.** The
  tree's *clear all* clears everything and the tree's *clear contents*
  and *clear formats* clear one thing each, and the tree's menu offers
  them as three items. Here the tree's *clear all* is already a
  command, so the other two are two commands — and a command in this
  tree says what it does.

### What it cost

- **Seven tests** in the grid battery (`tests/clearing.rs`): the
  contents being cleared and the format kept, the format being cleared
  and the contents kept, a formula being a content, the style being
  cleared with the format, the clearing of the whole cell still being
  here, a cell that is not there not being refused, and a cell that is
  not a cell refused.
- **Two new commands**: `grid.cell.clear.contents` and
  `grid.cell.clear.format`. The grid battery now carries **52**
  commands and the MCP server **480**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's comments and hyperlinks are not here.** The tree's
  *clear comments* and *clear hyperlinks* clear two more things that a
  cell may hold, and a cell here holds a value, a formula, a format
  and a style.
- **The tree's checkboxes are not here.** The tree's *clear contents*
  unchecks a checkbox before it empties the cell, because the box is
  the cell's value there; here a cell holds a value and there is no
  box.

## 363. The reading of a range of cells

A range of cells may be **read**: the answer is the values of the cells,
row by row.

### What was built

- The command `grid.range.read` reads a range of a sheet and gives the
  values of the cells, row by row, and says which range it read.
- A cell that holds a **formula** has the value its formula computes —
  the value is **derived**, so it is computed every time the range is
  read and it cannot be wrong.
- Without a range, the **used range** is read: the stretch of the sheet
  that holds something. A sheet that holds nothing has no used range,
  and the answer is empty.
- The **formulas** may be asked for instead of the values, and a cell
  without a formula then shows its value.
- A range that is **not a range of cells** is refused, and so is a node
  that is **not a sheet**, and a sheet that is **not there**.

### What the port found

- **The tree's bound is a million cells and this tree's bound is the
  sheet.** The tree refuses to read a range of more than a million
  cells and says *read it in parts*; here the bound of the reading is
  the **sheet** itself — a sheet is a million rows tall and sixteen
  thousand columns wide — and a range may not leave the sheet.
- **The tree's read may show the text the cells show, and here it does
  not.** The tree's read takes a `formatted` flag and gives the text
  the cells show, with the format and the conditional format and the
  date system of the workbook in it. Here the **text** is what
  `grid.cell.text` is for — one cell at a time — so the read gives the
  **values**.
- **The tree's read narrows a whole row or a whole column to the used
  range, and this one does not.** The tree intersects a full-column
  range with the used range, so `A:A` reads the cells that hold
  something and no more; here the range is the range that was named.
- **The tree's range may be the selection and this one may not.** The
  tree's read takes the range from the selection when the parameter is
  not given; here there is no selection, and the default is the used
  range.

### What it cost

- **Seven tests** in the grid battery (`tests/reading.rs`): a range
  being read, the value of a formula cell being computed, the formulas
  being asked for instead, the used range being read when no range is
  given, a sheet that holds nothing reading nothing, a range that is
  not a range refused, and a node that is not a sheet refused.
- **One new command**: `grid.range.read`. The grid battery now carries
  **53** commands and the MCP server **481**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's spill and its arrays are not here.** The tree's read gives
  the value of a spilled range and an array cell as the tree holds it;
  here a cell holds a value, a formula, a format and a style, and a
  spilled range is not a thing this tree has.
- **The tree's read of a picture cell is not here.** A cell may hold a
  picture in the tree and the read of it is the picture; here a picture
  is not a cell value.

## 364. The choice of a value

A formula may **choose**: `IF` takes a condition and the values it
chooses between, and only the branch that is taken is computed.

### What was built

- The function `IF` takes a condition and the two values it chooses
  between: `IF(A1>2,"big","small")`.
- **Only the branch that is taken is computed.** So a formula like
  `IF(A1=0,"",1/A1)` does not divide by zero when the condition is
  false — the false branch is never worked out.
- The **truth** of the condition is the tree's: an empty cell is false,
  a number is true when it is not zero, a boolean is itself, and the
  text `TRUE` or `FALSE` is the boolean it names. Any other text is an
  error, and so is an error that is the condition.
- A formula of **one argument** is the truth of its condition, and a
  formula of **two arguments** has `FALSE` for the false branch. A
  formula of **more than three** arguments is an error.

### What the port found

- **The tree's choice is lazy and so is this one — and here it costs
  nothing.** The tree computes a formula's value and writes it beside
  the formula, so a lazy branch is a branch the tree must remember not
  to compute; here a formula's value is **derived** and is worked out
  every time it is asked for, so the branch that is not taken is never
  worked out because it is never reached.
- **The tree has an argument that is not there and this tree does
  not.** The tree's formula language has a *missing* argument, and the
  tree's `IF` gives a missing argument the value zero; here an argument
  that is not written is an argument that is not there, so `IF(A1,1)`
  is `FALSE` when the condition does not hold and never zero.
- **The tree's condition may be an array and this tree's may not.** The
  tree's `IF` over a range of conditions is an **array formula** that
  spills; here a range is a range of cells and a condition is one
  value, so a spilled `IF` is not a thing this tree has.
- **The tree's text is `TRUE` or `FALSE` and nothing else.** The tree's
  truth of a text is the text `TRUE` or `FALSE`, in any case, and any
  other text is a `#VALUE!`; so is this one.

### What it cost

- **Nine tests** in the grid battery (`tests/choice.rs`): a condition
  that holds taking the first branch, a condition that does not hold
  taking the second, the branch that is not taken not being computed,
  a formula of one argument being the truth of its condition, a
  formula of two arguments having `FALSE` for the false branch, a
  formula of more than three arguments being an error, a condition
  that is text being an error, a condition that is an error being that
  error, and an empty cell as the condition being false.
- **No new command**: the choice is a function of the formula
  language. The grid battery still carries **53** commands and the MCP
  server **481**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's other choices are not here.** The tree has `IFS`,
  `IFERROR`, `IFNA`, `SWITCH` and `CHOOSE`, and each of them chooses
  too; here there is one choice, and the others would be the same
  choice written again.
- **The tree's array formulas are not here.** A condition that is a
  range of cells is a spilled formula in the tree and is not a thing
  this tree has.

## 365. The counting of a condition

A formula may **count** what meets a condition: `COUNTIF` counts the
cells that meet it and `SUMIF` adds them.

### What was built

- The function `COUNTIF` takes a range of cells and a condition, and
  counts the cells that meet it.
- The function `SUMIF` takes a range of cells, a condition and — with
  the third argument — the **sum range**: the cells that are added are
  the ones of the sum range that stand opposite the cells of the
  first range.
- The **condition** is a value:
  - a **number** is the number, and so is a **boolean** and so is an
    **error**: the cell that holds it matches;
  - an **empty** value is the number zero;
  - **text** is a condition written out, and it may begin with an
    operator — `=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` — and what follows it is
    what the cell is compared with. So `">2"` is *greater than two* and
    `"<>apple"` is *anything that is not the text apple*.
- The **wildcards** are the tree's: `*` is any run of characters, `?`
  is any one character, and `~` is the escape. The comparison of text
  is without case.
- A number **written as text** matches **only for equality**:
  `COUNTIF(range,1)` counts the cell that holds the text `1`, and
  `COUNTIF(range,">1")` does not.
- An **empty cell** is not counted by a number condition, and the
  **bare empty** condition — `""` — counts the empty cells and the
  empty texts.
- The **sum range** is sized like the range it is summed over and is
  anchored at its own top left cell, so a sum range that is smaller
  than the range is read past its own end.

### What the port found

- **The tree has two wildcards and this tree had one.** The tree's
  matcher takes `*`, `?` and the escape `~`, and the tree uses it for
  the finding, the filtering and the criteria alike. This tree's
  **filter** had a matcher that knew only `*` — so a question mark in
  a filter was a question mark and not any one character. There is
  **one wildcard in this crate now**, and it is the tree's.
- **The tree's criterion has a length bound and this tree's has it
  too.** The tree refuses a text criterion of more than two hundred
  and fifty-five characters, and says it checked it on two versions of
  its own application; here the bound is the same, and a criterion
  over it is an error and not a truncated criterion.
- **The tree's criterion may be a date and this tree's is not.** The
  tree reads a criterion that looks like a date as the number of that
  date; here a criterion is a number, a boolean or text, and a date is
  not one of them.
- **The tree's condition that is an error is not raised.** An error
  criterion is the condition *that the cell holds that error*, and a
  cell that holds it matches; so does this one.

### What it cost

- **Ten tests** in the grid battery (`tests/counting.rs`): the cells
  that meet a number condition being counted, the cells that meet a
  text condition being counted without case, the wildcards being the
  tree's, a number written as text matching only for equality, an
  empty cell not being counted by a number condition and the bare
  empty condition counting it, the cells that meet the condition being
  added, the sum reading another range, the sum range being sized
  like the range, a criterion over the bound being an error, and a
  range that is not there being an error.
- **No new command**: the counting is a function of the formula
  language. The grid battery still carries **53** commands and the MCP
  server **481**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's other counting functions are not here.** The tree has
  `COUNTIFS`, `SUMIFS`, `AVERAGEIF`, `AVERAGEIFS`, `MAXIFS` and
  `MINIFS`, and each of them counts with a condition or with two; here
  there is one condition and one counting pair.
- **The tree's lookup functions are not here.** `VLOOKUP`, `HLOOKUP`,
  `MATCH` and `INDEX` find a cell by a condition or by a place, and
  they are a different thing: they do not count, they find.

## 366. The finding of a cell

A sheet may be **searched**: the answer is the cells whose text holds
what was looked for.

### What was built

- The command `grid.find` searches a sheet — or the whole workbook,
  when no sheet is named — and gives the cells that hold what was
  looked for, each with its address and its text.
- The **case** does not matter unless the search says it does, and when
  it does not matter both sides are folded.
- A search that holds a **wildcard** is a wildcard search: `*` is any
  run of characters and `?` is any one character, and the escape is
  `~`. Such a search looks for the pattern **inside** the text unless
  the search says the **whole cell** must match.
- A search without a wildcard looks for the text **inside** the cell's
  text, and for the whole text when the whole cell must match.
- What is searched is the **text the cell shows**, unless the search
  asks for the **formulas** — and then a cell that holds a formula is
  searched by its formula and a cell that holds a value is searched by
  its value.
- The hits are in the order a reader reads them in: the rows first,
  and the columns in a row.
- Nothing to look for is **refused**, and what is **not found** is an
  empty answer and not an error.

### What the port found

- **The tree's find moves the selection and this tree's does not.** The
  tree's find puts the cursor on the first hit and changes the
  selection, and its *find next* is a second command. Here there is no
  selection — the sheet is a node and the cells are its cells — so the
  hits are the answer and the next hit is the next hit in the list.
- **The tree's find refuses when nothing is found and this tree's does
  not.** The tree says *we couldn't find what you were looking for*;
  here a search that finds nothing gives a count of zero and no hits,
  because "nothing here" is an answer and not a failure.
- **The tree's find looks in the active sheet and this tree's looks in
  the whole workbook.** The tree has no sheet to name — it has the
  active one — and it has a flag that widens the search to the
  workbook. Here a sheet may be named, and a search without one looks
  in every sheet of the workbook.
- **The tree's find may look in the values or in the formulas, and the
  choice is a flag.** The tree's flag is *look in values*, and the
  default is the formulas — a cell that holds a formula is searched by
  its formula unless the search asks for the values. Here the flag is
  *formulas*, and the default is the values, because the values are
  what a reader sees.

### What it cost

- **Eight tests** in the grid battery (`tests/finding.rs`): a text
  being found, the case not mattering unless it is asked for, the
  wildcards being the tree's, the whole cell being asked for, the
  formulas being searched, the whole workbook being searched, what is
  not found being an empty answer, and nothing to look for being
  refused.
- **One new command**: `grid.find`. The grid battery now carries **54**
  commands and the MCP server **482**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's replacing is not here.** The tree's find and its
  replacing are one pair, and the replacing writes what the find found;
  here a search finds and says.
- **The tree's hidden formulas are not here.** The tree hides the
  formula of a cell when the sheet says the formulas are hidden, and
  then the search finds the value and not the formula; here the
  formulas of a sheet are always there and always searchable.

## 367. The note on a cell

A cell may carry a **note**: a piece of text that says something about
the cell and is not the cell's value.

### What was built

- The command `grid.cell.note.set` writes a note on a cell: the text
  of it, and — with the `author` parameter — who wrote it.
- A note that is already on the cell is **edited**: the text is the
  new text, and the author is kept unless a new one is given.
- The command `grid.cell.note.get` gives the note of a cell, and the
  command `grid.cell.note.delete` takes it away. A cell that holds no
  note is not refused: there is nothing to take away.
- A note with **no text** is refused, and so is a node that is not a
  sheet and a sheet that is not there.
- A note **survives** the cell being written to: the value of a cell
  may change and the note stays.
- The note goes with the **whole cell** being cleared — `grid.cell.clear`
  takes it — and it stays when the **contents** are cleared.

### What the port found

- **The tree's comment is a thread and this tree's note is a text.** The
  tree's comment carries an author, the replies of a thread, a flag
  that says the thread is resolved, a flag that says the box is
  shown, the dates and the place of the box. Here a note is a text and
  an author, and the thread is not here.
- **The note belongs to the sheet and not to the cell, and that is the
  tree's own shape.** The tree keeps its comments in a map of the
  sheet and not in the cell, because a cell in the tree is a value and
  a formula and a style. Here the note is in the sheet's own map too,
  and that is why a note survives the cell being written to.
- **The tree's clear all takes the comment with it, and its clear
  contents does not.** So does this one: `grid.cell.clear` takes the
  note and `grid.cell.clear.contents` keeps it.
- **The tree's author is the name in its preferences and this tree's
  is what was given.** The tree has a user name and writes it on every
  comment; here there are no preferences, and the author is the one the
  note was written with — and the author of an edited note is kept.

### What it cost

- **Nine tests** in the grid battery (`tests/notes.rs`): a note being
  written, a note being edited and the author kept, a note surviving
  the cell being written to, the note going with the whole cell being
  cleared, the note staying when the contents are cleared, a note being
  taken away, a cell that holds no note not being refused, a note with
  no text being refused, and a node that is not a sheet being refused.
- **Three new commands**: `grid.cell.note.set`, `grid.cell.note.get`
  and `grid.cell.note.delete`. The grid battery now carries **57**
  commands and the MCP server **485**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's threads are not here.** A comment in the tree may have
  replies, and a thread may be resolved; a note here is one text and
  one author.
- **The tree's note box is not here.** The tree remembers where the
  box of a note sits and how big it is, and the dates of the thread;
  here a note is text, and where it is shown is the panel's business.

## 368. The link on a cell

A cell may carry a **link**: a target that something else may open.

### What was built

- The command `grid.cell.link.set` puts a link on a cell: where it
  goes — a place in this workbook or a place outside it — and, with
  the `tooltip` parameter, the text that is shown when the mouse
  rests on it.
- A link that is already on the cell is **edited**: the target is the
  new target, and the tooltip is kept unless a new one is given.
- The command `grid.cell.link.get` gives the link of a cell, and the
  command `grid.cell.link.delete` takes it away. A cell that holds no
  link is not refused: there is nothing to take away.
- Whether the target is **inside this workbook** is **derived**: a
  target that names a sheet of this workbook and a cell in it is
  inside, and everything else — a web address, a `mailto:`, a file —
  is outside.
- A link **survives** the cell being written to, and it goes with the
  **whole cell** being cleared.
- A link that goes **nowhere** is refused, and so is a node that is
  not a sheet and a sheet that is not there.

### What the port found

- **The tree's flag is read from a file and this tree's is derived.**
  The tree's hyperlink carries a flag that says whether the target is
  outside the workbook, and the tree reads it from the file the link
  was written in — a relationship in the file, and not a `location`.
  Here the flag is **derived**: this tree knows the sheets it has, so
  a target that names one of them and a cell in it is inside.
- **The tree cannot tell a bare file name from a defined name.** The
  tree says so in its own note, and so does this one: a target with no
  `!` in it is outside, whatever it is.
- **The link belongs to the sheet and not to the cell, and that is the
  tree's own shape.** The tree keeps its hyperlinks in a map of the
  sheet, and so does this one — and that is why a link survives the
  cell being written to and goes only when the whole cell is cleared.
- **The tree's clear all takes the hyperlink with it.** So does this
  one: `grid.cell.clear` takes the link and `grid.cell.clear.contents`
  keeps it.

### What it cost

- **Seven tests** in the grid battery (`tests/links.rs`): a link being
  written, a link being edited and the tooltip kept, a link that goes
  to a place in this workbook being inside, a link surviving the cell
  being written to and going with the whole cell being cleared, a link
  being taken away, a link that goes nowhere being refused, and a node
  that is not a sheet being refused.
- **Three new commands**: `grid.cell.link.set`, `grid.cell.link.get`
  and `grid.cell.link.delete`. The grid battery now carries **60**
  commands and the MCP server **488**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's links are not opened here.** The tree's file carries a
  relationship for every link that is outside the workbook, and a
  target that is a file is a relationship and not a path; here the
  target is the text that was given.
- **The tree's defined names are not here.** A target may name a
  defined name in the tree, and a bare name cannot be told from a file
  name; here a target names a sheet and a cell, or it is outside.

## 369. The shaping of a text

A formula may **shape** a text: take a part of it, count it, fold it
or clean it.

### What was built

- `LEFT(text, [count])` — the **first** characters of the text, and
  the first one when the count is not given.
- `RIGHT(text, [count])` — the **last** characters of the text.
- `MID(text, start, [count])` — the characters from the **start**, and
  the start is counted from one. A start that is not one is an error.
- `LEN(text)` — how many characters the text holds.
- `TRIM(text)` — the text without the spaces that are not between
  words.
- `UPPER(text)` and `LOWER(text)` — the text in one case or the other.
- `PROPER(text)` — the text with every **word** capitalised and the
  rest of it in small letters.
- The text of a value is the text it is **written** as: a number is
  written as a number, a boolean as `TRUE` or `FALSE`, and an empty
  value as nothing at all.
- A count that is **negative** is an error, and a value that is an
  **error** is that error: the shaping of an error is the error.

### What the port found

- **The tree's text is measured in characters and so is this tree's.**
  The tree counts the characters and takes the characters, and a
  character that is not a byte — an emoji, a letter outside the Latin
  — is one character and not four; here the text is taken and counted
  the same way.
- **The tree's count that is not there is a count of one, and a count
  that is there and holds nothing is a count of zero.** The tree's
  `LEFT` takes one character when the count is not given, and the
  tree's *an explicit empty is zero* rule applies to the count: an
  argument that is there and holds nothing is zero. So does this one,
  and `MID` without a count is an empty text.
- **The tree's start is counted from one and a start below one is an
  error.** The tree says `#VALUE!` for a start of zero and for a
  negative one; so does this one.
- **The tree's `TRIM` removes the spaces that are not between words.**
  The tree's `TRIM` splits the text on spaces and joins the words with
  one space, so a run of spaces is one space and the text is trimmed
  at both ends; so does this one.

### What it cost

- **Ten tests** in the grid battery (`tests/texts.rs`): the first
  characters being taken, the last characters being taken, the
  characters from the start being taken, a start that is not one being
  an error, the characters being counted, the text being trimmed, the
  text being folded into a case, the text of a number being the text
  it is written as, a count that is negative being an error, and a
  value that is an error being that error.
- **No new command**: the shaping is a function of the formula
  language. The grid battery still carries **60** commands and the MCP
  server **488**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's other text functions are not here.** The tree has
  `CONCAT`, `CONCATENATE`, `TEXTJOIN`, `FIND`, `SEARCH`, `SUBSTITUTE`,
  `REPLACE`, `T`, `CLEAN`, `TEXTBEFORE`, `TEXTAFTER` and `TEXTSPLIT`,
  and each of them works on a text; here a text is taken apart, folded
  and cleaned, and it is not put together again.
- **The tree's bound on the length of a text is not here.** The tree
  refuses a text that is longer than the limit of a cell, and it says
  so; here a text is as long as it is.

## 370. The finding of a value in a range

Three functions look for something in a range of cells: `MATCH`,
`VLOOKUP` and `INDEX`.

### What was built

- `MATCH(needle, range)` gives the **place** of the needle in the
  range, counted from one.
- `VLOOKUP(needle, table, column, [exact])` gives the value of the
  **column** of the row whose first column holds the needle.
- `INDEX(range, row, [column])` gives the value at a **place**.
- The search is the tree's: two numbers are equal when they are the
  same number, two texts are equal when they are the same text
  **without case**, a **text** needle may hold the tree's wildcards,
  a needle of one kind does not match a value of another kind, and the
  **first** match is the match.
- A value that is **not found** is `#N/A`, and a place or a column
  that is **not there** is `#REF!`.

### What the port found

- **The tree's default is the approximate search and this tree's
  default is the exact one.** The tree's `MATCH` and the tree's
  `VLOOKUP` look for the largest value that is not greater than the
  needle when nothing else is said, and so a lookup must **say** that
  it is exact here — `VLOOKUP(2,A1:B3,2,FALSE)` — and a lookup that
  does not say is refused with *not supported yet: an approximate
  search*. The tree's `MATCH` has no such default here: it looks for
  the exact match when no match type is given.
- **The tree's approximate search is a bisection and not a rule.** The
  tree says so in its own words: it probes the middle of what is left
  and answers what the tree's own application answers on data that is
  not sorted, and it skips the entries of other kinds. That is not a
  rule that can be written down in a sentence, and so it is not here.
- **The tree's needle may hold the wildcards and so does this one's.**
  The tree's exact search matches a text needle with the wildcards,
