  and `B*` matches `banana`; so does this one, and the text is
  compared without case in both.
- **The tree's `INDEX` may give a whole row or a whole column, and
  that is an array.** The tree's `INDEX` with a zero gives the array
  of the row or the column; this tree has no arrays, so it says *not
  supported yet: an array*.

### What it cost

- **Ten tests** in the grid battery (`tests/lookups.rs`): the place of
  a value being found, the wildcards being the tree's, a value that is
  not there being not found, the approximate search being refused, the
  value of a column being found, a lookup that does not say that it is
  exact being refused, a column that is not there being an error, the
  value at a place being taken, a place that is not there being an
  error, and a needle that is an error being that error.
- **No new command**: the finding is a function of the formula
  language. The grid battery still carries **60** commands and the MCP
  server **488**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's other lookups are not here.** The tree has `HLOOKUP`,
  `LOOKUP`, `XLOOKUP`, `XMATCH`, `ROWS`, `COLUMNS`, `TRANSPOSE` and
  `ADDRESS`, and each of them finds something in a range; here three
  do.
- **The tree's search may go backwards.** The tree's `MATCH` with a
  negative match type looks for the smallest value that is not less
  than the needle, in a range that is sorted the other way; that is
  the approximate search again, and it is not here.

## 371. The parts of a date

A formula may **make a date** and take a date apart.

### What was built

- The function `DATE(year, month, day)` gives the **serial** of the
  date — the days since the beginning of the calendar of the
  workbook.
- The functions `YEAR(serial)`, `MONTH(serial)` and `DAY(serial)` give
  the **parts** of the date the serial is, and the parts may be put
  together again.
- The month and the day **roll over**: the 13th month is the January
  of the next year, and the 32nd day of January is the 1st of
  February.
- A year **below 1900** is a year after 1900: the year 24 is the year
  1924.
- The **date system** is the workbook's: the 1900 system counts from
  the 1st of January 1900 and the 1904 system from the 1st of January
  1904, where the serial 0 is that day.
- A date outside the calendar is an **error**, and so is a serial that
  is not one.

### What the port found

- **The tree's `DATE` rolls over and a cell that holds a date does
  not.** The tree's `DATE(2026,2,30)` is the 1st of March, and this
  tree's `DATE` rolls the same way; but a **cell** that holds a date
  holds a date that *happened* — the 30th of February is refused when
  it is put in a cell, because a cell is a fact and a formula is a
  rule. That is the tree's own distinction too, and it is in this
  tree's `grid.cell.date` and in this formula.
- **The serial is the tree's serial, and it is not the count of the
  days.** In the 1900 system the serial 0 is the day *before* the 1st
  of January 1900, and the **fictitious** 29th of February 1900 — a
  leap day that never happened — is the serial 60, because the tree's
  calendar has it in it.
- **The tree's date system belongs to the workbook and so does this
  one's.** The tree's `DATE` reads the calendar of the workbook the
  formula is in; here the calendar is the workbook's too, and a
  workbook in the 1904 system counts the 1st of January 1904 as the
  zeroth day.

### What it cost

- **Seven tests** in the grid battery (`tests/datetimes.rs`): a date
  being made, the month and the day rolling over, a year below 1900
  being a year after 1900, a date being taken apart, the parts being
  put together again, a date outside the calendar being an error, and
  the 1904 system counting from another day.
- **No new command**: the dates are a function of the formula
  language. The grid battery still carries **60** commands and the MCP
  server **488**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's other date functions are not here.** The tree has
  `TIME`, `HOUR`, `MINUTE`, `SECOND`, `WEEKDAY`, `WEEKNUM`,
  `EDATE`, `EOMONTH`, `DATEVALUE`, `TIMEVALUE` and `DAYS`, and each of
  them works with a date or a time; here a date is made and taken
  apart, and the times are not here.
- **The tree's now is not here.** The tree has `NOW` and `TODAY`, and
  a formula that asks for the day it is read on is a fact about when
  it was read; here a date is a date.

## 372. The sorting of a range

A range of cells may be **sorted**: the rows of it are put in order by
the values of one of its columns.

### What was built

- The command `grid.sort` sorts a range — or the used range, when no
  range is named — by the values of one of its columns, and the order
  may be **descending**.
- What a row holds travels with it: the **value**, the **formula**,
  the **format** and the **style** of every cell of the row, and the
  **note** and the **link** of a cell.
- A formula's **relative** references move with the cell that holds
  it, and its **anchored** references — the `$` — stay where they
  are.
- The **order** is the tree's: the numbers, then the text, then the
  booleans, then the errors, and the **empty** cells last whatever the
  order is. The text is compared without case.
- The first row of the range is a **header** when it is guessed to be
  one — a column whose first cell is text and whose second cell is
  not votes for it — and the header stays where it is. The guess may
  be said otherwise.
- A **column that is not in the range** is refused, and so is a range
  with a **merge** in it: a merged region is one cell, and a row of a
  range is not.

### What the port found

- **The tree's sort moves whole lines and so does this one.** The
  tree's sort takes the cells of a row and puts them where the row
  goes, and a formula's relative references are **adjusted** for the
  move, so that a formula still reads the row it is on; so does this
  one, and the adjustment is done on the **text** of the formula —
  parsed, moved and written out again.
- **The tree's sort guesses the header with the boldness of the cells
  as well as with their text.** The tree's guess votes for a header
  when a column's first cell is text and its second is not, and when
  the first row is in bold and the second is not. Here a cell has a
  format and a style and no weight, so the guess is the **text** vote
  alone.
- **The tree's sort has many levels and this one has one.** The tree
  sorts by up to sixty-four keys, and a key may be a list of the
  tree's own words and a colour of a cell. Here there is one column
  and its values.
- **The tree's sort may sort by columns.** The tree's sort has an
  *orientation*, and the columns of a range may be sorted instead of
  its rows; here the rows of a range are sorted, and a column that is
  not in the range is refused.

### What it cost

- **Ten tests** in the grid battery (`tests/sorting.rs`): the rows
  being put in order, the order being descending, the empty cells
  being last, the text being compared without case, a header being
  guessed and staying where it is, a formula moving with its row, an
  anchored reference not moving, the note and the link travelling with
  the row, a column that is not in the range being refused, and a
  range with a merge in it being refused.
- **One new command**: `grid.sort`. The grid battery now carries **61**
  commands and the MCP server **489**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's sort of a protected sheet is not here.** The tree
  refuses to sort a sheet that is protected, and a sheet may be
  protected in the tree; this tree has no protection yet.
- **The tree's sort by a custom list is not here.** The tree may sort
  by a list of words of its own, so that the months come out in the
  order of the year; here the values are the values.

## 373. The protection of a sheet

A sheet may be **protected**.

### What was built

- The command `grid.sheet.protect` protects a sheet, and the
  protection says what may still be done to it: the **sorting**, the
  **filtering** and the **formatting**. What is not said is not
  allowed.
- The command `grid.sheet.unprotect` takes the protection away.
- The **cells** of a protected sheet are **locked**: a command that
  changes what a cell holds — its value or its formula — refuses, and
  so does the clearing of the contents of a cell and the filling of a
  range.
- A command that is not allowed says so and does nothing: *sorting is
  not allowed on this protected sheet: unprotect it with
  grid.sheet.unprotect*.
- A node that is **not a sheet** is refused, and so is a sheet that is
  not there.

### What the port found

- **The tree's cells are locked by their own style and this tree's are
  locked by the sheet.** The tree's style carries a *locked* flag and
  a *hidden* one, and a cell of a protected sheet may not be changed
  when its style is locked — and the tree has *Allow Edit Ranges*, a
  set of ranges of a protected sheet that may still be changed. Here
  the protection of the sheet locks the **cells of the sheet**, and
  there is no range that is let through: the whole sheet is locked.
- **The tree's protection may carry a password and this one's may
  not.** The tree stores the **hash** of the password and never the
  password, and the tree's *unprotect* asks for it. Here a sheet may
  be unprotected by anyone who may change it — which is what the
  tree's protection is when it has no password.
- **The tree's protection says more than this one.** The tree's
  protection carries a flag for the selecting, the inserting, the
  deleting, the formatting of the rows and of the columns, beside the
  sorting and the filtering. Here there are three, and they are the
  three that the commands of this tree do.
- **The tree's refusal names the menu and this one's names the
  command.** The tree says *sorting isn't allowed on this protected
  sheet (Review › Unprotect Sheet)*; here the refusal says which
  command undoes it, because an agent drives commands and not menus.

### What it cost

- **Seven tests** in the grid battery (`tests/protection.rs`): the
  cells of a protected sheet being locked, a formula not being put in
  a locked cell, the sorting being allowed and not being allowed, the
  filtering being allowed and not being allowed, the formatting being
  allowed and not being allowed, a sheet being unprotected and its
  cells being changed again, and a node that is not a sheet being
  refused.
- **Two new commands**: `grid.sheet.protect` and
  `grid.sheet.unprotect`. The grid battery now carries **63** commands
  and the MCP server **491**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's locked style is not here.** The tree's style says
  whether a cell is locked and whether its formula is hidden, and a
  cell of a protected sheet may be changed when its style says it is
  not locked; here the lock is the sheet's and there is no style that
  says otherwise.
- **The tree's ranges that may still be changed are not here.** The
  tree's *Allow Edit Ranges* lets a part of a protected sheet be
  changed, with or without a password of its own; here the whole
  sheet is locked.

## 374. The time and the days of a date

A formula may work with the **time** of a day and with the **days**
between two dates.

### What was built

- The function `TIME(hour, minute, second)` gives the **fraction of a
  day** a time is: the half of the day is noon, and the quarter is six
  in the morning.
- The functions `HOUR(serial)`, `MINUTE(serial)` and `SECOND(serial)`
  give the parts of the time of a day.
- The function `WEEKDAY(serial, [kind])` gives the **day of the week**
  as a number, and the number says where the week begins: one is a
  week that begins on the Sunday, two is a week that begins on the
  Monday, three is a week that begins on the Monday and counts from
  zero, and the eleven to seventeen are the weeks that begin on a day
  and count from one. A kind that is not one of those is an error.
- The functions `EDATE(start, months)` and `EOMONTH(start, months)`
  give a date a number of **months** away, and the day of the month is
  **clamped** to the length of the month it lands in — the 31st of
  January plus a month is the 28th of February — and the months are
  always counted from the **original** date, so a series does not
  drift.
- The function `DAYS(end, start)` gives the number of **days** between
  two dates.
- A time that is **before the midnight** is an error, and so is a
  number over thirty-two thousand seven hundred and sixty-seven.

### What the port found

- **The tree's `EDATE` drops the time of the day and so does this
  one.** The tree's `EDATE` is a **date** and not a moment: the time
  of the day is not carried over, and only the day of the month is.
- **The tree's February 1900 has its real twenty-eight days in `EDATE`
  and in `EOMONTH`, and this tree's calendar has the fictitious
  twenty-ninth.** The tree says so in its own note: it gives
  February 1900 its real twenty-eight days, though the sheet's
  calendar has a 29 February 1900 in it — the serial 60. Here the
  **calendar** is the one that counts, so the last day of February
  1900 is the fictitious twenty-ninth here, and the two rules are not
  two rules.
- **The tree's `WEEKDAY` has ten kinds and so does this one.** The
  kinds are the ones, the two, the three and the eleven to seventeen,
  and a kind that is not one of them is an error; the tree's error is
  a `#NUM!` and so is this one's.
- **The tree's `TIME` cuts the numbers to whole ones and so does this
  one.** The tree's rule: the hour, the minute and the second are cut
  to whole seconds, a number over thirty-two thousand seven hundred
  and sixty-seven is an error, and a time before the midnight is an
  error — and a time that is more than a day is a day and a bit.

### What it cost

- **Seven tests** in the grid battery (`tests/timesofday.rs`): a time
  being a fraction of a day, the parts of a time being taken, the
  day of the week being a number, a date a number of months away
  being found, the number of days between two dates, a kind that is
  not one of the tree's being an error, and a time that is not a time
  being an error.
- **No new command**: the times are a function of the formula
  language. The grid battery still carries **63** commands and the MCP
  server **491**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's other date functions are not here.** The tree has
  `WEEKNUM`, `ISOWEEKNUM`, `DATEVALUE`, `TIMEVALUE`, `DAYS360`,
  `DATEDIF`, `NOW` and `TODAY`, and each of them works with a date or
  a time; here a date is made and taken apart, a time is made and
  taken apart, and the days between two dates are counted.

## 375. The taking away of a media item

A media item may be taken away.

### What was built

- The command `film.item.remove` takes a media item away.
- An item that **no clip plays** is taken away, and it goes out of its
  bin with it.
- An item that a clip **plays** is not taken away: the answer says how
  many clips are in the way and which ones they are, so that they may
  be taken away first.
- A node that is **not an item** is refused, and so is a node that is
  not there.

### What the port found

- **The tree removes an item that a clip plays and this tree refuses.**
  The tree's *clear* takes the item out of the project and the clip
  that played it is left behind, and the tree has an **offline** flag
  for a media file that is not there. Here the removal is refused,
  because a **clip that plays nothing is not a clip** — and the
  refusal names the clips, so the order of the work is plain.
- **The tree's clear takes many items at once and this one's takes
  one.** The tree's clear takes the selection, and it may take the
  items to a **bin** instead of away. Here a bin is where the items
  are, and one item is taken away at a time.
- **The tree's *remove unused* is not here.** The tree may remove
  every item that no clip plays, in one step. Here the refusal says
  which clips are in the way of **this** item, and the items are taken
  away one by one.

### What it cost

- **Four tests** in the film battery (`tests/itemremoval.rs`): an
  item that no clip plays being taken away, an item that a clip plays
  not being taken away, the item being taken away when the clip is
  taken away first, and a node that is not an item being refused.
- **One new command**: `film.item.remove`. The film battery now
  carries **44** commands and the MCP server **492**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's project is not here.** The tree's project holds the
  items in **bins**, and its clear may take them to a bin and its
  *remove unused* may empty a bin; here the items are in bins and a
  bin is where they are.
- **The tree's offline item is not here.** The tree's item may be
  marked **offline** — made offline on purpose, with the media file
  not there — and a clip that plays an offline item is a clip that
  plays nothing; here the item is either there or not.

## 376. The reading of a project

A project may be **read**: the answer is the bins, the items in them,
and the clips that play them.

### What was built

- The command `film.project` gives the **bins** of the project, the
  **items** in them, and for every item what it is and what plays it.
- For every item the answer says its **name**, its own id in the
  editor, the **path** of the media, its **duration**, whether it is
  **offline**, the **bin** it is in, the **tracks** it holds and the
  **clips** that play it.
- Everything in the answer is **derived**: the bins are the nodes of
  the tree, the items are the nodes under them, and the clips that
  play an item are the edges that name it.
- A project with nothing in it is empty, and not an error.

### What the port found

- **The tree's project is a panel and this tree's project is a
  command.** The tree's project is a window with the items in bins, a
  **thumbnail** of every item, the **kind** of every item — a media, a
  sequence, a graphic — and a **selection** that the mouse chooses.
  Here the project is read by a command, and what it says is the
  names, the ids, the durations and the relations.
- **The tree's items may be of many kinds and this tree's items are
  media and sequences.** The tree's item may be a media file, a
  sequence, a graphic, an adjustment layer; here the item is a media
  and a sequence is an item with tracks in it — which is the tree's own
  shape, and the tree's kind is not said here.
- **The tree's bins may be in bins and this tree's are not.** The
  tree's bins are a tree of their own — a bin may be in a bin — and
  the tree's panel shows that; here the bins are flat and the items
  are under them.

### What it cost

- **Four tests** in the film battery (`tests/project.rs`): the bins
  and the items being read, the clips that play an item being derived
  and said, an item that no clip plays having no clips, and a project
  with nothing in it being empty.
- **One new command**: `film.project`. The film battery now carries
  **45** commands and the MCP server **493**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's pictures are not here.** The tree's panel shows a
  **thumbnail** of every item, and the tree's item carries one; here
  an item carries a path and a duration and no picture.
- **The tree's selection is not here.** The tree's project panel
  holds a **selection** of items, and the tree's commands act on the
  selection; here every command names what it acts on.

## 377. The joining and the finding of texts

A formula may **join** texts and **find** one text in another.

### What was built

- The functions `CONCATENATE` and `CONCAT` join the texts of their
  arguments.
- The function `TEXTJOIN(delimiter, ignore_empty, …)` joins the texts
  with a **delimiter**, and the empty texts may be left out.
- The functions `FIND(needle, text, [start])` and `SEARCH` give the
  **place** of a text in another, counted from one, and the search may
  begin later. `FIND` is exact; `SEARCH` folds the case and takes the
  tree's **wildcards**.
- The function `SUBSTITUTE(text, old, new, [instance])` changes a part
  of a text — and with the instance the change is made to the *second*
  change and not to the first.
- The function `REPLACE(text, start, count, new)` changes the part of
  a text that is counted from one.
- The function `T(value)` gives the text of a value when it is a
  text, and nothing at all when it is not: a number is a number and
  not a text.
- The function `CLEAN(text)` takes the **control characters** away.
- A text that is not found is an error, and a text that is longer
  than the tree's bound is an error too.

### What the port found

- **The tree's `CONCAT` takes the arrays apart and the tree's
  `CONCATENATE` does not.** Here there are no arrays, so the two are
  the same thing: both join the texts of their arguments.
- **The tree's `SEARCH` is a different search from the tree's `FIND`,
  and the two are here.** The tree's `FIND` is exact — the case
  matters — and the tree's `SEARCH` folds the case and takes the
  tree's wildcards; so does this one.
- **The tree's texts have a bound and so do these.** The tree refuses
  a text of more than thirty-two thousand seven hundred and sixty-seven
  characters; so does this one, and the bound is in the characters and
  not in the bytes.
- **The tree's `T` gives a number as nothing and so does this one.**
  The tree's `T` is the text of a value when the value is a text, and
  nothing at all when it is not — and an **error** is still an error.

### What it cost

- **Nine tests** in the grid battery (`tests/joining.rs`): the texts
  being joined, the texts being joined with a delimiter, a text being
  found in another, the search folding the case and taking the
  wildcards, a text that is not there not being found, a part of a
  text being changed, a part of a text being replaced, the text of a
  value that is not a text being nothing, and the control characters
  being cleaned away.
- **No new command**: the joining and the finding of texts are
  functions of the formula language. The grid battery still carries
  **63** commands and the MCP server **493**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's other text functions are not here.** The tree has
  `REPT`, `EXACT`, `CHAR`, `CODE`, `UNICHAR`, `TEXTSPLIT`,
  `TEXTBEFORE`, `TEXTAFTER`, `TEXTBEFOREAFTER` and `FIXED`, and each
  of them works on a text; here a text is joined, found and changed.
- **The tree's `TEXTSPLIT` gives an array and this tree has no
  arrays.** A text that is split into its parts is a list of texts,
  and a list is not a thing this tree has.

## 378. The name of a thing in the project

A media item may be **named**, and a bin may be **named**.

### What was built

- The command `film.item.rename` names a media item, and the command
  `film.bin.rename` names a bin.
- The name is the thing's **own**: it does not follow the thing, and
  it is not derived from it. The name of an item is what the project
  says.
- A name that is **nothing** is refused, and the thing keeps the name
  it had.
- A node that is **not an item** and a node that is **not a bin** are
  refused, and so is a node that is not there.

### What the port found

- **The tree's rename renames an item or a clip and this tree's are
  two commands.** The tree's `clip.rename` takes an item or a clip,
  and one command does both. Here a command is one thing: the clip is
  named by `film.clip.rename` and the item by `film.item.rename` — and
  the rule they share is the tree's: a name that is nothing is
  refused.
- **The tree's rename of a bin is not a command and this tree's is.**
  The tree's bins are renamed in the **panel**, and the tree has no
  command for it; here the bin is a node like any other and it is
  named by a command.

### What it cost

- **Five tests** in the film battery (`tests/itemnaming.rs`): a media
  item being named, a bin being named, the name of an item being said
  by the project, a name that is nothing being refused, and a node
  that is not an item being refused.
- **Two new commands**: `film.item.rename` and `film.bin.rename`. The
  film battery now carries **47** commands and the MCP server **495**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's selection is not here.** The tree's rename renames the
  **selected** clip when no clip is named, and the tree's panel
  renames what is selected; here every command names what it acts on.
- **The tree's names may be of many kinds and this tree's are plain
  texts.** The tree's project has a name and a **label** for an item,
  and the tree's clip has a name that the timeline shows; here the
  name is the name.

## 379. The taking away of a bin

A bin may be taken away, and what is **in** it goes with it.

### What was built

- The command `film.bin.remove` takes a bin away, and the **items** of
  the bin go with it: an item of a bin is the bin's child, and a child
  goes with its parent.
- A bin that holds an item that a clip **plays** is not taken away:
  the answer says which item is played by which clip, so that the clip
  may be taken away first.
- A node that is **not a bin** is refused, and so is a node that is
  not there.

### What the port found

- **The tree's bins are a tree and this tree's are not.** The tree's
  `file.newBin` takes a **parent** — a bin may be in a bin — and the
  tree's items live in the bins of that tree. Here a bin holds the
  items and there is no bin in a bin, so the removal of a bin takes
  the items of it and nothing else.
- **The tree's clear of the project takes the items and the bins and
  this tree's takes them apart.** The tree's `project.delete` takes
  the **selection** — items and bins — and the tree's *remove
  unused* takes the items no clip plays. Here a bin is taken away on
  its own, and the rule is the same rule the removal of an item has:
  an item that a clip plays may not be taken away.

### What it cost

- **Four tests** in the film battery (`tests/binremoval.rs`): a bin
  being taken away with its items, a bin whose item is played not
  being taken away, the bin being taken away when the clip is taken
  away first, and a node that is not a bin being refused.
- **One new command**: `film.bin.remove`. The film battery now
  carries **48** commands and the MCP server **496**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's bins in bins are not here.** The tree's bins are a
  tree of their own, and a bin may be in a bin; here a bin holds the
  items and nothing else.
- **The tree's moving of an item to a bin is not here.** The tree may
  move an item from one bin to another; here an item is in the bin it
  was added to.

## 380. The reading of a cell

A cell may be read whole: the answer is everything the cell holds and
everything that is said about it.

### What was built

- The command `grid.cell.get` gives the **value** of a cell and its
  **type**, the **formula** it holds, the **text** it shows, the
  **format** and the **style** it carries, the **note** and the
  **link** that are on it, and the **merge** that covers it.
- A cell that holds a formula has the value its formula **computes**,
  because the value is derived.
- The **text** is the value written with the format of the cell: the
  conditional format that matches it, and the format of the style it
  names, and its own format otherwise.
- A cell that is **not there** is empty, and not an error.
- A node that is **not a sheet** is refused, and so is a sheet that is
  not there.

### What the port found

- **The tree's cell may hold a picture and this tree's cell does
  not.** The tree's `cell.get` says whether the cell holds a picture
  and gives the picture; here a cell holds a value, a formula, a
  format and a style, and the picture is not one of them.
- **The tree's cell may be part of a spilled range and this tree's
  cell does not.** The tree's `cell.get` says where a spilled range
  began and which range a cell belongs to; here a formula that spills
  is not a thing this tree has.
- **The tree's merge covers every cell of the region and this tree's
  covers the ones that are not the top left.** The tree's merged
  region is one cell and every cell of it is in it; here the **value**
  of a merged region is the value of its top left cell, and so the
  other cells of it are the ones that are covered.

### What it cost

- **Six tests** in the grid battery (`tests/cellread.rs`): a cell that
  holds a value being read, a cell that holds a formula having the
  value the formula computes, the format, the style, the note and the
  link being said, a cell that is covered by a merge saying so, a cell
  that is not there being empty, and a node that is not a sheet being
  refused.
- **One new command**: `grid.cell.get`. The grid battery now carries
  **64** commands and the MCP server **497**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's pictures and its spilled ranges are not here.** A cell
  may hold a picture in the tree and a formula may spill over the
  cells below it, and the tree's `cell.get` says both.
- **The tree's input text is not here.** The tree's `cell.get` says
  the **input** of a cell — what was typed into it, which is the
  formula and not the value — and here the formula is said and the
  input is not a thing a cell holds apart from it.

## 381. The shape and the name of a format

A format says how a number is written. It may be given by its **code**
— `0.00`, `"$"#,##0.00`, `yyyy-mm-dd` — or by its **name**, the way the
tree's ribbon names its formats.

### What was built

- A format may be given by its **code** or by its **name**. The names
  are `general`, `number`, `currency`, `percentage`, `fraction`,
  `scientific`, `short date` and `time`.
- A name says a **code**, and the **code is kept**: the name is a way
  of saying the code, and the cell is written with the code.
- The **scientific** format is here: `0.00E+00` — a mantissa and an
  exponent, and the exponent moves one place at a time. A mantissa
  that rounds up to ten moves the exponent one place on, and a zero
  has no exponent to move.
- The names this tree **does not write** — `accounting`, `comma`,
  `long date` and `text` — are **refused with the reason**: the
  tree's fills, the tree's long date and the tree's text.
- Every door that takes a format takes a name: `grid.cell.format`,
  `grid.style.add`, `grid.style.set`, `grid.conditional.set`, and the
  `format` of `grid.cell.date` and `grid.cell.time`.

### What the port found

- **The tree's names are a ribbon over a mapping, and the mapping has
  a fallback.** The tree's `format_code_for` maps a name to a code, and
  a name that is not in its table is taken **as a code**. Here a name
  that is not one of ours is refused: a format that is quietly ignored
  is a format the user believes in and the program does not have.
- **The tree's scientific code is a language and here it is a shape.**
  The tree's step may be more than one place, and its `?` placeholders
  pad with spaces — `#.#E+#` gives `0.E+0`. Here the whole part of the
  mantissa is a single placeholder and the exponent moves one place at
  a time.
- **The tree's accounting and comma codes are fills.** They write
  spaces where the number is not and put the symbol at the edge; this
  tree has no fill and writes no spaces that are not there.
- **The tree's text format keeps the text a number was written with**,
  and this tree does not: a cell keeps its **value** and its **format**,
  and the text of a number is written by the format.

### What it cost

- **Fourteen tests** in the grid battery (`tests/formatnames.rs`): a
  name saying the code it names, the number, percentage, fraction and
  scientific names, the short date and the time names, a name given to
  a style and to a conditional format, the accounting and text names
  refused with their reasons, a name that is not one refused, and a
  code that is still a code.
- **One new module**: `formatnames`. **No new command**: the grid
  battery still carries **64** commands and the MCP server **497**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's fills, its long date and its text format are not here.**
  Each of them is refused with the reason, and the reason is a
  statement about this tree and not about the tree.
- **The tree's scientific step is not here.** A code whose mantissa has
  more than one whole placeholder is refused.
- **The tree's locale tags are not here.** The tree's `Time` is
  `[$-F400]h:mm:ss AM/PM`, and here the time is `h:mm:ss AM/PM`: the
  clock of twelve is the clock, and the locale of it is a thing this
  tree does not keep.

## 382. The reading of a media item

A media item may be read whole: the answer is everything the item
holds and everything that is said about it.

### What was built

- The command `film.item.get` gives the **name** of an item, the **id**
  it has in the editor, the **path** of the media, how long it is in
  **frames**, whether it was made **offline** on purpose, and the
  **label** it carries.
- The **bin** the item is in is derived: it is the item's place in the
  tree.
- The **clips** that play the item are derived: they are the edges
  that name it.
- A fact that is **not there** is said as nothing: an item with no
  path has no path, and an item with no label is in no group — the
  tree's own rule.
- A node that is **not there** is refused, and so is a node that is
  not an item.

### What the port found

- **The tree's item carries much more than this tree's item.** The
  tree's item holds the **media** it points at, an **interpretation**,
  the **marks** in and out, the **markers** on it, a **proxy**, and the
  **identity** of the file — its size and a fingerprint, so that a
  relinking may tell a moved original from another file of the same
  name. Here an item holds four facts and a label: the id it has in
  the editor, the path, the length and the offline flag.
- **The tree's offline is two things and this tree's is one.** The
  tree's item may be made offline **on purpose**, and a file that is
  merely missing is found out at run time by the media pool. Here the
  flag says that the item was made offline on purpose and says
  nothing about whether the file is there.
- **The tree's marks are not here.** A mark in and a mark out belong to
  the media, and a clip plays the material between them; here the
  material a clip plays is the clip's own **source in**.

### What it cost

- **Six tests** in the film battery (`tests/itemreading.rs`): an item
  being read whole, the bin of an item being derived, the clips that
  play an item being derived, a label being said, a node that is not
  there being refused, and a node that is not an item being refused.
- **One new command**: `film.item.get`. The film battery now carries
  **49** commands and the MCP server **498**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's media, its proxies and its identity are not here.** An
  item here says where the media is and how long it is, and the tree
  says much more about the file itself.
- **The tree's media pool is not here.** The tree's pool lists the
  media of a project with the columns it chooses, and it finds the
  media that is missing; here the project is read node by node.
- **The tree's relinking is not here**, and so the fingerprint that
  would tell a moved original from another file of the same name is
  not here either.

## 383. The reading of a name

A name is a word that stands for a range of cells, and a name may be
read: the answer is the range it stands for and the values of the cells
of that range.

### What was built

- The command `grid.name.get` gives the **range** a name stands for,
  the **sheet** it is in, and the **values** of the cells of the range,
  row by row.
- The values are **derived**: the book computes them, so a cell that
  holds a formula has the value the formula computes.
- A name that is **not there** is refused, and so is a workbook that
  is not there, a node that is not a workbook, and a name whose **sheet
  is gone** — the name stands for a range of a sheet that is not there.

### What the port found

- **The tree's name may be more than a range.** The tree's name holds
  a **formula** and not only a range of cells, so a name may be a
  constant — the tree's own macro names hold constants — or an
  expression. Here a name stands for a range of cells and nothing else:
  the range names its sheet, so a name is never a name for "the sheet
  it was written on".
- **The tree's name has a scope and this tree's does not.** The tree's
  name may belong to a sheet or to the workbook, and the sheet's own
  name wins. Here a name is **workbook** wide, and every sheet of the
  workbook may use it.
- **The tree's name may be hidden and may carry a comment, and this
  tree's does not.** The tree keeps a hidden flag and a comment on a
  name; here a name is a word and the range it stands for.

### What it cost

- **Five tests** in the grid battery (`tests/namereading.rs`): a name
  being read, the values of a name being derived, a name that is not
  there being refused, a workbook that is not there and a node that is
  not a workbook being refused, and a name whose sheet is gone being
  refused.
- **One new command**: `grid.name.get`. The grid battery now carries
  **65** commands and the MCP server **499**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's formulas in names are not here**, and so a name that is
  a constant is not here either.
- **The tree's sheet-scoped names are not here**: a name here belongs
  to the workbook and to every sheet of it.
- **The tree's hidden names and its comments on names are not here.**

## 384. The reading of a sheet

A sheet may be read whole: the answer is everything the sheet holds
and everything that is said about it.

### What was built

- The command `grid.sheet.get` gives the **name** of a sheet, the
  **workbook** it is in, its **used range**, how many **cells** hold
  something, its **view** — the gridlines, the headings, the zeros,
  the direction it runs in and the **frozen panes** — its **zoom**, the
  **rows** and **columns** that are hidden, its **protection**, and the
  **calendar** its dates are counted in.
- The **used range** and the number of cells are **derived**: the used
  range is the stretch of the sheet that holds something, and it is
  computed every time the sheet is read.
- A sheet that holds **nothing** has no used range, and that is said
  as nothing and not as an empty range.
- A sheet that is **not there** is refused, and so is a node that is
  not a sheet.

### What the port found

- **The tree's sheet is a whole struct and here it is a node with a
  payload.** The tree's sheet carries the cells, the columns and the
  rows, the merges, the freeze, the zoom, the conditional formats, the
  validations, the tables, the autofilter, the comments, the
  hyperlinks, the charts, the images, the shapes, the sparklines, the
  slicers, the pivot tables and the protection — a great deal that is
  here a fact of another kind, or is not here at all.
- **The tree's view has more flags than this tree's.** The tree's
  sheet may show the formulas, may show the outline symbols, may put
  the summary rows below and the summary columns to the right, and it
  has a **view mode** — normal, page layout, page break preview. Here
  a view is the gridlines, the headings, the zeros, the direction the
  sheet runs in and the frozen panes.
- **The tree's protection names the ranges that may still be edited,
  and a cell's locked flag comes from its style.** Here a protected
  sheet is locked as a whole, and the protection says what may still
  be done to it — the sorting, the filtering and the formatting.

### What it cost

- **Six tests** in the grid battery (`tests/sheetreading.rs`): a sheet
  being read whole, a sheet that holds nothing having no used range,
  the view being said, the hidden rows and columns being said, the
  protection being said, and a sheet that is not there and a node that
  is not a sheet being refused.
- **One new command**: `grid.sheet.get`. The grid battery now carries
  **66** commands and the MCP server **500**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's edit ranges are not here**, and so the locked flag of a
  cell's style is not here either: a sheet here is locked as a whole.
- **The tree's charts, images, shapes, sparklines, slicers and pivot
  tables are not here**, and neither are its tables and its autofilter
  as things a sheet carries.
- **The tree's page layout and its page break preview are not here**:
  the view here is the view of the grid.

## 385. The reading of a clip

A clip may be read whole: the answer is everything the clip holds and
everything that is said about it.

### What was built

- The command `film.clip.get` gives the **name** a clip is shown by,
  where it **starts**, how long it is, where in the media it
  **begins**, how fast it **plays**, whether it **plays** at all, its
  **label**, its **link** to the clip beside it, the **frame hold** in
  it, and whether it runs **backwards**.
- Three of the facts of the answer are **derived**: where the clip
  **ends** is its start and its length, the **material** it plays is
  its length times its speed, and the **track**, the **sequence** and
  the **item** it belongs to are its place in the tree and the edges
  that name it.
- A fact that is **not there** is said as nothing: a clip with no
  label has no label, and a clip with no frame hold holds no frame.
- A clip that is **not there** is refused, and so is a node that is
  not a clip.

### What the port found

- **The tree's clip is a value in a list and here a clip is a node.**
  The tree's track holds a vector of clips, and a clip is a value with
  an id of the editor's own. Here a clip is a **node** of the kind
  `film.clip`, so that a clip may be named, labelled and read on its
  own, and the order of the timeline is derived rather than the order
  of the tree.
- **The tree's clip carries more than this tree's clip.** The tree's
  clip carries its **effects**, its **markers**, its **group**, the
  **gain** of an audio clip in decibels, the **scale to frame size**
  flag, the **essential sound** settings of an audio clip, the
  **multi-camera** selection and the **time interpolation** — how the
  frames are made when the speed is changed. Here a clip carries the
  timing and the flags and nothing else.
- **The tree's speed may be negative and this tree's is not.** In the
  tree a negative speed is the reverse and the clip has a `reverse`
  flag beside it; here the speed is a positive number and the reverse
  is its own flag.

### What it cost

- **Five tests** in the film battery (`tests/clipreading.rs`): a clip
  being read whole, the track, the sequence and the item being
  derived, a label and a frame hold being said, a clip that does not
  play saying so, and a clip that is not there and a node that is not
  a clip being refused.
- **One new command**: `film.clip.get`. The film battery now carries
  **50** commands and the MCP server **501**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's effects on a clip are not here**, and neither are its
  markers, its group or its gain.
- **The tree's multi-camera and its time interpolation are not here.**
- **The tree's negative speed is not here**: a clip that runs
  backwards says so with its own flag.

## 386. The reading of a track

A track may be read whole: the answer is everything the track holds and
everything that is said about it.

### What was built

- The command `film.track.get` gives the **name** of a track, its
  **kind** — a video track or an audio one — and whether it is
  **locked**.
- Three of the facts of the answer are **derived**: the **clips** on
  the track are its children in the order they **start**, the
  **length** of the track is the end of its last clip, and the
  **sequence** the track is in is its place in the tree.
- A track that holds **no clip** is not long, and its length is said
  as zero because a track that holds nothing has no end.

### What the port found

- **The tree keeps two lists of tracks and here a track has a kind.**
  The tree's sequence holds a list of video tracks and a list of audio
  tracks, and the kind of a track is which list it is in. Here a track
  is a node and it **says** what it is — `video` or `audio` — in its
  payload, and the two kinds are one kind of thing with a name.
- **The tree's track carries the mixer and this tree's does not.** The
  tree's track has a **mute**, a **solo**, an **output toggle**, a
  **sync lock**, the **channel format**, the **volume** and the
  **pan**, and the track-level **effects** — the mixer's inserts. Here
  a track has its name, its kind and whether it is locked.
- **The tree's track holds its transitions and here it does not.** The
  transitions between the clips of a track are the tree's own; here a
  transition is a thing of its own and not a part of the track.

### What it cost

- **Four tests** in the film battery (`tests/trackreading.rs`): a
  track being read whole, the clips of a track being in the order they
  start, a locked track saying so, and a track that is not there and a
  node that is not a track being refused.
- **One new command**: `film.track.get`. The film battery now carries
  **51** commands and the MCP server **502**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's mixer is not here**, and so a track's mute, solo,
  volume, pan and channel format are not here.
- **The tree's track-level effects are not here**, and neither are the
  tree's transitions as parts of a track.
- **The tree's two lists of tracks are not here**: a track says what
  it is, and that is the whole of it.

## 387. The reading of a bin

A bin may be read whole: the answer is everything the bin holds and
everything that is said about it.

### What was built

- The command `film.bin.get` gives the **name** of a bin, the **items**
  in it and the **bins** in it.
- One fact of the answer is **derived**: the **parent** of a bin is the
  bin that holds it.
- A bin that is **not there** is refused, and so is a node that is not
  a bin.

### What the port found

- **The tree's bin holds its items and its bins in one list, and here
  the tree holds them apart.** The tree's bin has a vector of
  children, and each child is either an item or a bin — the kind of
  the child is in the child. Here a bin has **children**, and the kind
  of each child says what it is: a bin is a node of the kind
  `film.bin` and an item is a node of the kind `film.item`.
- **The tree's bin has no parent and this tree's bin has none
  either.** The tree's bin does not say which bin holds it — the parent
  is found by walking the tree from the root — and so the parent here
  is derived and not written down.
- **The tree's bin is a value inside a value and here a bin is a
  node.** The tree's project holds a root bin, and the root bin holds
  the bins, and the whole of it is a value in the project's file. Here
  a bin is a node of the tree, so it may be named, read and taken away
  on its own.

### What it cost

- **Three tests** in the film battery (`tests/binreading.rs`): a bin
  being read whole, a bin holding a bin and the bin in it knowing
  where it is, and a bin that is not there and a node that is not a
  bin being refused.
- **One new command**: `film.bin.get`. The film battery now carries
  **52** commands and the MCP server **503**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's project panel shows the bins as a tree and the project
  read here lists them flat.** The bin read says what a bin holds and
  where it is, and the project read lists every bin of the document.
- **The tree's bin has no other facts and neither has this one**: the
  tree's bins carry nothing but their name and their children.

## 388. The reading of a workbook

A workbook may be read whole: the answer is everything the workbook
holds and everything that is said about it.

### What was built

- The command `grid.workbook.get` gives the **name** of a workbook, its
  **sheets** — each with its name, its used range and how many cells
  hold something — the **names** it defines, the **styles** it carries,
  the **lists of words** of its own, and the **calendar** its serials
  are counted in.
- The sheets and their used ranges are **derived**: the sheets of a
  workbook are its children, and the used range of a sheet is the
  stretch of it that holds something.
- A workbook that is **not there** is refused, and so is a node that
  is not a workbook.

### What the port found

- **The tree's workbook carries much more than this tree's.** The
  tree's workbook carries a **theme**, the **calculation settings**,
  the **active sheet**, the **document properties**, the **structure
  protection** and its password, the **named cell styles** of the
  gallery, the **phonetic** readings of the shared strings, the **VBA
  project** carried through untouched, and the **separator** of the CSV
  it was read from. Here a workbook carries its sheets, its names, its
  styles, its lists of words and its calendar.
- **The tree's named style is a whole style and this tree's is a
  format.** The tree's style carries the font, the colour, the
  alignment and the number format; here a style carries a **number
  format** and nothing else, because the format is the only thing
  this tree writes on a cell.
- **The tree's sheets are a list and here they are children.** The
  tree's workbook holds a vector of sheets and the sheets hold their
  cells; here a workbook holds its sheets as children of the tree, and
  the order of the tabs is a fact of its own.

### What it cost

- **Three tests** in the grid battery (`tests/workbookreading.rs`): a
  workbook being read whole, its names and its styles being said, and
  a workbook that is not there and a node that is not a workbook being
  refused.
- **One new command**: `grid.workbook.get`. The grid battery now
  carries **67** commands and the MCP server **504**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's theme is not here**, and so the colours a workbook
  gives by name are not here.
- **The tree's structure protection is not here**, and neither is its
  password.
- **The tree's document properties and its calculation settings are
  not here.**

## 389. The rate of a sequence

A frame is a number, and the **rate** of a sequence says how many
frames there are in a second.

### What was built

- The command `film.sequence.rate.set` puts a **rate** on a sequence:
  the tree's own name — `25`, `23.976`, `29.97` — or the fraction
  behind it, `30000/1001`.
- The command `film.sequence.rate.get` reads it, and gives the length
  of the sequence in **frames** and in **seconds**.
- The length in seconds is **derived**: it is the frames and the rate.
- A sequence with **no rate** has no length in seconds, and that is
  said as nothing and not as a zero.
- A rate that is **not a rate** is refused, and so is a rate that is
  not positive, a sequence that is not there, and a node that is not
  an item.

### What the port found

- **The tree's rate is a fraction and this tree's is too.** The tree's
  frame rate is a numerator over a denominator, and the rates it
  offers are `24000/1001`, `24`, `25`, `30000/1001`, `30`, `48`, `50`,
  `60000/1001`, `60`, `120000/1001` and `120`. Here a rate is the same
  fraction, and it may be written with the name the tree shows or with
  the fraction behind it.
- **The tree has a rate in two places and this tree has it in one.**
  The tree's **sequence** carries a rate in its settings, and the
  tree's **media item** carries an **interpretation** with a rate of
  its own — the rate of the file, which may be different from the rate
  of the timeline it is cut into. Here a rate belongs to the sequence
  and to the timeline that hangs on it.
- **The tree's drop frame is not a rate and it is not here.** The
  tree's sequence may count 29.97 frames a second and **drop** the
  numbers of the frames it skips, so that the timecode keeps pace with
  the clock. A rate here is a rate and nothing else.

### What it cost

- **Seven tests** in the film battery (`tests/rates.rs`): a rate being
  set and read, the tree's rational rates being written two ways, the
  length in seconds being derived, a sequence with no rate having no
  length in seconds, a rate that is not a rate and a rate that is not
  positive being refused, and a sequence that is not there and a node
  that is not an item being refused.
- **Two new commands**: `film.sequence.rate.set` and
  `film.sequence.rate.get`. The film battery now carries **54** commands
  and the MCP server **506**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's timecode is not here**, and so the start timecode of a
  sequence and the drop frame are not here.
- **The tree's interpretation is not here**, and so the rate of a
  **media** file — as against the rate of the timeline it is cut into
  — is not here.
- **The tree's resolution and its pixel aspect ratio are not here**:
  the tree's sequence settings carry them beside the rate.

## 390. The comment on a block

A comment is something somebody said about a piece of a document: who
said it and what they said.

### What was built

- The command `prose.comment.set` puts a **comment** on a block, the
  command `prose.comment.get` reads it, and the command
  `prose.comment.delete` takes it away.
- A block has at most one comment, and a comment put on it again
  **replaces** the one that was there.
- The comment belongs to the **document** and names the **block** it is
  on, so it lives in the **payload** of the document: comments are
  numerous, and they hold nothing.
- The comment goes with the **block**: a block that is taken away takes
  its comment with it, and a comment on a block that is not there is a
  comment on nothing.
- A block with **no comment** has no comment, and that is said as
  nothing and not as an error. A comment with **no author** is
  refused, and so is a comment that is taken away that is not there.

### What the port found

- **The tree's comment anchors to a range of words and here it names a
  block.** The tree's comment is a range in a story — the words it
  covers are marked in the text — and a comment may be in the middle of
  a sentence. Here a comment is on a **block**, and the block is the
  smallest thing a comment may be on.
- **The tree's comment carries more than this tree's.** The tree's
  comment has the **initials** of its author, the **date** it was
  made, the comment it is a **reply to**, whether it is **resolved**,
  and the **durable id** Word keeps it by. Here a comment has who said
  it and what they said.
- **The tree's comment text lives in a part and here it lives in the
  comment.** The tree's document holds its parts beside it and a
  comment names the part its words are in; here the words are in the
  comment itself, which is in the payload of the document.

### What it cost

- **Eight tests** in the prose battery (`tests/comments.rs`): a comment
  being put and read, a block with no comment having none, a comment
  put again replacing the one that was there, a comment being taken
  away, a comment with no author being refused, a comment that is not
  there not being taken away, the comment going with the block, and a
  node that is not a block being refused.
- **Three new commands**: `prose.comment.set`, `prose.comment.get` and
  `prose.comment.delete`. The prose battery now carries **18** commands
  and the MCP server **509**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's replies are not here**: a comment that answers another
  comment is not a thing this tree has.
- **The tree's resolved flag is not here**, and neither is the tree's
  date.
- **The tree's comment on a range of words is not here**: a comment
  here is on a block and not on a range.

## 391. The numbering of a block

A list says what its items are numbered like — `1.`, `a)`, `i.` or a
bullet — and a block is in a list at a level. The number shown beside
the block is **derived**.

### What was built

- The command `prose.list.add` puts a **list** in a document, of one
  of the tree's nine kinds — or of a **single character**, which is a
  bullet of its own.
- The command `prose.block.numbering` puts a **block** in a list at a
  **level**, and the command `prose.block.number` reads the number.
- The number is **derived**: it is the count of the blocks of the list
  before it and the format of the level. So a block that is moved is
  renumbered, and nothing is written down that could be wrong.
- The **levels** are the tree's: a list kind says what each of its
  nine levels looks like, and the kinds that cycle — `1. a. i.` —
  cycle every three.
- A block that is in **no list** has no number, and that is said as
  nothing. A kind that is **not a kind** is refused, and so is a level
  beyond the ninth, a list that is not there and a node that is not a
  block.

### What the port found

- **The tree has two lists where this tree has one.** The tree keeps
  an **abstract** list — the definition with its levels — and the
  **lists** that use it, each with its own overrides. Here a list is
  one thing: its kind, and the blocks that are in it.
- **The tree's list is on the paragraph's properties and this tree's
  is on an edge.** The tree's paragraph carries the number of its list
  and its level in its properties; here the block names the list with
  a **relation**, the way it names a style — the third time an edge
  has answered "what is this relationship?".
- **The tree counts in sixty-two formats and this tree counts in
  six.** The tree's number formats include the Japanese, the Chinese,
  the Korean, the Hebrew, the Hindi and the Thai; the ones a list
  needs are decimal, upper and lower roman, upper and lower letters,
  and the bullet.
- **The tree's letters repeat and do not count in twenty-sixes.** The
  tree writes `a` to `z` and then `aa` to `zz` and then `aaa` — the
  twenty-seventh item is `aa`, not `ba`. Here the letters are the
  tree's.

### What it cost

- **Ten tests** in the prose battery (`tests/numbering.rs`): a block
  in a list being numbered, the number counting the blocks before it,
  the number being derived when a block is moved, a level counting in
  its own format, a bullet list showing a bullet, a list being a
  bullet of its own, a block in no list having no number, and a kind
  that is not a kind, a level that is not a level, a list that is not
  there and a node that is not a block being refused.
- **Three new commands**: `prose.list.add`, `prose.block.numbering`
  and `prose.block.number`. The prose battery now carries **21**
  commands and the MCP server **512**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's abstract lists are not here**, and so a list's own
  override of a level is not here either.
- **The tree's sixty-two number formats are not here**: the six that
  a list needs are here and the rest are not.
- **The tree's restart rules are not all here**: a deeper level
  restarts when a shallower level is used again, and the tree's own
  `lvlRestart` is not here.

## 392. The page of a document

A document is printed on pages, and a page has a size and margins.

### What was built

- The command `prose.page.set` puts the **page** of a document, and the
  command `prose.page.get` reads it.
- The size and the margins are in **points** — a seventy-second of an
  inch — because that is the tree's own unit.
- A document that has no page has the **tree's default page**: US
  Letter, 612 by 792 points, with an inch of margin on every side.
- A margin that is not given keeps the one the page has.
- Whether the page is a **landscape** one is **derived**: it is wider
  than it is tall.
- A page that is **not a page** is refused: a size of nothing, a
  negative margin and a page too big are all refused. A document that
  is not there is refused, and so is a node that is not a document.

### What the port found

- **The tree keeps a flag and a size that say the same thing.** The
  tree's section carries a `landscape` flag **and** a width and a
  height that are **already swapped** for it — two facts where one is
  enough, and two that can disagree. Here the page carries the size
  and the flag is derived.
- **The tree's page belongs to a section and here it belongs to the
  document.** The tree's document holds a body of blocks and the
  properties of the **last** section, and a document may have many
  sections. Here a document has one page.
- **The tree's page carries much more than a size.** The tree's page
  has the **header** and **footer** distances, the **gutter**, the
  **columns**, the **headers** and **footers** themselves, the **title
  page** flag, the **page numbering**, the **line numbers**, the
  **borders** and the **direction** the text runs in. Here a page has
  a size and four margins.

### What it cost

- **Five tests** in the prose battery (`tests/page.rs`): a document
  having the tree's default page, the page being set, a landscape page
  being derived, a page that is not a page being refused, and a
  document that is not there and a node that is not a document being
  refused.
- **Two new commands**: `prose.page.set` and `prose.page.get`. The
  prose battery now carries **23** commands and the MCP server **514**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's sections are not here**, and so a document with more
  than one page setup is not here either.
- **The tree's headers and footers are not here**, and neither are the
  header and footer distances or the gutter.
- **The tree's columns and its page borders are not here**, and neither
  is the tree's page numbering.

## 393. The links of a block

A run may carry a link: the target it points at. Whether that target
may be **opened** is derived.

### What was built

- A run may carry a **link**, and the runs of a block say it.
- The command `prose.block.links` gives every run that carries a link,
  with the **words** it covers — derived — the **target** it points at,
  and whether the target **may be opened**.
- The rule is the **tree's own**: a link the system may follow is a
  **web link** or a **mail link** — `http`, `https` and `mailto` — and
  nothing else.
- Each kind of target is refused for its own **reason**: a script, a
  `data:` link, a `file:` link, a link to **another machine** and a
  relative link each say why they may not be opened.
- The rule is **exact**: a leading space or a control character makes
  the target not a link at all.
- A target that is not a text is refused, and so is a target too long
  to be a target.

### What the port found

- **The tree has two rules and this tree has one.** The tree has a
  rule for a link the system may **follow** — a web link or a mail
  link — and another for a link that may be **written out** as an
  `href`: that one allows a bookmark and a relative path as well. The
  tree's two rules serve two purposes, and a kit that opens links has
  the first of them.
- **The tree's target is read the way a browser reads a URL, and the
  rule is exact.** The tree drops ASCII control characters and spaces
  before it reads the scheme, so `java\nscript:` is a script; and the
  rule it uses for following does not drop them, so ` https://…` is
  not a link at all. Here the exact rule is the one that is ported,
  and a target with a space in front of it is not a link.
- **The tree's link to another machine is refused for the reason it
  is refused.** A protocol-relative `//host` and a UNC `\\host` name
  another machine, and following one on Windows would send the user's
  own credentials with it. Here the refusal says that.
- **The tree keeps the link in the run's own properties and this tree
  keeps it in the run's payload.** The tree's hyperlink is a character
  property with a target and an anchor; here a run is an interval over
  the text with the formatting on it, and the link is one of the
  things a run carries.

### What it cost

- **Eight tests** in the prose battery (`tests/links.rs`): a web link
  being opened, a mail link being opened, a script and a link to
  another machine and a relative link not being opened, the rule being
  exact, a run with no link not being a link and a link that is not a
  text being refused, and a block that is not there and a node that is
  not a block being refused.
- **One new command**: `prose.block.links`. The prose battery now
  carries **24** commands and the MCP server **515**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's export rule is not here**: a bookmark and a relative
  path may be written into an exported file in the tree, and here a
  link that is not a web link or a mail link may not be opened.
- **The tree's anchor is not here**: the tree's hyperlink names a place
  in the document as well as a target, and here a link is a target.

## 394. The revisions of a block

A run may be marked as a revision: it was inserted, it was deleted, or
its format was changed — and by whom.

### What was built

- A run may carry a **revision**, and the runs of a block say it.
- The command `prose.block.revisions` gives every run that carries a
  revision, with its **kind**, its **author**, its **date** and the
  **words** it covers — the words are derived.
- The kinds are the **tree's own**: an insertion, a deletion and a
  format change.
- A revision with **no author** is refused, and so is a revision of a
  kind that is not one of the three, and a date that is not a text.
- The date is the text the caller gives, because this tree has **no
  clock of its own**.

### What the port found

- **The tree's revisions are of the document and this tree's are of
  the run.** The tree keeps a list of revisions on the document and
  the runs point into it by number, so a revision is a thing of the
  document that a run refers to. Here a revision is **on the run**,
  beside the link and the formatting — a run is an interval over the
  text with the things that are true of it.
- **The tree has three kinds and this tree has three kinds.** The
  tree's are an insertion, a deletion and a format change, and they
  are the three here.
- **The tree's move is not here.** The tree's revision has a **move
  name** that links a deletion to the insertion that replaced it — the
  two ends of a move. Here a revision is one of the three kinds and
  nothing else.

### What it cost

- **Five tests** in the prose battery (`tests/revisions.rs`): a run
  being an insertion, the kinds being the tree's own, a revision
  carrying a date, a revision with no author and a revision of a kind
  that is not one being refused, and a block that is not there and a
  node that is not a block being refused.
- **One new command**: `prose.block.revisions`. The prose battery now
  carries **25** commands and the MCP server **516**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's move is not here**: the two ends of a move are not
  linked, and so a moved paragraph is a deletion and an insertion and
  not a move.
- **The tree's revisions live on the document and here they live on
  the run**, and so a revision is not a thing the document keeps a
  list of.

## 395. The footnotes of a document

A footnote is a note that belongs to the foot of the page, and the text
that points at it is a reference.

### What was built

- The command `prose.footnote.add` puts a **footnote** in a document,
  and a **run** may point at one.
- The command `prose.block.footnotes` gives every run that points at a
  footnote, with the **number** of the footnote, what it **says**, and
  the **words** that point at it — the words are derived.
- The **number** is **derived**: it is where the footnote is referenced
  in the document, and the first reference gives the footnote its
  number. A footnote that is referenced again is not renumbered, and a
  footnote that is not referenced has no number at all.
- A reference to a footnote that is **not there** is refused, and so
  is a reference to a node that is not a footnote.

### What the port found

- **The tree's footnote is a part of the file and here it is a node.**
  The tree keeps the footnotes of a document in a **part** beside it —
  the file's own `footnotes.xml` — and the paragraph points at it by
  an inline object that carries the footnote's number. Here a footnote
  is a **node** of the tree, and a run names it.
- **The tree's number is a fact of the section and here it is
  derived.** The tree's note options say where the notes go — the
  bottom of the page or the end of the document — and how they are
  numbered: the **format**, the **start** and the **restart**. Here
  the number is worked out from where the footnote is referenced.
- **The tree has footnotes and endnotes and this tree has footnotes.**
  The tree's endnote is the same kind of note at the end of the
  document, and the two have their own options each.

### What it cost

- **Five tests** in the prose battery (`tests/footnotes.rs`): a
  paragraph pointing at a footnote, the number of a footnote being
  derived, a footnote that is not referenced having no number, a
  reference to a footnote that is not there and a reference to a node
  that is not a footnote being refused, and a block that is not there
  and a node that is not a block being refused.
- **Two new commands**: `prose.footnote.add` and `prose.block.footnotes`.
  The prose battery now carries **27** commands and the MCP server
  **518**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's endnotes are not here**, and so the two kinds of note
  are one kind here.
- **The tree's note options are not here**: the format of the number,
  the number it starts at, and the rule that restarts it are all the
  tree's own and none of them is here.
- **The tree's footnotes are counted in the word count and here they
  are not**: a footnote is a note and not words of the document.

## 396. The bookmarks of a document

A bookmark is a name for a place in a document, so that a link may
point at it: `#the-name`.

### What was built

- The command `prose.block.bookmark` puts a **bookmark** on a block and
  the command `prose.block.bookmark.delete` takes it away.
- The command `prose.document.bookmarks` gives the **bookmarks** of a
  document: they are **derived**, and they are the blocks that carry a
  name.
- A name has the rule Word has: it begins with a letter or an
  underscore, the rest of it is letters, digits and underscores, and
  it is at most forty characters long.
- A name another block of the document already carries is **refused**:
  two places with one name are one place, and a link to that name
  would be a link to nothing in particular.
- A link to a **place in this document** may be opened, and a link to
  a place that is **not there** may not — and the refusal says which
  place is missing.

### What the port found

- **The tree's bookmark is an inline object and here it is the
  block's own name.** The tree's bookmark is a `BookmarkStart` object
  in the paragraph, with a matching `BookmarkEnd`, and a paragraph may
  carry many. Here a block carries at most one name, in its payload.
- **The tree's bookmarks may be read in order and here they are
  derived.** The tree walks the body and gives every bookmark's name
  with the position it is at. Here the bookmarks are the blocks that
  carry a name.
- **The tree's rule for a link that leaves the document is not the
  rule for a link that stays inside it.** The tree's rule for
  **following** a link is web or mail; a bookmark is a link that stays
  in the document and is not handed to the system at all. Here a link
  to a place of this document may be opened when the place is there.

### What it cost

- **Six tests** in the prose battery (`tests/bookmarks.rs`): a block
  carrying a bookmark, a name that is not one being refused, a name
  that is already there being refused, a bookmark being taken away and
  a block with no bookmark being refused, a link to a place being
  opened and a link to a place that is not there not being opened, and
  a block that is not there and a node that is not a block being
  refused.
- **Three new commands**: `prose.block.bookmark`,
  `prose.block.bookmark.delete` and `prose.document.bookmarks`. The
  prose battery now carries **30** commands and the MCP server **521**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's bookmark ranges are not here**: the tree's bookmark has
  a beginning and an end and may cover a range of text, and here a
  bookmark names a block.
- **The tree keeps a bookmark name as it is and here a name has a
  rule.** The tree writes the name into the file and leaves the
  application's rules to the application; here a name that may not be
  one is refused, and a name that is already in the document is
  refused too.
- **The tree's links to places are not followed here either**: a link
  to a place of this document may be opened, and nothing follows it.

## 397. The statistics of a formula

A formula may ask about the **shape** of a set of numbers.

### What was built

- The functions `MEDIAN`, `MODE`, `STDEV`, `STDEVP`, `VAR`, `VARP`,
  `LARGE`, `SMALL`, `RANK`, `PERCENTILE`, `QUARTILE` and `COUNTBLANK`.
- The **middle** is the middle number, and the mean of the two middle
  ones when the count is even; the **mode** is the number that occurs
  most often; the **spread** is the deviation and the variance, the
  sample one and the population one.
- The **order statistics** are the k-th largest and the k-th smallest,
  and the **place** of a number in a list is its rank, counting from
  the largest unless the order says otherwise.
- The **percentile** is the value at a fraction of the way through the
  numbers, and the **quartile** is the quarter of it.
- The errors are the **tree's**: a middle of no numbers is `#NUM!`, a
  spread of fewer than two numbers is `#DIV/0!`, a k that is not in
  the numbers is `#NUM!`, a number that is not in the list has no
  place and is `#N/A`, and a set with no number twice has no mode and
  is `#N/A`.

### What the port found

- **The tree's statistics are in three places and this tree's are in
  one.** The tree has the **descriptive** statistics — the middle, the
  mode, the spread, the order statistics — and the **distributions**
  — the percentile and the quartile — and the **regression** — the
  correlation, the slope and the intercept — as three modules of their
  own. Here the first two are one module.
- **The tree's percentile has an inclusive and an exclusive form and
  here there is one.** The tree has `PERCENTILE.INC` and
  `PERCENTILE.EXC`, and the two differ in where the fraction is
  measured from. Here the **inclusive** one is the one that is
  ported, and the name is `PERCENTILE` — the tree's own name for the
  inclusive form.
- **The tree's quartile is the percentile of a quarter.** The tree
  reads the quarter, rounds it down, and asks for that fraction of
  the numbers; here it is the same, and a quarter that is not one of
  the four is `#NUM!`.
- **The tree's mode may be many and here it is one.** The tree has
  `MODE.SNGL` and `MODE.MULT`, and the second gives every value that
  occurs most often. Here the mode is the first of them — the tree's
  `MODE.SNGL` — and a set with no number twice has no mode.

### What it cost

- **Nine tests** in the grid battery (`tests/statistics.rs`): the
  middle of the numbers, the most frequent of them, the spread, the
  k-th largest and smallest, the place of a number in a list, the
  value at a fraction of the numbers, the cells that hold nothing,
  and the tree's errors — a middle of no numbers, a spread of fewer
  than two numbers, a k that is not in the numbers, a number that is
  not in the list and a set with no number twice.
- **One new module**: `statistics`. **No new command**: a function is
  not a command, and the grid battery still carries **67** commands and
  the MCP server **521**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's regression statistics are not here**: the correlation,
  the slope and the intercept are not here.
- **The tree's exclusive percentile is not here**, and neither is the
  tree's `MODE.MULT` with every value that occurs most often.
- **The tree's distributions are not here**: the normal, the binomial
  and the Poisson distributions the tree has are not here.

## 398. The arithmetic of a formula

A formula may do arithmetic on a number, and the rules are the tree's
own.

### What was built

- The functions `ROUND`, `ROUNDUP`, `ROUNDDOWN`, `TRUNC`, `INT`,
  `MROUND`, `CEILING`, `FLOOR`, `MOD`, `QUOTIENT`, `ABS`, `SIGN`,
  `SQRT`, `POWER`, `EXP`, `LN`, `LOG`, `LOG10`, `PI`, `PRODUCT`,
  `SUMSQ`, `GCD` and `LCM`.
- `ROUND` rounds **halves away from zero**, and it does so on the
  number written with **fifteen significant digits** — so `2.675`
  rounds to `2.68` and not to `2.67`.
- `ROUNDUP` rounds away from zero, `ROUNDDOWN` toward zero, `TRUNC` is
  the same as `ROUNDDOWN`, and `INT` is the floor.
- `MOD` is the rest of a division and it keeps the **sign of the
  divisor**, so `MOD(-3,2)` is `1`.
- The errors are the **tree's**: zero to a negative power is
  `#DIV/0!`, zero to the zeroth is `#NUM!`, a negative number to a
  half power is `#NUM!`, the root of a negative number is `#NUM!`,
  the logarithm of a number that is not positive is `#NUM!`, a base
  of one is `#DIV/0!`, and `GCD` and `LCM` are the **whole** numbers
  and a number that is not one is `#NUM!`.

### What the port found

- **The tree's rounding is careful and a naive rounding is not.** The
  tree does not scale a number and round it — it writes the number
  with fifteen significant digits, rounds those digits, and reads them
  back. That is why `2.675` rounds to `2.68` and not to `2.67`, and
  why `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.3`. Here the same fifteen digits are written
  and the same rounding is done on them.
- **The tree has a family of rounding functions and here the family is
  the same.** The tree has `CEILING`, `CEILING.MATH`,
  `CEILING.PRECISE`, `FLOOR`, `FLOOR.MATH` and `FLOOR.PRECISE`, and
  the ones that differ are the ones that take a **mode** — how a
  negative number rounds. Here `CEILING` and `FLOOR` are the
  tree's own, and the ones with a mode are not here.
- **The tree's remainder has a rule of its own.** The tree's `%` is
  an exact remainder, and the tree adds the divisor back when the
  signs differ — so the rest always keeps the sign of the divisor and
  is never as big as the divisor. Here the same.
- **The tree's `QUOTIENT` cuts and does not round**, and it divides
  by nothing with `#DIV/0!`. Here it is the same.

### What it cost

- **Nine tests** in the grid battery (`tests/arithmetic.rs`): a half
  rounding away from zero on the fifteen digits, the rounding up and
  down and the cut and the floor, a number rounded to a multiple, the
  rest of a division and the whole of it, the root and the power and
  the sign, the logarithms, the product and the sum of the squares,
  the divisor and the multiple, and the constant.
- **One new module**: `arithmetic`. **No new command**: a function is
  not a command, and the grid battery still carries **67** commands and
  the MCP server **521**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's trig functions are not here** — the sines and the
  tangents and their inverses — and neither are its hyperbolic ones.
- **The tree's `CEILING.MATH` and `FLOOR.MATH` are not here**, and
  neither are the precise ones: a rounding with a mode is not here.
- **The tree's combinatorial functions are not here**: the factorial,
  the combinations and the permutations.

## 399. The trigonometry of a formula

A formula may ask about an angle.

### What was built

- The functions `SIN`, `COS`, `TAN`, `ASIN`, `ACOS`, `ATAN`, `ATAN2`,
  `SINH`, `COSH`, `TANH`, `ASINH`, `ACOSH`, `ATANH`, `COT`, `COTH`,
  `CSC`, `CSCH`, `SEC`, `SECH`, `ACOT`, `ACOTH`, `DEGREES` and
  `RADIANS`.
