  tree's pen tool makes a mask of a path, and a path of nothing is
  nothing.

### What it cost

- **Five tests** in the fx battery (`tests/masks.rs`): a mask may be
  made on a layer, a mask with no vertices is refused, the mode of a
  mask may be set, a mask may be inverted and locked, and a mask may
  be taken away.
- **One new module** (`masks`): the masks of a layer are their own.
  The fx battery now carries **36** commands and the MCP server
  **542**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's tangents of a mask are not here**: the vertices and the
  closed flag are here and the curve between the vertices is a line.
- **The tree's feather, opacity and expansion are not proved here**
  by a test, though the mask carries them.

## 430. The time of a composition

A compositing application has a **time cursor**: the place in the
composition where it is looking.

### What was built

- The commands `fx.time.set`, `fx.time.get`, `fx.time.start`,
  `fx.time.end` and `fx.time.step`.
- The time is a **frame** of the composition. `set` puts it at a
  frame, `get` says where it is, `start` and `end` take it to the
  beginning and the end, and `step` moves it by a number of frames —
  a negative number steps back.
- The **rules** are the tree's: the time is never before the start of
  the composition, the **end** is the end of the composition, and a
  step that would go before the start stops at the start.

### What the port found

- **The tree's time is measured in seconds and this tree's in
  frames**: a composition here is a number of frames long, and a time
  that is not a whole number of frames is refused. This is a
  difference and not a mistake, and it is written down here.
- **The tree keeps the time in its session**, one for each
  composition, and so the time of a composition is not saved with it.
  Here the time is a **fact of the composition** — its payload
  carries the frame — and so it is saved with it and read back with
  it.
- **The tree's time may be set beyond the last frame** of a
  composition and is not refused for it. Here the same.

### What it cost

- **Three tests** in the fx battery (`tests/time.rs`): the time may be
  set and read, it may go to the start and to the end, and it may be
  stepped.
- **One new module** (`time`): the time of a composition is its own.
  The fx battery now carries **41** commands and the MCP server
  **547**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's ten frames back and ten frames on** are not here as
  commands: a step of ten frames is a step of ten frames.
- **The tree's time of the source of a layer** is not here: a
  composition has one time and that is the one.

## 431. The stack of layers of a composition

A compositing composition is a **stack**: the layers stand in an
order, and the front of the stack is drawn over the rest of it.

### What was built

- The commands `fx.layer.list`, `fx.layer.arrange` and
  `fx.layer.rename`.
- `fx.layer.list` reads the stack, **the front first**. `fx.layer.
  arrange` moves a layer in it: `forward` is one step towards the
  front, `backward` is one step towards the back, `front` is the front
  of the stack and `back` is the back of it. `fx.layer.rename` gives
  a layer a name.
- The **rules** are the tree's: a layer that is already at the front
  and is told to go forward stays there, a layer that is already at
  the back and is told to go back stays there, a place that is not one
  of the four is refused, and a layer with no name is refused.

### What the port found

- **The tree arranges a selection of layers at once**, and its rules
  for a selection that is not contiguous are careful: each layer
  moves one step and the layers keep their order among themselves.
  Here a command arranges **one** layer — a command that takes a
  selection is a command that does not say what it does, and the
  tree's own rule is that a command does one thing (§ the registry).
- **The tree's order is the front first** — the layer that was added
  last is at the front — and here the children of the composition are
  in the order they were added, and so the front is the last of them.
  The test here says so.
- **The tree's `front` and `back` keep the order of the layers that
  are moved**, and here one layer is moved and there is no order to
  keep.

### What it cost

- **Four tests** in the fx battery (`tests/stack.rs`): the stack may
  be read, a layer may be moved in it, a place that is no place is
  refused, and a layer may be renamed.
- **One new module** (`stack`): the order of the layers is their own.
  The fx battery now carries **44** commands and the MCP server
  **550**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's arranging of a locked layer is not here**: a layer has
  no lock in this tree, and the refusals of a locked layer are the
  refusals of a track that is locked (§ §426).
- **The tree's layer selection is not here**: a command names the
  layer it acts on.

## 432. The selection of layers

The **selection** is what a person has picked out, or what an agent
has named.

### What was built

- The commands `fx.layer.select`, `fx.layer.deselect` and
  `fx.selection.get`.
- `fx.layer.select` **selects** layers — it replaces the selection —
  and `fx.layer.deselect` **takes layers out** of it and does not take
  the selection away. `fx.selection.get` reads what is selected, and
  may name it as well as count it.
- The **rules** are the tree's: a layer that is not in the document is
  not selected, and a node that is not a layer is refused.

### What the port found

- **The tree's selection is of the session and not of the document**,
  and here the same: the selection lives in the session, and the
  document is the truth and the selection is of the document. A
  selection that is not in the document is not a selection.
- **The tree's `selectNext` and `selectPrevious` walk the stack** —
  the layer above and the layer below the one that is selected — and
  here the stack is the stack of the composition (§ §431), but the
  walk itself is not here: a command that says which layer it means
  is a command that does one thing (§ the registry).

### What it cost

- **Three tests** in the fx battery (`tests/selection.rs`): layers may
  be selected, they may be taken out of the selection, and a layer
  that is not there is refused.
- **One new module** (`selection`): the selection of layers is its
  own. The fx battery now carries **47** commands and the MCP server
  **553**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's selection of a property is not here**: a selection here
  is of a node, and a property is a path in a node and not a node of
  its own.
- **The tree's walking of the stack with the selection is not here**:
  a command names the layer it acts on.

## 433. The settings of a layer

A CAD layer is more than a name: it has **settings**.

### What was built

- The commands `cad.layer.on`, `cad.layer.freeze`, `cad.layer.lock`,
  `cad.layer.color`, `cad.layer.fill`, `cad.layer.linetype`,
  `cad.layer.lineweight` and `cad.layer.list`.
- A layer may be **on** or off, **frozen** or not, **locked** or not;
  it may have a **colour** — an index or a name — the colour it is
  **drawn in** as `#rrggbb`, a **line type** and a **line weight** in
  millimetres. `cad.layer.list` reads the layers of a drawing and
  their settings.
- The **rules** are the tree's: a layer that is off or frozen is **not
  drawn**, a layer that is locked is drawn and may not be edited, a
  colour index of nothing is refused, and the words `ByLayer` and
  `ByBlock` are refused — a layer's colour is its own.

### What the port found

- **The tree's off layer and its frozen layer are not drawn, and so
  they are not in the extents**: the extents of a drawing are the box
  that holds what is drawn. Here the same, and the evaluator skips
  the entities of a layer that is off or frozen — so the extents
  change when a layer is turned off, which is the tree's rule and not
  a thing this tree decided.
- **The tree's `layer.set` is one command that sets any of the
  settings**, and here they are **one command each**: the tree's own
  rule is that a command does one thing (§ the registry), and a
  command that may set eight things is a command that does eight
  things.
- **The tree's colour of a layer may be an index or a name, and never
  `ByLayer` or `ByBlock`**: here the same, and the refusal says which
  colour was refused.

### What it cost

- **Four tests** in the cad battery (`tests/layersettings.rs`): the settings
  of a layer may be set, the flags of a layer may be set, a colour
  that is no colour is refused, and a layer that is off is not drawn.
- **One new module** (`layersettings`): the settings of a layer are their
  own. The cad battery now carries **16** commands and the MCP server
  **561**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's current layer is not here**: an entity names the layer
  it is on, and there is no layer that everything goes on.
- **The tree's plot flag and its transparency are not here**: what a
  drawing is plotted with is the host's business.

## 434. The curves of a drawing

A CAD drawing has **curves**: the ellipse and the polyline.

### What was built

- The commands `cad.entity.ellipse.add` and
  `cad.entity.polyline.add`, and the entity kinds `cad.entity.ellipse`
  and `cad.entity.polyline`.
- An **ellipse** is the tree's own: its **centre**, its **major
  axis** — a vector from the centre to the end of the major axis —,
  the **ratio** of the minor axis to the major one, and the two
  **angles** it runs from and to. A **polyline** is a list of
  **points** and whether it is **closed**.
- The **rules** are the tree's: the major axis is not of no length,
  the ratio is above nothing and at most one, and a polyline is made
  of at least two points.

### What the port found

- **The tree's ellipse is DXF-shaped**: the major axis is a **vector**
  and not a length, so an ellipse may be turned — and here the same,
  and the minor axis is the major one turned a quarter and made
  shorter by the ratio.
- **The tree's bounds of a whole ellipse are exact**, and here they
  are: the box of an ellipse is the box of its centre and its two
  half axes, and the test here says so.
- **The tree's bounds of an elliptical arc are exact** and are worked
  out from the derivative of the curve. Here the bounds of an **arc**
  are **sampled** — a difference, and it is written down here.
- **The tree's polyline may bulge** — a vertex may carry an arc — and
  here a polyline is straight between its vertices.

### What it cost

- **Four tests** in the cad battery (`tests/curves.rs`): an ellipse
  may be put in a block, an ellipse with a bad ratio is refused, a
  polyline may be put in a block, and a polyline of no points is
  refused.
- **One new module** (`curves`): the curves of a drawing are their
  own. The cad battery now carries **18** commands and the MCP server
  **563**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's polyline with a bulge is not here**: a polyline here
  is straight between its vertices.
- **The tree's bounds of an elliptical arc are not exact here**: they
  are sampled, and the test here does not claim otherwise.

## 435. The order the entities are drawn in

The entities of a block are drawn in an **order**, and an entity may
be moved in it.

### What was built

- The commands `cad.entity.list`, `cad.entity.front`,
  `cad.entity.back`, `cad.entity.forward` and `cad.entity.backward`.
- `cad.entity.list` reads the entities of a block in the order they
  are drawn. `front` and `back` move an entity to the front or to the
  back, and `forward` and `backward` move it one step.
- The **rules** are the tree's: the **front** is the top of the
  drawing and the top is drawn **last**, the **back** is drawn
  **first**, and an entity that is already at the front and is told
  to go to the front stays there.

### What the port found

- **The tree's entities live in a flat store and their order is a
  list**, and here the entities are the **children** of a block and
  the children are drawn in the order they stand in. So the order is
  the shape of the tree and not a field, and moving an entity is
  moving a child.
- **The tree's draw order moves a selection of entities at once** and
  here a command moves **one**: a command that takes a selection is a
  command that does not say what it does (§ the registry).

### What it cost

- **Four tests** in the cad battery (`tests/order.rs`): the order may
  be read, an entity may be brought to the front and sent to the
  back, an entity may be moved one step, and a node that is not an
  entity is refused.
- **One new module** (`order`): the order the entities are drawn in is
  their own. The cad battery now carries **23** commands and the MCP
  server **568**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's `above` and `under` are not here**: they move an entity
  above or below another one that is named, and here the order is
  moved by steps and not against a reference.
- **The tree's text to front is not here**: a text and an entity are
  the same thing here, and the order is the order.

## 436. The modification of an entity

A drawing is not a picture: things in it may be **moved**, **turned**
and **scaled**, and they may be **taken away**.

### What was built

- The commands `cad.entity.move`, `cad.entity.rotate`,
  `cad.entity.scale` and `cad.entity.remove`.
- A **move** takes a **vector**; a **turn** takes a **point** and an
  **angle in degrees**; a **scale** takes a **point** and a **factor**
  above nothing. A change of the geometry is a change of the geometry
  and of nothing else: the name of the entity stays, and the layer it
  is on stays.
- The **rules** are the tree's: a circle that is scaled gets a bigger
  radius and a circle that is turned keeps its radius, an ellipse
  that is scaled keeps its **ratio** and an ellipse that is turned has
  its **major axis** turned with it, a text that is scaled is a bigger
  text, and a factor of nothing is refused.

### What the port found

- **The tree's entities are a closed union and their modification is a
  change of the variant's fields.** Here an entity is a node of an
  **open kind**, and its modification is a change of the **geometry in
  its payload** — so a new kind of entity is modified by writing one
  more case and not by touching four places at once (§ the header).
- **The tree's turn of a text turns the text's own angle** and here
  the same: a text carries its angle and the turn adds to it.
- **The tree's turn is in degrees** and here the same, and the answer
  is **near** the number and not the number — a turn is a sine and a
  cosine, and the test here says so.

### What it cost

- **Four tests** in the cad battery (`tests/modify.rs`): an entity may
  be moved, it may be turned, it may be scaled, and it may be taken
  away.
- **One new module** (`modify`): the modification of an entity is its
  own. The cad battery now carries **27** commands and the MCP server
  **572**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's mirror was not here when this section was written**: an
  entity could be moved, turned and scaled, and not yet turned over a
  line. It is built now (§440).
- **The tree's copy of an entity was not here when this section was
  written**: an entity was made by a command that makes one, and there
  was no copy of it. It is built now (§439).


## 437. The measure of a drawing

A drawing is not only a picture of things: it is a set of things whose
**sizes** may be asked for.

### What was built

- The commands `cad.measure.length`, `cad.measure.area`,
  `cad.measure.radius` and `cad.measure.angle`.
- A **length** is the length of a path: a line is the distance between
  its ends, a polyline is the sum of its segments, a circle is its
  **circumference**, an arc is the piece of it that the arc is, and an
  ellipse is sampled along its curve.
- An **area** is the area **enclosed**: a circle is pi times the radius
  squared, an ellipse is pi times the two half axes, and a polyline is
  enclosed **only when it is closed**.
- A **radius** is the radius of a circle or an arc, and the
  **diameter** is twice it. An **angle** is the angle at a point
  between two directions, in **degrees**, and never more than a
  straight one.
- Every number is **derived**: it is worked out from the geometry in
  the payload every time it is asked for, and it is never stored. A
  stored measurement would be a second copy of the geometry, and a
  second copy is a copy that can be wrong.

### What the port found

- **The tree's measures are commands of their own, each answering about
  a different kind of thing.** Here the same: a length, an area, a
  radius and an angle are four commands and not one command with a
  mode. A command that asks "what do you want measured?" has already
  made the caller do the work the command should do.
- **The tree's area of an open polyline is nothing, and the tree says
  so.** Here the same, and the measure is **refused** rather than
  answered with a zero: a zero is a number, and a number that means
  "this was not asked properly" is a lie.
- **The tree's angle is worked out from two lines and their
  intersection.** Here the **vertex** is given: the angle is at a
  point, between two directions. Working the vertex out means extending
  two lines until they meet, and two parallel lines never meet — a
  case the tree answers with an error and this one does not have.

### What it cost

- **Ten tests** in the cad battery (`tests/measurements.rs`): the
  length of a line, of a circle and of a polyline, the area of a circle
  and of a closed polyline, the radius of a circle, the angle at a
  point, and the three refusals — the area of an open polyline, the
  radius of a line, and an angle whose direction has no length.
- **One new module** (`measurements`): the measure of a drawing is its
  own. The cad battery now carries **31** commands and the MCP server
  **576**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's arc was not here when this section was written**: the
  kind existed and the measure knew what an arc is, but no command
  made one. It is built now (§438), and the measure answers for it.
- **The tree's volume is not here**: a solid may be measured for its
  size, and this measures a drawing in two dimensions.
- **The tree's perimeter of a region is not here**: the area is
  measured, and the outline of an area that is not an entity is not.

## 438. The arc of a drawing

The cad battery had a kind of entity it could not make: an **arc** was
a kind, and nothing put one in a drawing.

### What was built

- The command `cad.entity.arc.add`: an arc is a **centre**, a **radius
  above nothing** and **two angles in radians**, and it runs from one
  to the other the way a circle does — counter-clockwise, and never
  more than a whole turn.
- The arc **carries its two ends**: the points where it begins and
  ends. The sweep of an arc is worked out from them every time, and it
  is never written down where it could go stale.
- An arc is **drawn** — as a curve, sampled — and a point on it is
  **on** it.
- The **box** of an arc is the box of the curve and not the box of its
  two ends: the bulge is in the box.
- The **length** of an arc is the radius times the sweep, and the
  measure of §437 answers it.

### What the port found

- **The tree's arc is two angles and a radius.** Here the arc is made
  with two angles too, and it carries its ends: the angles are worked
  out from them, and they are worked out every time.
- **The tree's arc is a variant of its own**, with its own fields, its
  own file mapping and its own transform. Here an arc is a node of an
  **open kind**, and a new kind of curve is a new kind and nothing
  else.

### What it cost

- **Seven tests** in the cad battery (`tests/arcs.rs`): an arc may be
  put in a block, its box includes the bulge, it is drawn, a point on
  it is on it, its length is the radius times the sweep, and the two
  refusals — a radius of nothing and an arc of no sweep.
- **One new module** (`arcs`): the arc of a drawing is its own. The cad
  battery now carries **32** commands and the MCP server **577**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's arc is measured in degrees and here it is in radians**:
  the angles of an ellipse in this battery are in radians too, and one
  convention is worth more than two.
- **The tree's arc may be turned the other way round**, and here it may
  not: the sweep is the way round the arc goes, and it is worked out
  from the ends.

## 439. The copy of an entity

A copy is a second entity of the **same kind**, with the same geometry
and the same layer, put somewhere else.

### What was built

- The command `cad.entity.copy`: it takes the entity, the **name** the
  copy goes by, the **vector** it is copied **by**, and the block it
  goes in — the block of the entity itself when it is not said.
- The copy is on the **same layer** as the entity it copies, and the
  layer is an **edge**: the edge is made again for the copy.
- A copy of an **insert** refers to the same block: the reference is
  an edge too, and the edge is made again.

### What the port found

- **The tree's copy is a command with a base point and a target, and
  it copies a whole selection.** Here one entity is copied at a time,
  and the **offset** is the vector it is copied by: a copy that is in
  the same place as the thing it copies is a copy that cannot be told
  from it, and the caller says where the copy goes.
- **The tree's copy carries the layer with it**, and here the same —
  and the layer being an edge is what makes the carrying possible:
  there is no field to copy, only an edge to make again.

### What it cost

- **Five tests** in the cad battery (`tests/copies.rs`): an entity may
  be copied, the copy is in the same block, it is on the same layer, it
  may be put in another block, and a node that is not an entity is
  refused.
- **One new module** (`copies`): the copy of an entity is its own. The
  cad battery now carries **33** commands and the MCP server **578**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's copy of a whole selection is not here**: one entity is
  copied at a time, and a command that copies many things is a command
  that says how many.
- **The tree's copy keeps the name and adds a number is not here**: the
  copy is given its name, so that two things in a block never share a
  name by accident.

## 440. The mirror of an entity

The same entity, turned over a line.

### What was built

- The command `cad.entity.mirror`: it takes the entity and **two
  points**, and the two points say where the line runs.
- Every point of the entity is turned over the line: the ends of a
  line, the centre of a circle, the centre and the two ends of an
  arc, the points of a polyline, the place of a text and of an insert.
- An ellipse is turned over with its **major axis turned over too**:
  the axis is a **vector**, and a vector turned over a line is not a
  point turned over a line. The **ratio** stays the ratio.

### What the port found

- **The tree's mirror is a line and a selection.** Here the line is
  **two points** and one entity is mirrored at a time: a line that
  runs through two points is a line, and a line that is a pair of
  directions is a line that has to be worked out first.
- **The tree's mirror turns the entity's own angle**, and here the
  same — and the reason it has to is the ellipse: its centre is a
  point and its axis is a vector, and the mirror knows which is which.

### What it cost

- **Five tests** in the cad battery (`tests/mirrors.rs`): a line may
  be turned over a line, an ellipse has its major axis turned over, a
  circle keeps its radius, and the two refusals — a line of no length
  and a node that is not an entity.
- **One new module** (`mirrors`): the mirror of an entity is its own.
  The cad battery now carries **34** commands and the MCP server
  **579**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's mirror of a whole selection is not here**: one entity is
  mirrored at a time.
- **The tree's mirror over a line at an angle is not tested here**:
  the line here is the vertical one and the horizontal one, and a
  line at any angle is the same sum.

## 441. The audit of a drawing

A drawing is a document, and a document can be wrong.

### What was built

- The command `cad.audit`: it reads a drawing and **reports** what is
  wrong with it. It changes nothing.
- The issues it finds are the ones a drawing can reach: **two layers
  with the same name**, an entity on a **locked** layer, an entity on a
  **frozen** layer, an **insert of a block of another drawing**, and an
  **insert of the block it is in**.

### What the port found

- **The tree's audit repairs as well as reports**, and it repairs by
  changing the drawing — a missing table row is recreated, a bad
  handle is given a new one, a broken reference is removed. Here the
  audit **reports and does not repair**: repairing is a change, and a
  change is a command that changes, and there is one command per
  thing.
- **The tree's audit is about a file**: it reads a drawing from disk
  and checks the tables it holds. Here a drawing is in the document,
  and the audit looks at the document — the same idea with the file
  taken out of it.
- **The tree's audit finds a block that refers to itself** and removes
  the reference. Here it is **reported**: the drawing is left as it
  is, and a person says what should happen to it.

### What it cost

- **Seven tests** in the cad battery (`tests/audits.rs`): a drawing
  with nothing wrong with it has no issues, two layers with the same
  name are an issue, an entity on a locked layer is an issue, an
  entity on a frozen layer is an issue, an insert of a block of
  another drawing is an issue, an insert of the block it is in is an
  issue, and a node that is not a drawing is refused.
- **One new module** (`audits`): the audit of a drawing is its own. The
  cad battery now carries **35** commands and the MCP server **580**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's repairs are not here**: the audit says what is wrong
  and nothing more. A command that repairs a drawing is a command
  that changes one, and it is not written yet.
- **The tree's audit of a file is not here**: this audit looks at the
  document, and a drawing that came from a file may hold faults that
  the commands cannot make.

## 442. What may be edited

A layer may be locked, and it may be frozen, and both of them are
about what may be changed.

### What was built

- The **rule**: an entity on a layer that is **locked** or **frozen**
  may not be **edited**. Every command that changes an entity — the
  move, the turn, the scale, the removal, the copy and the mirror —
  **refuses** it, and the refusal names the layer and says why.
- The rule lives in one place (the module `editable`), so every
  command that changes an entity asks the same question of the same
  kind of answer.
- An entity on **no layer** may be edited: there is no layer to lock
  it.

### What the port found

- **The tree's locked objects are skipped, not refused.** Its cut
  copies the objects that are not on locked layers and says how many
  were left alone; its edits filter the locked ones out of the set
  they work on. Here an edit of a locked entity is **refused**: a
  command that silently does nothing to half of what it was given is a
  command whose answer is a lie, and an entity that cannot be edited
  should say so.
- **The tree's layer is a name and the lock is a property of the
  name.** Here the layer is a **node**, the lock is a fact in its
  payload, and an entity is on a layer through an **edge** — so the
  question is answered by following the edge, and the edge is the
  only place the answer comes from.

### What it cost

- **Seven tests** in the cad battery (`tests/editable.rs`): an entity
  on a locked layer may not be moved, taken away or copied, an entity
  on a frozen layer may not be turned, an entity on a layer that is
  not locked may be moved, an entity on no layer may be moved, and a
  layer that is unlocked lets its entities be edited again.
- **One new module** (`editable`): what may be edited is its own
  question, and every command that changes an entity asks it. No new
  command: the cad battery still carries **35** commands and the MCP
  server **580**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's block reference may be locked too**: a block that is
  being edited may not be inserted. Here the lock of a layer is the
  lock of what is on it, and that is all.
- **The tree's layer that is frozen may not be changed either**: here
  the settings of a frozen layer may still be set, and only what is on
  it is held still.

## 443. The resolution of a revision

A revision is a mark on a run. Resolving it is the decision about the
mark: accept it, and the change becomes part of the text; reject it,
and the change never happened.

### What was built

- The commands `prose.revision.accept`, `prose.revision.reject`,
  `prose.revision.accept.all` and `prose.revision.reject.all`.
- An **accepted insertion** is ordinary text: the words stay and the
  mark goes. An **accepted deletion** is really deleted: the words go
  and the run goes with them. A **rejected insertion** is taken away,
  and a **rejected deletion** is restored.
- The block's **text and runs are rewritten together**, because the
  runs describe slices of the text: a text and a set of runs that
  disagree are a block that says two things at once.
- A **rejected format change is refused**: the format a run had before
  the change is not kept, and so there is nothing to put back.

### What the port found

- **The tree resolves a revision by editing the text.** An accepted
  deletion deletes the words; a rejected insertion deletes them
  instead. Here the same — and the runs are rewritten with the text,
  which is what makes the two agree.
- **The tree keeps the format a run had before the change**, so it can
  put it back. Here the old format is **not kept**, and so a rejected
  format change is **refused**: there is no old format to put back,
  and a resolution that guesses is a resolution that is wrong.

### What it cost

- **Nine tests** in the prose battery (`tests/resolving.rs`): an
  accepted insertion is ordinary text, a rejected insertion is taken
  away, an accepted deletion is really deleted, a rejected deletion is
  restored, a rejected format is refused, every revision of a block
  may be accepted at once and rejected at once, a run with no revision
  is refused, and a block with no revisions has nothing to accept.
- **One new module** (`resolving`): the resolution of a revision is
  its own. The prose battery now carries **33** commands and the MCP
  server **584**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's rejection of a format change is not here**: the old
  format is not kept, so there is nothing to put back.
- **The tree's resolution of a revision may name the author**: here a
  revision is resolved by the number of its run, and the author is
  said by the revision itself.

## 444. The ease of a keyframe

Two eases are worth naming, because they are the ones a person asks
for by name.

### What was built

- The command `fx.keyframe.easy`: the **easy ease**. The influence is
  a **third** of the segment and the speed is nothing, and the
  keyframe stops being an **auto bezier** — the ease is written down
  instead of coming from its neighbours. It may be given to one side
  (`in` or `out`) or to both.
- The command `fx.keyframe.hold`: the **hold**. The value does not
  move at all until the next keyframe, and turning the hold off again
  gives back the **bezier** the keyframe had — when it eases — or a
  **straight line** when it does not.

### What the port found

- **The tree's easy ease is a number, not a calculation**: the
  influence is a third and the speed is nothing. Here the same — and
  a survey of the tree said it was worked out from the neighbours, and
  it is not: it is a third, and a third is a third.
- **The tree's hold is turned off again by a rule**: the keyframe gets
  its bezier back when it eases — when it is an auto bezier, when it
  is continuous, when its in side is a bezier, or when it has an ease
  of its own — and a straight line when it does not. Here the same,
  and "it has an ease of its own" means "its ease is not the default
  one": the tree's ease is a list and an empty list is how it says "no
  ease", and here the ease is always there and the default one is how
  it says the same thing.

### What it cost

- **Eight tests** in the fx battery (`tests/eases.rs`): the easy ease
  is a third and no speed, it may be given to one side, it stops the
  keyframe being an auto bezier, a hold keyframe does not move the
  value, the hold turned off again gives a straight line back or a
  bezier back, a side that is not a side is refused, and a keyframe
  that is not there is refused.
- **One new module** (`eases`): the ease of a keyframe is its own. The
  fx battery now carries **46** commands and the MCP server **586**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's smooth is not here**: the tree can replace a run of
  keyframes with the fewest auto beziers that stay within a
  tolerance, and that is a search and not a setting.
- **The tree's keyframe assistant is not here**: it moves and deletes
  keyframes in bulk, and those are commands of their own.

## 445. The cells of a table

A table is a **grid**: rows of cells, and every row as long as every
other row.

### What was built

- The commands `prose.table.cell.get`, `prose.table.cell.set`,
  `prose.table.row.add`, `prose.table.row.remove`,
  `prose.table.column.add` and `prose.table.column.remove`.
- A **cell** is found by its **row and its column**, and it may be
  read and written. A **row** that goes in pushes the rows below it
  down, and a **column** that goes in pushes the columns beside it
  right.
- A table whose rows are **not the same length** is **refused** — by
  the command that makes a table and by every command that works on
  one. A table that is nearly a grid is a table whose cells cannot be
  addressed.

### What the port found

- **The tree's table is a tree**: every cell holds paragraphs, and a
  cell has an identity of its own that a row or a column insert moves
  about. Here a cell is a **value in a row**, and a cell is found by
  its **row and its column** — there is no cell identity to keep, and
  a row that goes in pushes the rows below it down.
- **The tree's table is a grid and says so**: a row of one length
  beside a row of another is not a table. Here the same, and the check
  is **refusal** rather than tidying up.

### What it cost

- **Nine tests** in the prose battery (`tests/tables.rs`): a cell may
  be read and written, a row may be put in and taken out, a column may
  be put in and taken out, a cell that is not there is refused, a
  table whose rows are not the same length is refused, and a row that
  is not a whole number is refused.
- **One new module** (`tables`): the cells of a table are their own.
  The prose battery now carries **39** commands and the MCP server
  **592**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's cells hold paragraphs and here they hold values**: a
  cell that holds blocks is a different thing, and this battery does
  not pretend to have one.
- **The tree's merged and split cells are not here**: a cell that
  covers two cells is a shape the grid does not have.
- **The tree's table formulas are not here**: `=SUM(ABOVE)` needs a
  formula in a cell, and this arc is about the cells and not about
  what a cell may say.

## 446. The synchronisation of a clip by its anchor

A clip has two clocks: where it starts on the **timeline** and where
it begins in the **media**. The frame of the media the clip begins at
is its **anchor**.

### What was built

- The command `film.clip.synchronise`: it takes the clip and the
  **reference** it lines up with, and the **method** — `in` for the
  **in points** and `out` for the **out points**.
- Two clips are **in step** when their anchors agree: each of them
  begins at the same moment of its own media. The **timeline** is left
  alone.
- The **link** is honoured: the tree moves the linked clips together,
  so that the picture and the sound stay in step, and this tree does
  the same.
- The **bounds** are the media's: a clip may not begin before the
  media and may not run past the end of it.

### What the port found

- **The tree's synchronisation is a common time**: every clip is
  reduced to an anchor, and the clips are moved in the timeline until
  their common times line up. Here the **media** lines up and the
  timeline is left alone: a clip that is in step shows the same thing
  as the clip it is in step with, and a synchronisation that moved
  clips about would be a second edit wearing the synchronisation's
  coat.
- **The tree has five methods and here there are two.** The tree's
  timecode and marker methods need a clock and a marker, and its audio
  method needs the waveforms; this tree has the frames of the media
  and nothing else.

### What it cost

- **Seven tests** in the film battery (`tests/anchors.rs`): a clip is
  put in step by its in points, it may be put in step by its out
  points, a clip longer than the reference cannot be in step by its
  out points, a clip that is already in step is refused, a method that
  is not a method is refused, a clip cannot be in step with itself,
  and a clip that would play past the end of the media is refused.
- **One new module** (`anchors`): the synchronisation of a clip is its
  own. The film battery now carries **70** commands and the MCP server
  **593**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's timecode, marker and audio methods are not here**: this
  tree has the frames of the media and nothing else.
- **The tree's common time is not here**: the clips are not moved in
  the timeline to line up, and the synchronisation is a change of the
  media and not of the place.

## 447. Finding and replacing in a block

A find is a **reading**: it says where the text is that matches a
pattern, and it changes nothing. A replace is a **change**.

### What was built

- The commands `prose.find` and `prose.replace`.
- The pattern may hold **wildcards**: a `*` for any text at all and a
  `?` for one character, and a `~` in front of one of them says that
  it is the character itself. The **case** does not matter unless it is
  asked for.
- A **replace** rewrites the text and the **runs** together, because
  the runs describe slices of the text and the two must agree. The
  replaced words carry the formatting of the run the match **begins**
  in.
- A **tracked change** is not replaced: a match that lies inside a run
  with a revision is **refused**, and the block is left as it was.

### What the port found

- **The tree's find has a language of its own** — `^p` for a paragraph
  mark, `^&` for the text that was found, the groups `\1` to `\9` —
  and it turns it into a **regular expression** so that a pattern
  cannot match for ever. Here the language is the wildcards and
  nothing else, and the matcher is **its own**: a pattern is matched by
  walking the text and the pattern together, and a `*` that matched
  too little takes one more character.
- **The tree's replace refuses to touch a tracked change**, and here
  the same.
- **The tree's find is a search and not a whole match**: the pattern
  is found somewhere in the text and not only when it is the whole of
  it, and here the same — a pattern that is done while the text goes
  on has matched the beginning of it.

### What it cost

- **Eight tests** in the prose battery (`tests/finding.rs`): a find
  says where the pattern is, a find does not mind the case unless it
  is told to, a wildcard stands for any text, a replace rewrites the
  text and the runs, the replaced words carry the formatting of the
  run, a tracked change is not replaced, a pattern that is nothing is
  refused, and a replace that finds nothing changes nothing.
- **One new module** (`finding`): finding and replacing are their own.
  The prose battery now carries **41** commands and the MCP server
  **595**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's pattern language is not here**: `^p`, `^&` and the
  groups `\1` to `\9` are not, and the wildcards are all there is.
- **The tree's find goes on through the blocks and the documents**: it
  finds in a document and this finds in a block.

## 448. The information of a document

A PDF file has a **trailer**, and the trailer may name an
**information dictionary**: the object that says who wrote the file,
what it is called and when it was made.

### What was built

- The command `pdf.info.set`: it says which object is the file's
  information, and the **trailer** of the written file names it:
  `/Info 2 0 R`.
- There is **one** information dictionary in a file, and a second one
  is refused: two answers to one question.
- The information dictionary is an **ordinary object**: its entries are
  set and read as the entries of any other object are.

### What the port found

- **The tree's information is a table of its own**: the properties of
  a document — its title, its author, its subject, its keywords, its
  creator — are fields with names, and a document that has one of them
  says so. Here the information is a **dictionary of entries**, and
  the entries are the object's own: the tree's names are the PDF's
  names, and the PDF's names are open.
- **The tree's trailer writes the information under a name of its own**
  (`DOCPROPS` in its own file format). Here the trailer writes
  `/Info`, which is what a PDF file says.

### What it cost

- **Five tests** in the pdf battery (`tests/information.rs`): an object
  may be made the information, the trailer names it, a file with no
  information says nothing about it, a second information dictionary
  is refused, and a node that is not an object is refused.
- **One new module** (`information`): the information of a document is
  its own. The pdf battery now carries **27** commands and the MCP
  server **596**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's page labels are not here**: the labels of the pages —
  their style, their prefix and the number they start at — are a
  number tree in the page tree, and they are not written.
- **The tree's document properties are named and here they are not**:
  the entries are the PDF's own names, and the PDF's names are open.

## 449. The stops of a gradient

A gradient is a list of **stops**, and a stop says where it is along
the gradient — its **offset**, from zero to one — and what **colour**
it is there, and how **solid** it is.

### What was built

- The commands `vector.gradient.read`, `vector.gradient.stop.add`,
  `vector.gradient.stop.set` and `vector.gradient.stop.remove`.
- The stops are a **list in order**: a stop at a smaller offset comes
  before a stop at a bigger one, and that is the order the gradient
  is read in.
- A gradient has **two stops or more**: one colour is a fill and not a
  gradient, and the last stop of a two-stop gradient may not be taken
  away.
- A path filled with **one colour** has no gradient, and the command
  says so.

### What the port found

- **The tree's stops have a midpoint and a swatch of their own**: a
  stop is a colour that may be shared with another stop, and the
  colour it shows is at a place along it. Here a stop is an **offset,
  a colour and an opacity**, and it is its own: there is no shared
  swatch and no midpoint, so there is nothing to keep in step with
  anything else.
- **The tree edits a gradient in place**: the stops are picked and
  moved and recoloured, and the gradient is the same gradient
  afterwards. Here the same: a stop is added, changed or taken away
  and the path keeps its gradient.

### What it cost

- **Nine tests** in the vector battery (`tests/gradients.rs`): the
  gradient of a path may be read, a stop may be added and the stops
  stay in order, a stop may be changed, a stop may be taken away, the
  last stop of a two-stop gradient may not be taken away, a path
  filled with one colour has no gradient, an offset that is not
  between zero and one is refused, and a stop that is not there is
  refused.
- **One new module** (`gradients`): the stops of a gradient are their
  own. The vector battery now carries **40** commands and the MCP
  server **600**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's midpoints are not here**: the colour of a stop is shown
  at the stop's own place and nowhere else.
- **The tree's shared swatches are not here**: two stops with the same
  colour are two stops, and changing one changes only that one.

## 450. The groups of a filter

A filter may be **groups** of criteria: the columns of a group are
judged together, and the groups are judged one by one.

### What was built

- The command `grid.filter.groups.set`: the **groups** of criteria, each
  criterion saying which **column** it judges, the **operation** and
  the **value**.
- The columns of a group are judged **together** — a row matches the
  group when it matches every criterion of it — and the groups are
  judged one by one: a row is **hidden** when it matches **none** of
  them.
- A **column filter** is one group of one criterion: the two filters
  hide the same rows, and the tree says so in one sentence.
- The rows a filter hides are still **derived**: they are worked out
  from the cells each time they are asked for.

### What the port found

- **The tree's filter is over a range and this one's is over a
  column.** The tree's filter has a range and a criterion for each
  column of it. Here a sheet has **one** filter, and it is either over
  one column (`grid.filter.set`) or over **groups** of criteria
  (`grid.filter.groups.set`) — and the rows it hides are the rows of
  the sheet either way.
- **The tree's criteria range is a range of cells and here it is a
  list.** The tree's criteria are written in cells above the data, and
  a row of them is a row of the sheet; here they are a **list** of
  groups, so the criteria are not part of the sheet and cannot be
  summed by accident.

### What it cost

- **Eight tests** in the grid battery (`tests/filtergroups.rs`): the
  columns of a group are judged together, the groups are judged one by
  one, a group of no criteria is refused, a filter with no group is
  refused, an operation that is not an operation is refused, a column
  that is not a column is refused, a comparison that needs a number and
  is given a word is refused, and a column filter is one group of one
  criterion.
- **One new module**: the filter of a sheet keeps its own module
  (`filters`), and the **filter** of the workbook is now **two kinds**
  of thing — a column or groups — so that both are one filter and not
  two filters that could both be there. The grid battery now carries
  **68** commands and the MCP server **601**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's criteria are written in cells and here they are a
  list**: a sheet cannot hold its own criteria and read them back.
- **The tree's filter copies the rows it keeps to another place**: it
  can take the rows that match and put them in another sheet. That is
  a change and not a filter, and it is not written yet.

## 451. The what-if of a sheet

A what-if asks a question of a sheet by **trying** values: the input
cell takes this number, and the result cell says what the sheet says
then.

### What was built

- The command `grid.whatif`: the **input** cell that is varied, the
  **result** cell that is read, and the **values** to try.
- The sheet is **not changed**: the trial is made in a **copy** of the
  workbook and the copy is thrown away when the table is done. A
  what-if that left the sheet changed would be a second edit wearing a
  question's coat.
- The number of values is **bounded**: a what-if may try 256 of them,
  because each one is an evaluation of the sheet.
- The input and the result may not be the **same cell**, and a value
  that is not a number is refused.

### What the port found

- **The tree's what-if has two forms**: a **data table**, which tries a
  list of inputs and says what each of them gives, and a **goal seek**,
  which tries inputs until the result reaches a target. Here the **data
  table** is the command, and the goal seek is not written yet: a goal
  seek is a search, and a search needs to say how far to look and when
  to stop.
- **The tree's data table takes a whole range of inputs and lays the
  results out beside them.** Here the inputs are a **list** and the
  results are a **list** too: one input, one result, in the order they
  were given.

### What it cost

- **Seven tests** in the grid battery (`tests/whatifs.rs`): a what-if
  says what the sheet would say, the sheet is not changed by it, the
  input and the result may not be the same cell, a cell that is not a
  cell is refused, a value that is not a number is refused, a what-if
  with no value is refused, and the result may be a cell that has
  nothing in it.
- **One new module** (`whatifs`): the what-if of a sheet is its own.
  The grid battery now carries **69** commands and the MCP server
  **602**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's goal seek is not here**: finding the input that gives a
  target is a search, and the search's bounds are not written.
- **The tree's data table lays its results out in cells and here they
  are a list**: a what-if here says what it would say and does not
  write it down.

## 452. The goal of a sheet

A goal seek asks the other question: not "what does the sheet say for
this input?" but "**what input gives this result?**"

### What was built

- The command `grid.goal`: the **input** cell that is varied, the
  **result** cell that is read, the **target** to reach, and the two
  **ends** of the range to look in.
- The answer is found by **narrowing**: the sheet is asked at the two
  ends, and if the target is between what they say, the range is
  **halved** and the sheet is asked again in the middle — and again,
  until the range is small enough to call the answer.
- The command says the **steps** it took and the **width** of the range
  it was left with, so a reader knows how close the answer is.
- The sheet is **not changed**: the search is made in the same copy of
  the workbook the what-if uses.

### What the port found

- **The tree's goal seek has its own limits and its own way of finding
  the answer**: it may scan the range in steps, or bisect it, and it
  stops when the answer is close enough. Here the range is **given**
  and the answer is found by **halving**: the work is one evaluation of
  the sheet for each halving, and the number of halvings is bounded.
- **The tree's goal seek says what it did.** Here it says the **steps**
  it took and the **width** of the range it was left with.

And the assumption is named, because it is an assumption: the sheet is
taken to move **one way** as the input moves. A sheet that does not is
not found, and the command says so rather than giving an answer that
is a coincidence.

### What it cost

- **Seven tests** in the grid battery (`tests/goals.rs`): the goal is
  the input that gives the result, the sheet is not changed by it, a
  target the sheet does not reach is refused, the goal may be at an
  end of the range, a range whose ends are the same point is refused,
  the input and the result may not be the same cell, and a result that
  is not a number is refused.
- **One new module** (`goals`): the goal of a sheet is its own. The
  grid battery now carries **70** commands and the MCP server **603**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's scan is not here**: the answer is found by halving, and
  a sheet that moves one way and then the other is not found.
- **The tree's goal seek may be told to stop at a tolerance and here
  the tolerance is the width of the range**: the number of halvings is
  bounded, and the width that is left is reported.

## 453. The labels of the pages

A PDF file may give its pages **labels** — the names a reader sees
beside them: `i`, `ii`, `iii` for the front matter and `1`, `2`, `3`
for the rest.

### What was built

- The command `pdf.page.labels`: the **pages** that are given labels
  and the **runs** of labels, each run saying which page it begins at,
  how the numbers are written (`D`, `R`, `r`, `A` or `a`), the
  **prefix** before the number and the number it **starts** at.
- The labels are written as the PDF's own **`/PageLabels`**: a number
  tree hanging from the page tree, and the pages name it.
- The runs are **in order** — the first is the page they begin at and
  the next is later — because a number tree is sorted and a tree that
  is not sorted is not a tree.
- The writer learned one **pair**: the two things of a number tree's
  entry are written one after the other and not in brackets, and the
  payload says so — `{"pair": […]}`, the way it already says what a
  reference and a text string are.

### What the port found

- **The tree's labels are a thing of their own** — a list of entries,
  each with a style, a prefix and the number it starts at, and the
  tree's own file format has a section for them. Here the labels are
  the **PDF's own** `/PageLabels`: a number tree with the entries the
  format says.
- **The tree's labels may be read back and the file's may not**,
  here: the labels are written into the file and the file is the place
  they live. A command that reads them back would be a second copy of
  them, and a second copy is a copy that can be wrong.

### What it cost

- **Six tests** in the pdf battery (`tests/labels.rs`): the pages may
  be given their labels and the file says so, the prefix of a label is
  written as text, a style that is not a style is refused, the labels
  must be in order, a label that does not say which page is refused,
  and a node that is not the pages is refused.
- **One new module** (`labels`): the labels of the pages are their
  own. The pdf battery now carries **28** commands and the MCP server
  **604**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's labels are read back and here they are not**: the file
  is the place they live, and a command that read them back would be
  a second copy of them.
- **The tree's labels may be any of its own kinds and here there are
  the PDF's five**: `D`, `R`, `r`, `A` and `a`.

## 454. The table of a sheet

A **table** is a named range of cells whose first row names the
**fields** of the table: `who`, `amount`, `when`. Every column of the
range is a field, and the header cell of that column is its name.

### What was built

- **Six commands** in the grid battery: `grid.table.create` to make a
  table, `grid.table.read` to read the tables of a sheet,
  `grid.table.fields` to read the fields of one, `grid.table.rename`,
  `grid.table.resize` and `grid.table.remove`.
- A table is a **fact of the sheet**: its name and the range it
  reaches, kept in the sheet's payload beside the merges and the notes.
- The **fields are derived**: they are the text of the header cells,
  and a header cell that is edited names another field. A table does
  not keep a copy of its own fields, because a second copy is a copy
  that can be wrong.
- The **rules**: the name is not nothing, does not look like a cell or
  a range, and is not another table's name on the same sheet; the range
  covers more than one cell, because a table of one cell is a cell;
  the header is a row of **text** — a cell that holds nothing, a
  number, a boolean, an error or a formula does not name a field, so
  the table is **refused** and the refusal says which cell; and two
  tables of a sheet do not **overlap**, because a cell that is in two
  tables is in none of them.

### What the port found

- **The tree's table is an object with a style.** The tree's table has
  a name, a range, a header row and a style — banded rows and banded
  columns, an emphasised first column and last column, a total row.
  Here the table is the **name, the range and the fields**, because a
  style is a drawing and a drawing is not a fact of the sheet.
- **The tree's table may remove the duplicate rows of its range.** Here
  it may not, and the reason is the rule the whole tree follows: the
  removal of the duplicates is a change of the **cells**, and a change
  of the cells is a change of the sheet — so it is another command, and
  not this one.

### What it cost

- **Ten tests** in the grid battery (`tests/tables.rs`): a table is
  made and read back, the fields are the text of the header, a header
  that holds a number is refused, a table of one cell is refused, two
  tables that overlap are refused, a name that looks like a cell is
  refused, a table is renamed, a table is resized, a table is taken
  away and the cells stay, and the fields follow the header when the
  header is edited.
- **One new module** (`tables`): the tables of a sheet are their own.
  The grid battery now carries **76** commands and the MCP server
  **610**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's table may be read in a formula by its name.** Here the
  name is a name of the sheet, and a formula cannot read it: the
  formula reads a range or a name of a workbook, and a table is
  neither.
- **The tree's table has a style and here it has none**: no banded
  rows, no emphasised first column, no total row.
- **The tree's table may be taken away and turned into a plain
  range.** Here a table that is taken away leaves the cells where they
  are, and nothing says they were a table.

## 455. The pivot of a sheet

A **pivot** summarises a range of cells: the rows are gathered by the
value of one **field**, and the numbers of another field are put
together — summed, averaged, or the largest or the smallest of them.

### What was built

- **Three commands** in the grid battery: `grid.pivot.create` to make a
  pivot of a sheet, `grid.pivot.read` to read its summary, and
  `grid.pivot.remove` to take it away.
- A pivot is a **fact of the sheet** — the range it reads, the field it
  gathers by, the field it spreads the groups over, the field it puts
  together and the way it puts them together — and the **summary is
  derived**: it is worked out every time it is asked for, so it cannot
  be out of date.
- The **five ways** of putting numbers together: `sum`, `average`,
  `min`, `max` and `count`. A way that is not one of them is refused.
- The **rules**: the fields are columns of the range and the range has
  a **header** — the header cell of a field names the field, and a
  cell that holds nothing or a number does not name one, so the pivot
  is refused and the refusal says which cell; a cell of the **value
  field** that holds **text** is not a number, and a number cannot be
  put together with a text, so the summary is refused and the refusal
  says which cell; and a group of rows that holds **no number** has
  **no value** — the answer is nothing, and nothing is written as
  nothing and not as a zero.
- The groups are in the **tree's order** — the numbers before the
  text, and the empty cells last — and a row whose key is empty is in
  the group **`(blank)`**, which says what it is.

### What the port found

- **The tree's pivot is a thing that is worked on.** The tree's pivot
  may be **filtered**, **sorted**, given **subtotals** and **refreshed**
  by a command, and what it shows is a summary that is kept. Here the
  pivot is the **definition** and the summary is worked out from the
  cells as they are, and the price of that is the price the tree's own
  rule asks for: a value that is never written down cannot be wrong.
- **The tree's pivot is refreshed by a command and here there is
  nothing to refresh.** The summary is derived, so it is always the
  summary of the cells as they are, and a refresh would be a command
  that changes nothing.

### What it cost

- **Ten tests** in the grid battery (`tests/pivots.rs`): the numbers of
  a group being summed, the groups being spread over the columns, the
  average, the count, a group with no number having no value, a
  header that does not name a field being refused, a value that is not
  a number being refused, a way that is not one of the five being
  refused, the summary following the cells, and a pivot being taken
  away.
- **One new module** (`pivots`): the pivots of a sheet are their own.
  The grid battery now carries **79** commands and the MCP server
  **613**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's pivot is written into the sheet and may be read back
  from it.** Here the pivot is a fact of the sheet, and the summary
  is derived from it, so there is no summary stored to be read.
- **The tree's pivot may be laid out, filtered, refreshed and drilled
  into.** Here it summarises and nothing else.
- **The tree's pivot may be a chart.** Here a pivot is a table of
  numbers, and a chart is not built.

## 456. The character of a run

The **character** of a piece of text is how it is written: bold,
italic, underlined, in what colour and in what size.

### What was built

- **One command** in the prose battery: `prose.run.format`, given a
  block, a **start** and a **length** — counted in characters and not
  in bytes — and the character it puts on that range.
- The runs are **split** so that the range lies in whole runs: the run
  that covers the range is cut at both ends, and the character is put
  on the piece in the middle and on no other.
- The **five characters** of the tree: `bold`, `italic`, `underline`,
  the `colour` and the `size`. A command that says nothing to change
  is refused, and the read of the runs says the character of each of
  them.
- The **rules**: the range must be **inside the text** — a range that
  reaches past the end is refused and not cut short; a **colour** is
  the kit's colour, `#rrggbb`, and a text that is not one is refused;
  a **size** is a number that is finite and above zero, and one that
  is not is refused; and a **tracked change** is not formatted, because
  a tracked change is somebody else's text.

### What the port found

- **The tree has a command for each of the characters.** The tree's
  `format.bold`, `format.italic`, `format.underline`, `format.color`
  and `format.size` are five commands over the **selection**. Here
  they are one command over a **range**, because the thing is the same
  thing: the character of a piece of text.
- **The tree's selection is a place in the text and this tree's is a
  number.** The tree's commands act on what is selected; here the
  range is **two numbers** — where the text begins and how long it is
  — and the runs are split to fit it.

### What it cost

- **Nine tests** in the prose battery (`tests/characters.rs`): the
  character being put on the range and on no other, the text not being
  changed, all five characters being set, a range past the end being
  refused, a command that changes nothing being refused, a colour that
  is not a colour being refused, a size that is not a size being
  refused, a tracked change not being formatted, and the character
  being read back with the blocks.
- **One new module** (`characters`): the character of a run is its
  own. The prose battery now carries **43** commands and the MCP server
  **614**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's character may be put on a selection and not only on a
  range of a block.** Here the range is given by two numbers, and
  there is no selection of the document to speak of.
- **The tree's character is the character of a whole run at a time.**
  Here the range may be any part of a run, and the run is split to
  fit it — which is more than the tree does and not less.
- **The tree's size is the size of a font in the tree's own units, and
  the tree's colour may be a theme colour.** Here the size is a number
  and the colour is the kit's `#rrggbb`.

## 457. The edit decision list of a sequence

An **EDL** is a list of cuts: it says, for every clip of a sequence,
what was cut, where it came from and where it sits on the timeline. It
is the oldest interchange format there is — CMX 3600 — and it is a
**text**, so anything can read it.

### What was built

- **One command** in the film battery: `film.export.edl`, given a
  sequence and, optionally, a title.
- The list is **derived**: it is worked out from the sequence as it is
  now, and it is never written down anywhere else.
- The shape of a line is the tree's shape: a **title**, the **frame
  count** (`NON-DROP FRAME`), and then one **event** for every clip —
  the number of the event, the **reel** it comes from, the **channel**
  it is on (`V` for a video track, `A`, `AA`, `A3` for the audio
  ones), the **edit** (`C` for a cut) and the four **timecodes**: the
  source in and out, and the record in and out.
- The **reel** is the name of the item in **eight characters** — the
  tree's rule — with everything that is not a letter or a digit turned
  into an underscore.
- The **rules**: a **transition** is a dissolve, and a dissolve is a
  line this tree does not write, so a sequence with a transition is
  **refused** rather than written wrongly; and a clip with **no item**
  has no reel and no source, so the list is refused too.

### What the port found

- **The tree writes the list to a file, and this tree returns it.**
  The tree's `file.exportEdl` asks for a path and writes the bytes.
  Here the list is a **reading** and it comes back as a text, because
  a command that writes a file is a command about the **machine** and
  not about the document — and the kit's rule is that a command
  changes the document or says something about it.
- **The tree's list is a whole interchange format** — it reads EDLs
  back as well as writing them, and it knows the dissolves, the wipes,
  the keys and the motion effects. Here the list is **written** and
  nothing is read back: a list that is read back would be a second
  copy of the sequence, and a second copy is a copy that can be wrong.

### What it cost

- **Eight tests** in the film battery (`tests/edl.rs`): the list saying
  what was cut and where it came from and where it sits, the reel
  being the name of the item in eight characters, the title being the
  one that was given, the timecodes being counted at the rate of the
  sequence, two events being numbered one after the other, an audio
  track being on an audio channel, a transition being refused, and a
  node that is not a sequence being refused.
- **One new module** (`edl`): the list of a sequence is its own. The
  film battery now carries **71** commands and the MCP server **615**.

### What it does not settle

- **The tree's list is read back as well as written.** Here it is
  written only.
- **The tree's list has dissolves, wipes, keys and motion effects,
  and here it has cuts.** A sequence with a transition is refused, and
  the refusal says that the list would be wrong.
- **The tree's list may be written per video track**, one file for
  each, and here the list holds every track of the sequence.
